title: Activate ForwardRPC auto-routing for RouteTargeted RPCs
description:
The routing interceptor is wired in and enforces strategy declarations, but RouteTargeted RPCs still pass through to handler-level routing (remoteNodeForVault → per-RPC Forward* handlers). The ForwardRPC generic dispatch mechanism exists but failed in real cluster testing — the internal mux dispatch (httptest.NewRecorder + Connect protocol) needs integration testing before activation.

Next steps:
1. Write a multi-node integration test (TestMultiNode_ForwardRPC) that exercises the full path: interceptor → ForwardRPC gRPC stream → internal mux dispatch → Connect handler → response
2. Debug why the dispatch fails (likely Connect protocol requirements beyond Content-Type and Connect-Protocol-Version)
3. Once the test passes, re-enable auto-routing in interceptor.go by uncommenting the RouteTargeted forwarding path
4. Verify all 29 existing multi-node tests still pass
5. Optionally: remove handler-level remoteNodeForVault checks once ForwardRPC is proven reliable

title: Logout should revoke only the current refresh token, not all sessions
description:
Currently `Logout` calls `InvalidateTokens` + `DeleteUserRefreshTokens`, which nukes every session for the user across all devices. This is because `LogoutRequest` is empty — the server doesn't know which refresh token to revoke.

Fix: add `refresh_token` field to `LogoutRequest`. The client sends its refresh token, the server deletes just that one via `DeleteRefreshTokenByHash(sha256(token))`. Remove the `InvalidateTokens` call from `Logout`.

Steps:
1. Add `string refresh_token = 1` to `LogoutRequest` in `auth.proto`
2. `buf generate`
3. Update `Logout` handler to delete only the provided token
4. Update frontend to send the refresh token in the logout call
5. Remove the `InvalidateTokens` call (keep it only in password change)
6. Add expired-token cleanup (periodic sweep of tokens past `ExpiresAt`)

title: Tiered Storage

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Vault replication question (gastrolog-3d5fy) resolved by the tier chain model — replication is per-tier, not per-vault. Object storage tiers get durability for free. Local tiers replicate via per-tier primary/secondary with sealed chunk copies. Memory tiers optionally mirror writes. See docs/vision.md Tiered Storage section.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Tiered Storage epic complete and superseded.

The original design — vaults as ordered chains of tiers with operator-driven inter-tier transitions — shipped end-to-end in March/April 2026 across ~50 child issues, then was deliberately collapsed in the vault refactor epic (gastrolog-55dej). The 1:1:1 vault/tier/storage model from Phase 5 (gastrolog-4kkoo) replaces tier chains with the routing table: inter-vault flow is now expressed as routes (with `_source = "retention"` on retention output, controlled per-vault by the disposition flag from gastrolog-18du3) rather than as transitions inside a tier chain.

What survives from this epic:
- The tier *infrastructure* (Raft groups, replication, sealed chunk transfers, primary election) carries forward as the per-vault control plane.
- The cloud-backing model (active chunk + warm cache locally, sealed chunks in object storage) is preserved and unified into GLCB by Phase 6 (gastrolog-69fd5).
- The placement system (storage classes, file storages, replication factors) is preserved and now lives directly on VaultConfig.

What was deliberately removed:
- Tier chains (multiple tiers per vault). One storage shape per vault.
- Inter-tier transition policies (time-based, size-based, access-based). Inter-vault flow via routes.
- Per-tier rotation/retention policies. Now per-vault.
- The transition receipt protocol. Phase 4 collapsed it into the routing event.
- Budget-based transition policy (gastrolog-31hep). Tier-chain framing obsolete; routing-budget concept could be redesigned later.

Closing.

title: Define storage types and areas in proto + config
description:
Define the storage model in proto and config:

1. StorageArea — per-node declaration of locally-attached storage. Has a path, a storage class (numeric — lower is faster), a capacity, and a label. Multiple per node. Example: NVMe at class 1, NAS at class 3.

2. CloudService — cluster-wide definition of a cloud storage endpoint. Provider, bucket, credentials, region, storage class. Multiple can exist. Not tied to any node.

3. Three tier types:
   - Memory tier: RAM-backed. Budget limits RAM usage.
   - Local tier: disk-backed. Has a storage class requirement — matched to StorageAreas on nodes.
   - Cloud tier: references a CloudService for sealed chunks. Has a storage class requirement for the active chunk (local disk for staging). Has a separate storage class requirement for the chunk cache (local disk for query cache).

4. Vault: contains one or more tiers, ordered.

This issue covers the proto messages, Go config types, Raft FSM commands, store interface, and store implementations for StorageArea and CloudService. The tier and vault config entities are separate follow-up issues.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Design discussion (2026-03-22):

CURRENT STATE:
- Vault is a struct with one ChunkManager, one IndexManager, one query Engine
- Vault type (memory/file/cloud) determined by which concrete ChunkManager is passed in
- Each vault has a specific storage directory assigned at creation time by the operator
- Each vault is assigned to a specific node

DECOUPLING CHANGES:

1. Storage configuration becomes per-node, not per-vault
   - Nodes declare what storage they have available on registration/startup
   - Each local storage area has a path, a speed class (free-form label like 'fast', 'standard'), and a capacity
   - Example node config:
     storage:
       - path: /data/nvme, class: fast, capacity: 200GB
       - path: /data/hdd, class: standard, capacity: 4TB
   - Multiple local storage paths per node supported (NVMe + HDD, etc.)
   - Speed class is an operator-assigned label, not a numeric ranking — avoids everyone inventing their own scale
   - Memory budget also per-node (how much RAM available for memory tiers)

2. Cloud storage config is cluster-wide (Raft-replicated)
   - S3 buckets, GCS buckets, credentials are shared config — not node-specific
   - Any node with local disk can be a cloud tier primary (cloud tiers need local disk for active chunks)
   - The S3/GCS bucket is accessible from any node — nothing node-local about cloud credentials

3. Vault creation flow changes
   - Operator no longer picks a type or path — just names the vault and configures the tier chain policy
   - Tier chain references speed classes, not paths: memory → local(fast) → local(standard) → s3(default)
   - The system places tier primaries on nodes that have the required medium/class available
   - If a node doesn't have a matching speed class, it can't be elected primary for that tier

4. Tier primary election is constrained by node capabilities
   - A node without 'fast' local storage can't be primary for a local(fast) tier
   - A node with a full disk shouldn't be elected for any local tier
   - Memory budget exhaustion prevents election for memory tiers

5. Open questions
   - What happens when a tier chain references a speed class that no node has? Fail vault creation? Warning?
   - Should there be a default tier chain so operators don't have to configure one for simple deployments?
   - How does the migration from current vault types work? Existing file vaults become single-tier (local) vaults with the current path as their storage area?

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Design discussion continued (2026-03-22):

STORAGE PRIORITY MODEL (replaces speed class labels):

1. Unified priority system
   - Every storage area has a numeric priority (0 = fastest/most expensive, higher = slower/cheaper)
   - Priority 0 is always memory-backed (RAM). Not declared by operator — implicit on every node
   - All other priorities declared by operator with a label, and either a path+capacity (local) or bucket+credentials (cloud)
   - Cloud storage areas declare which local priority to use for their active chunk buffer
   - Example node storage config:
     priority 0: Memory (implicit)
     priority 1: label=NVMe, path=/data/nvme, capacity=200GB
     priority 3: label=NAS, path=/mnt/nas, capacity=10TB
     priority 5: label=S3 Production, bucket=logs-prod, active-buffer=3
     priority 7: label=Glacier, bucket=logs-archive, active-buffer=3

2. Vault tier chain is just a list of priorities
   - Example: [0, 1, 5] = memory -> NVMe -> S3
   - No distinction between local tier and cloud tier in the chain
   - The storage area definition tells the system whether it is RAM, disk, or object storage
   - Operator can skip priorities (e.g. [0, 1, 5] skips 3)
   - Operator can omit memory tier if desired (start at priority 1)

3. No special tier types
   - S3/GCS/Glacier are not special — they are storage areas with a priority like any other
   - The only thing that differentiates them is the storage area definition (bucket vs path)
   - Cloud tiers need local disk for active chunks — the active-buffer field points to another priority

4. Failure handling
   - Configuration time: fail hard. If vault references a priority that no node has, reject the config
   - Runtime (node failure): stall, don't reroute. The upstream tier holds data per durability handoff protocol. This effectively fails up — data stays on faster storage until the downstream tier is available again. Storage pressure alerts tell the operator to fix the tier chain
   - Permanently missing priority: upstream tier fills up, pressure alerts fire, operator reconfigures. System never silently reroutes to a different priority

5. Why not freeform labels or fixed enum
   - Freeform labels (like CockroachDB attrs): system can't reason about ordering. Can't validate that tier chain priorities are ascending
   - Fixed enum (nvme/ssd/hdd like HDFS): doesn't accommodate SAN, NAS, USB, NVMe-oF, or any future storage medium. A network NVMe-oF array might outperform local SATA SSD — device type != performance
   - Numeric priorities: operator defines the ordering based on their actual hardware. System validates ascending order in tier chains. Labels for human readability in UI

6. Single-node deployments
   - Everything still works. All tier primaries on the same node, no secondaries, no replication for local tiers. The tier chain is an in-process pipe. Cloud tiers still get S3 durability

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Industry research on storage classification and tiered placement (2026-03-22):

INFRASTRUCTURE SYSTEMS:

Kubernetes StorageClasses: Fully operator-defined taxonomy. StorageClass has a name, provisioner, and opaque parameters bag. PVCs reference by name. K8s deliberately avoids modeling storage capabilities — pushes all semantics to CSI drivers. Maximum flexibility, zero cross-provider portability.

Ceph CRUSH maps: Device classes (hdd/ssd/nvme) auto-detected from kernel, with operator override. Custom classes allowed. CRUSH rules select device classes via shadow hierarchies — filters the placement tree by class. Elegant reuse of existing placement algorithm.

HDFS storage policies: Fixed enum of 4 types (RAM_DISK > SSD > DISK > ARCHIVE) with implicit ranking. Policies define placement + fallback chains (what to use when preferred tier is full). Background Mover reconciles actual placement with declared policy. Fallback chain concept is useful for GastroLog.

ZFS: No tiering taxonomy. Devices assigned to architectural roles (data/slog/cache/special). Special vdev steers metadata and small files to fast media via block-size threshold. Not a cache — first-class storage with overflow to regular vdevs.

CockroachDB: Two label systems — locality (hierarchical location) and store attributes (freeform capability tags). Zone configs use +/- prefix constraints. Inheritance hierarchy: cluster > database > table > index > partition. Freeform attrs mean no validation — referencing a nonexistent attr silently under-replicates.

TiKV: Freeform key-value labels on stores. Placement policies in SQL with constraint syntax. Unique feature: dictionary constraints ({+disk=ssd: 1, +disk=nvme: 2}) for per-tier replica counts. Kubernetes-style filter primitives (in/notIn/exists/notExists).

Cloud providers (AWS/GCP/Azure): All converge on small fixed enum of named tiers with performance profiles. Trend toward decoupled provisioning (independently set IOPS and throughput). Users cannot create new types.

DATABASE AND LOG SYSTEMS:

Kafka tiered storage: Two tiers (local/remote), binary. Metadata tracked in internal Kafka topic. Two-retention model: local.retention.ms (how long on fast disk) + retention.ms (how long total). Clean separation. Active segments never tiered.

Cassandra: No tiered storage. All data directories treated as equal peers. Deliberately chose NOT to support heterogeneous storage — data safety argument (tombstone resurrection risk if disks fail independently).

Elasticsearch ILM: Four tiers (hot/warm/cold/frozen) as first-class node roles. Evolved FROM arbitrary labels TO fixed roles because freeform was error-prone. Frozen tier uses searchable snapshots (local cache over S3, no replicas needed — snapshot is source of truth). _tier_preference has fallback chain.

ClickHouse: Three-level hierarchy (disk -> volume -> policy). Dual migration triggers: space pressure (move_factor) + time (TTL MOVE rules). Per-table policies. Most granular model in survey. TTL MOVE can also change compression codec on migration.

Splunk: Raw path-based (homePath/coldPath/thawedPath). Volumes as named paths with size caps. Hot+warm share same path. Frozen is terminal (delete or external archive via script hook). No abstraction for storage type.

Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift: Fully opaque. No operator knobs. BigQuery tiering is purely a billing change (50% discount after 90 days). Redshift RA3 uses local SSD as transparent cache over S3 with temperature-based eviction.

KEY TAKEAWAYS FOR GASTROLOG:

1. Freeform labels are flexible but error-prone (Elasticsearch abandoned them, CockroachDB silently under-replicates)
2. Fixed enums are predictable but don't accommodate diverse hardware
3. Numeric priorities (our chosen model) sit between these — operator defines ordering, system can validate
4. Fallback chains (HDFS) and _tier_preference (Elasticsearch) are important — we handle this via durability handoff stall
5. ClickHouse's dual trigger model (space pressure + TTL) maps to our time-based + size-based transition policies
6. Kafka's metadata-in-own-system approach validates storing chunk metadata in Raft
7. Elasticsearch's searchable snapshots (frozen tier = cache over object store) validates our on-demand promotion design
8. Background reconciliation (HDFS Mover, MinIO ILM) is the common pattern — declare intent, async process migrates

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Cloud storage considerations (2026-03-22):

CLOUD STORAGE IS NOT LIMITLESS — COST CONSTRAINTS:

1. Per-request costs
   - S3: PUT/GET/LIST priced per-request. Thousands of tiny chunks = thousands of LIST calls
   - This is why cloud tiers need their own chunking schedule producing fewer, larger objects
   - Key prefix partitioning needed at scale (S3: ~5,500 PUT/s, ~3,500 GET/s per prefix)

2. Egress costs
   - Downloading data from S3 costs money per GB
   - On-demand promotion (cold -> warm) incurs egress on every fetch
   - Frequent promotion/eviction cycling can negate storage savings
   - Access-based transition policy must account for this: don't demote frequently-queried data

3. Minimum retention charges
   - Glacier: 90-day minimum charge regardless of actual retention
   - Glacier Deep Archive: 180-day minimum
   - Delete early and you still pay for the full minimum period

4. Budget-based policy must include total cost
   - Storage cost (GB-months) + request costs (PUT/GET/LIST) + egress costs (downloads)
   - A vault's $30/month budget is the total, not just storage

LOCAL CACHE FOR CLOUD CHUNKS:

Cloud-stored sealed chunks should be cached locally on-demand to avoid repeated egress costs and latency:

1. Query hits a cloud-stored chunk -> download to local disk -> serve from local -> keep in cache
2. Cache uses the on-demand promotion mechanism (issue 1.20) with a local storage priority for cache location
3. Cache eviction policy: LRU or TTL-based (issue 1.21)
   - LRU: evict least-recently-queried chunks when cache fills up
   - TTL: evict chunks not accessed within N hours/days
   - Hybrid: TTL floor (keep at least 1 hour) + LRU when space pressure hits
4. Cache is purely a performance optimization — the cloud copy is the source of truth
5. Cache hit avoids egress cost entirely. Cache sizing directly impacts cloud cost
6. This is the same pattern as Elasticsearch's frozen tier searchable snapshots and Redshift RA3's managed storage — local SSD as transparent cache over object store
7. Cache should be shared across all vaults using the same cloud priority — not per-vault caches competing for the same disk

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
CONSOLIDATED DESIGN (2026-03-22) — supersedes comments c1 and c2:

STORAGE PRIORITY MODEL:

Every storage area has a numeric priority (0 = fastest, higher = slower/cheaper).

Priority 0 is memory-backed (RAM), implicit on every node. The per-node memory budget constrains how much RAM is available for priority 0 tiers.

All other priorities are declared per-node:
  - Local storage: priority, label, path, capacity
  - Cloud participation: priority, label, active-buffer priority (which local priority to use for unsealed chunks and cache)

Cloud backend definitions (bucket, credentials, region) are cluster-wide config in Raft. Per-node declarations reference these backends and specify local resources for active chunks and caching.

Example node declaration:
  priority 0: Memory (implicit, budget: 4GB)
  priority 1: label=NVMe, path=/data/nvme, capacity=200GB
  priority 3: label=NAS, path=/mnt/nas, capacity=10TB
  priority 5: cloud backend=s3-prod, active-buffer=3, cache=3
  priority 7: cloud backend=glacier-archive, active-buffer=3, cache=3

Example cluster-wide cloud backends:
  s3-prod: bucket=logs-prod, region=eu-west-1, credentials=...
  glacier-archive: bucket=logs-archive, region=eu-west-1, storage-class=GLACIER

VAULT TIER CHAIN:

A list of ascending priorities: [0, 1, 5] = memory -> NVMe -> S3.

No distinction between local and cloud tiers in the chain. The storage area definition determines the implementation. Operator can skip priorities or omit memory.

FAILURE HANDLING:

Config time: fail hard if a referenced priority doesn't exist on any node.
Runtime: stall (upstream tier holds data via durability handoff). Effectively fails up. Storage pressure alerts fire. System never silently reroutes.

SINGLE-NODE:

All tier primaries on same node. No secondaries, no local replication. Cloud tiers still get provider durability. Tier chain is an in-process pipe.

CLOUD STORAGE COSTS AND CACHING:

Budget-based policies must include storage + request + egress costs. Cloud-stored sealed chunks cached locally (LRU/TTL, shared across vaults on same cloud priority) to avoid repeated egress. Cache location uses the active-buffer priority. See comment c4 for details.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Live tier chain reconfiguration (2026-03-22):

Reconfiguration affects the future, not the past.

Adding a tier: new data streams to the inserted priority. Existing data in downstream tiers stays put — no back-migration.

Removing a tier: the removed priority enters wind-down state. No new writes. Existing sealed chunks remain part of the vault — queryable, visible in inspector, counted in storage metrics. Chunks drain forward to the next active priority in the background. Once empty, the tier is fully removed.

Key invariant: orphaned data in a removed tier still belongs to the vault. Never invisible, never silently discarded.

Changing transition policies: new thresholds apply to future evaluations only.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Implementation approach (2026-03-22):

The current Vault struct is just a component tuple (ChunkManager + IndexManager + query Engine) registered with the orchestrator. All lifecycle behavior (seal, compress, rotate, retain) lives in the orchestrator, not the vault.

Step 1: Create a Tier entity
- Extract the current Vault struct into a Tier
- Move lifecycle operations (seal, compress, rotate, retain, schedule) from the orchestrator into the Tier
- Tier owns: ChunkManager, IndexManager, query Engine, rotation policy, retention policy, node assignment, state (active/wind-down/empty)
- The orchestrator calls into Tiers instead of directly manipulating chunk managers

Step 2: Create the new Vault entity
- Vault owns: ID, name, ordered list of Tiers (by priority), transition policies
- Vault manages: inter-tier record streaming, durability handoff, tier chain reconfiguration
- Vault delegates queries to all its Tiers and merges results
- The orchestrator manages Vaults, which manage their Tiers

This is a refactor of existing code first, new functionality second. The Tier does exactly what the current Vault+orchestrator does today. The new Vault adds the tier chain on top.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Implementation context from replication work (gastrolog-18ybo):

Current behavior:
- Sealed-chunk replication runs in post-seal pipeline: seal → compress → index → replicate to secondaries
- Tier 1 primary deletes chunk immediately after transitioning records to Tier 2
- Tier 1 secondaries retain their copies until their own retention sweep expires them (all actions forced to expire on secondaries)
- Tier 2 primary receives records, seals, then replicates to Tier 2 secondaries in its own post-seal pipeline
- During the handoff window: Tier 1 secondaries (RF-1 copies) + Tier 2 primary (1 copy) = RF total, but Tier 2 alone has only 1 copy until replication completes

What this issue needs to add:
- TransitionAck mechanism: after Tier 2 confirms RF-complete replication, it sends an ack back to Tier 1
- Pending handoff state on chunks: Tier 1 marks transitioned chunks as 'awaiting ack' instead of deleting immediately
- Tier 1 retention sweep skips chunks in pending-handoff state
- Timeout policy: if ack doesn't arrive within a configurable window, either hold indefinitely (safe) or expire with a warning (see open question in comment 1)
- The ack could piggyback on the existing ForwardImportRecords response, or be a separate RPC

Key files:
- orchestrator/replication.go — replicateSealedChunk (the completion callback would trigger the ack)
- orchestrator/transition.go — transitionChunk / transitionLocal / transitionRemote (need to track pending handoff instead of immediate delete)
- orchestrator/retention.go — sweep needs to skip pending-handoff chunks
- cluster/chunk_transferrer.go — ReplicateSealedChunk (could return a completion signal)

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
REWORKED: This issue now covers ack gating AND the durability handoff for tier transitions.

Part 1 — Ack gating: Delay the IngestMessage.Ack until RF-1 secondaries confirm receipt (depends on gastrolog-4h7og for the forwarding). Opt-in: only fires for ingesters with non-nil Ack (RELP, HTTP X-Wait-Ack). Fire-and-forget ingesters stay async.

Part 2 — Tier transition handoff: Tier 1 should not delete a transitioned chunk until Tier 2 has RF-complete sealed-chunk replication. TransitionAck mechanism, pending-handoff state on chunks.

Part 3 — Sealed-chunk handoff on secondaries: When sealed-chunk replication delivers a canonical sealed chunk to a secondary, the secondary must discard its active chunk (raw records from fire-and-forget forwarding). Without this, the active chunk is never sealed (rotation disabled on secondaries), never cleaned by retention (only processes sealed chunks), and grows forever. Trigger: ImportToTier on a secondary discards the active chunk before importing.

Key files: lifecycle.go:244 (ack point), transition.go (handoff state), vault_ops.go ImportToTier (active chunk discard).

comments.text:
Document the interaction between rotation and retention timing:
- Retention only acts on sealed chunks; the active chunk is never touched
- Age is measured from WriteEnd (last record written), not WriteStart
- Effective minimum data lifetime = rotation period + retention age + sweep interval (1 min)
- If retention age < rotation period, the rotation period is the effective floor
- Operators should ensure rotation period ≤ retention age for predictable behavior

- Rotation policy dropdown on TierEntryCard (used in both vault creation and vault card inline tier creation)
- Show assigned rotation policy in the tier row on the vault card
- PutTier already accepts rotation_policy_id — just needs the UI wiring

title: Rename 'local' tier type to 'file' throughout the stack
description: The tier type 'local' describes where storage is relative to a node, not what it is. The factory already uses 'file'. Rename TierTypeLocal → TierTypeFile, 'local' → 'file' in proto enums, Go constants, frontend labels, UI dropdowns, help docs, and tests. Full-stack rename.

title: Tier replication (record-level write mirroring to secondaries)
description:
Each tier's primary replicates sealed chunks to secondary nodes. The mechanism is the same regardless of tier type: after a chunk is sealed, compressed, and indexed, it's copied to secondary nodes.

For cloud tiers, sealed chunks are uploaded to object storage (S3/GCS/Azure) — the cloud provider handles AZ redundancy. But the active chunk (buffered on local disk before seal+upload) still needs cluster-level replication so it survives a node failure before the upload completes.

Replication enables:
- Failover: if the primary dies, a secondary is promoted with identical data
- Read scaling: secondaries can serve queries
- Durability: data exists on multiple nodes before the source tier drops it (prerequisite for gastrolog-4xeh4)

Design considerations:
- Replication factor is per-tier (not per-vault)
- Secondary nodes are chosen from eligible nodes (same storage class requirements as primary)
- Replication is asynchronous — the primary doesn't wait for secondaries before accepting new writes
- Memory tiers: sealed chunk data is serialized and sent to secondaries (not live write mirroring — that's a future optimization if failover latency matters)
- File tiers: post-seal chunk files copied to secondaries
- Cloud tiers: sealed chunks go to object storage (provider-managed redundancy); active chunk on local disk replicated to secondaries for crash safety

title: Ingester high availability (automatic failover)
description:
Epic: Ingester high availability (automatic failover).

Ingesters are a single point of failure. If the node running an ingester dies, that ingester is gone — no failover, no automatic restart on another node, incoming logs are dropped until someone manually reconfigures.

## Design

Operators select allowed nodes per ingester via multi-select checkboxes. The scheduling strategy depends on the ingester mode:

- **Passive (listeners)**: attempt to run on ALL selected nodes. Port bind is the natural distributed lock — nodes that can bind succeed, others retry with 3-5s jitter. Automatic failover when a node dies and its port frees up.
- **Active (collectors)**: run on exactly ONE selected node, Raft-coordinated. Prefer non-leader nodes. Checkpoint state replicated via system Raft group for seamless failover.

## Child Issues

1. ~~gastrolog-4js27 — Ingester classification field (passive/active)~~ ✓ CLOSED
2. gastrolog-2ty8a — Ingester node selection and placement infrastructure (shared)
3. gastrolog-4pn18 — Passive ingester HA (listen on all selected nodes with retry)
4. gastrolog-1dex0 — Active ingester HA (Raft-placed single-node with checkpoint replication)
5. gastrolog-4z596 — Per-node local ingesters (self + metrics)

Superseded: gastrolog-53gal, gastrolog-5b5qd (closed, replaced by 2/3/4 above).

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Industry Research: Ingester/Agent HA Across Comparable Systems

### Universal Finding
**No mainstream log management system does coordinated agent failover for file-tailing or pull-based collection.** Every system treats agents as independent per-host processes with local-only checkpoint state. HA is achieved through infrastructure-level restarts and output-level redundancy, not through distributed agent coordination.

### Per-System Breakdown

**Grafana Loki**
- Agents (Promtail/Alloy): Independent per-node, local positions file, no cross-node failover for file tailing
- Ingesters (server-side): Hash ring placement, RF=3 quorum writes via distributor, WAL for local crash recovery
- WAL is local-only — not replicated across ingesters
- Grafana Alloy has a clustering mode for service-discovery targets but NOT for file tailing
- Key insight: Loki separates collection (agents, no HA) from ingestion (server-side, full HA with replication)

**Vector / Fluentd / Fluent Bit**
- All three are fully independent per-node agents with zero cluster awareness
- Checkpoint state: Vector uses SQLite, Fluent Bit uses SQLite, Fluentd uses a pos_file — all local-only
- No active-passive or active-active agent pairs for the same input source
- Fluentd has output-level failover (standby servers in out_forward) but not agent-level
- Vector has end-to-end acknowledgements (checkpoint advances only after downstream ACK) — reduces duplicate window
- All provide at-least-once delivery, none provide exactly-once

**Elasticsearch / Filebeat / Logstash**
- Filebeat: Node-local registry (log-structured SQLite), no cluster awareness, no work reassignment
- Registry tracks inode+device+offset; lost if disk is lost
- Logstash: Local persistent queues (disk-backed), no shared state between instances
- Recommended HA: Kafka as intermediate buffer, Logstash consumer groups for processing HA
- Elastic Agent (Fleet): Fleet Server manages config but does NOT store cursor state or reassign work on failure
- Key insight: Elastic's real HA comes from Kafka, not from their own agents

**Splunk**
- Universal Forwarders: Per-host with local fishbucket (CRC + offset per file), no cluster coordination
- Fishbucket is local-only, not replicated — loss means re-ingestion or data gaps
- Load balancing: Client-side autoLB across indexers (time-based rotation, not load-aware)
- Heavy Forwarders: Full Splunk instances with persistent queues, typically run active-active behind LB
- Deployment Server manages config distribution but is itself a SPOF
- Key insight: HA is 'make the forwarder reliable' (auto-restart), not 'make the forwarder distributed'

**Graylog**
- Global inputs run on every node — LB distributes incoming logs across nodes
- Each node has a local disk-based message journal (Kafka-like) for durability
- Journal survives Graylog crashes; on restart, replays unindexed messages
- Journal is local and unreplicated — permanent node loss = journal data lost
- Sidecars manage collectors (Filebeat etc.) but have no HA themselves
- Built-in LB status endpoint for graceful drain before maintenance
- Key insight: Graylog's journal provides single-node crash resilience but not multi-node durability

### Key Takeaways for GastroLog

1. **No one does distributed checkpoint replication for file-tailing agents.** The complexity is apparently not worth the benefit. All systems accept at-least-once delivery with local checkpoints.

2. **Push-based ingestion HA is solved** — Loki's distributor replication and Graylog's journal pattern are the two approaches. GastroLog's record forwarding already does something similar.

3. **Pull-based collection HA is unsolved industry-wide.** The universal answer is 'restart the agent on the same host.' If the host is gone, accept the gap or re-read from the beginning.

4. **The Kafka/buffer pattern** is the gold standard for decoupling collection from ingestion. Filebeat→Kafka→Logstash is the most robust pipeline in the Elastic world.

5. **End-to-end acknowledgements** (Vector's approach) are the most sophisticated agent-side mechanism — tying checkpoint advancement to downstream confirmation.

6. **If GastroLog wants to replicate ingester cursor state via Raft, it would be novel** — no comparable system does this. The question is whether the complexity justifies the benefit for pull-based ingesters that are inherently node-local.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Design Direction: Passive vs Active Ingesters

Ingesters should be classified into two categories:

### Passive Ingesters (listeners)
Push-based — they listen on a port and passively accept incoming data. Examples: syslog, RELP, HTTP, GELF.

- Can run on ALL nodes simultaneously (Graylog 'global inputs' pattern)
- No failover needed — every node accepts traffic, LB distributes
- NodeID should be optional: empty = run on all nodes
- Records are routed to the correct tier via the existing record forwarder regardless of which node receives them
- This is the simplest and most robust HA model

### Active Ingesters (collectors)
Pull-based — they actively read from local data sources. Examples: tail (file), docker, journald.

- Inherently tied to the host where the data lives
- Must be pinned to a specific node (NodeID required)
- Failover only makes sense if the data source is on shared storage (NFS/EFS)
- Checkpoint state (file offset, cursor position) is local — replicating via Raft would be novel but only useful with shared storage
- For most deployments, the answer is auto-restart (systemd/k8s), same as the rest of the industry

### The Self Ingester
Special case — captures local slog output. Inherently node-local, not a failover candidate, not configurable. Runs on every node automatically.

### What Changes
1. Add an ingester classification field: passive (listener) or active (collector). Derive from ingester type — the factory knows whether it binds a port or reads files.
2. Passive ingesters with empty NodeID run on ALL nodes (current behavior only runs on the node that created them).
3. The UI should make this visible — passive ingesters show 'all nodes' instead of a node selector.
4. The ingester placement manager (if built) only needs to handle active ingesters. Passive ingesters don't need placement — they run everywhere.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Metrics Ingester: Move to Per-Node Local Collection

The metrics ingester is currently assigned to a single node and collects metrics from all nodes via gossip. This should change to match the self ingester pattern:

- Each node runs its own metrics ingester locally
- Each node ingests only its own metrics (CPU, memory, disk, goroutines, etc.)
- No gossip-based metric collection — the data is already local
- Queries fan out across all nodes to get the full cluster picture (same as log search)
- Removes a single point of failure (if the metrics node dies, all metric collection stops)
- Reduces unnecessary gossip traffic

Both the self ingester and the metrics ingester should be reworked together as part of this issue — they're both active ingesters that should run on every node automatically, ingesting only local data.

title: Active record forwarding to secondaries (fire-and-forget)
description:
## Problem

Sealed-chunk replication (gastrolog-18ybo) only replicates immutable chunks after seal. The active chunk on each tier exists solely on the primary — RF=1 regardless of configured replication factor. If the primary dies, the active chunk's records are lost.

This also undermines the durability handoff (gastrolog-4xeh4): transitioned records land in Tier 2's active chunk with no replicas, so even if Tier 1 waits for an ack, the data is vulnerable until Tier 2 seals.

The exposure window is bounded by the rotation policy (e.g. 100 records or 1 minute), which is acceptable for most log workloads but not all.

## Prior art: record-level replication (attempted and reverted)

We implemented and reverted real-time record mirroring in this session. The approach was: primary streams every appended record to secondaries via async buffered channels, with synchronized seals. It produced correct results in unit tests but had cascading production issues:

1. **Streaming handler gap**: The RecordForwarder used the StreamForwardRecords streaming RPC, but the streaming handler didn't route tier_id/chunk_id — records went to the vault's active tier instead of the target tier. Secondaries created independent chunks.

2. **Chunk ID divergence**: Each secondary's ChunkManager generated its own UUIDv7 via NewChunkID(). We added SetNextChunkID() to synchronize IDs, but it only worked for the first chunk — subsequent rotations happened inside Append() atomically, bypassing the hook.

3. **Seal-before-records race**: Seal commands were sent via direct sync RPC while records were buffered in an async channel. The seal could arrive before all records, creating orphaned 1-record chunks. Fix: route seals through the same channel.

4. **Map iteration reordering**: sendBurst grouped records by vault+tier into a Go map. Random iteration order could send post-rotation records before pre-rotation records, causing chunk ID mismatches on secondaries.

5. **Double-seal from rotation policy**: Secondaries ran the same rotation policy as the primary. Both independently sealed at 100 records. The primary's seal command (now redundant) arrived and sealed the secondary's new active chunk at 1 record.

6. **Triple-transition from retention**: Secondaries ran retention sweeps independently, causing RF×N transitions to the next tier. Fix: force all retention actions to expire on secondaries.

7. **Buffer overflow drops**: Replication shared the ingestion forwarding channel (cap 1000) with immediate-drop semantics. Under load, replication records were silently dropped — defeating the purpose.

## Design constraints

- Active chunks are mutable and append-only — replicas must stay in sync record-by-record
- ChunkManager.Append() checks rotation and may seal+open atomically under one lock — no external hook between seal and open
- Rotation policies are per-ChunkManager, so secondaries rotate independently
- Seal boundaries must match exactly across replicas (same records in same chunks)

## Possible approaches

### A. WAL shipping
Primary writes a tier-local write-ahead log alongside the chunk. The WAL is shipped to secondaries, which replay it. Simpler than record-level streaming because:
- WAL entries are immutable once written
- Replay is deterministic (includes seal markers)
- No chunk ID sync needed — WAL carries the primary's chunk ID
- No rotation policy on secondaries — they replay seals from the WAL
- Backpressure is natural (WAL is persistent, secondaries catch up at their own pace)

Trade-off: additional disk I/O for the WAL on the primary.

### B. Disable rotation on secondaries
Keep record-level streaming but disable rotation policies on secondary ChunkManagers entirely. Secondaries only seal when the primary sends a seal command. This eliminates problems 5 and 6 above. Combined with the channel-ordering fixes (3, 4), this might be viable.

Trade-off: requires careful ordering guarantees in the forwarding channel.

### C. Synchronous replication
Primary blocks on each append until RF-1 secondaries confirm. Strongest guarantees but adds latency to every write. Likely unacceptable for a log system.

### D. Accept the gap
Keep sealed-chunk replication only. Bound the risk with aggressive rotation (seal every N records or M seconds). Document that active chunk data has RF=1. For log management, this is often acceptable — sources can retry, and sub-minute gaps are operationally tolerable.

## Recommendation

Option A (WAL shipping) is the cleanest path. It decouples the replication transport from the ChunkManager internals and avoids all the mutable-state synchronization issues we hit with record-level mirroring. Option D is acceptable as an interim.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
Preferred approach: ack-gated replication (discovered during gastrolog-18ybo)

The IngestMessage already has an `Ack chan<- error` field. Today it fires immediately after local Append (lifecycle.go:244). RELP and HTTP (X-Wait-Ack) ingesters block on this channel before confirming to the sender.

The idea: delay the ack until the record is replicated to RF-1 secondaries. No ChunkManager changes needed — replication happens at the orchestrator level between ingest and ack.

Flow:
1. Orchestrator appends record to local chunk (as now)
2. If msg.Ack is non-nil AND tier has secondaries: forward the record to RF-1 secondaries, collect confirmations
3. Once all secondaries confirm (or timeout): fire msg.Ack
4. If msg.Ack is nil (fire-and-forget ingesters like syslog UDP): replicate best-effort, don't wait

This avoids all the problems from the reverted record-level replication because:
- No chunk ID synchronization needed — secondaries create their own chunks, dedup happens at query time or is irrelevant (the point is durability, not identity)
- No seal ordering — secondaries seal independently via their own rotation policy
- No mutable state sync — each node's ChunkManager is autonomous
- The only coordination point is the ack channel, which already exists

The replication itself can reuse ForwardToTier (record forwarding to a specific tier). The difference from the reverted approach: we don't care about chunk ID matching or seal synchronization. We only care that RF nodes have the record bytes. Sealed-chunk replication (already implemented) handles the long-term storage; ack-gated replication handles the active-chunk durability window.

Trade-offs:
- Ingesters with Ack (RELP, HTTP wait-ack) get full RF durability — sender doesn't purge until confirmed
- Ingesters without Ack (UDP syslog, stdin, self-ingester) stay fire-and-forget — active chunk is RF=1
- Latency: ack-gated mode adds one network RTT per record (parallel to RF-1 nodes, wait for slowest)
- Timeout policy needed: if a secondary is unreachable, ack after timeout with a warning (don't block ingestion indefinitely)

Key files:
- orchestrator/lifecycle.go:244 — the ack firing point (delay this)
- orchestrator/ingest.go — ingest path, where replication would be triggered
- ingester/relp/ingester.go:174-196 — RELP ack flow (already correct, just needs the orchestrator to delay)
- ingester/http/ingester.go:195-198 — HTTP ack flow (same)

This supersedes WAL shipping (approach A in the issue description) as the preferred path. WAL shipping solves a broader problem but this is simpler and leverages existing infrastructure.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
REWORKED: This issue is now scoped to just the forwarding plumbing.

Forward each appended record to secondaries as fire-and-forget. Secondaries create their own independent chunks (no ID sync, no seal sync). These chunks are invisible to search (PrimaryTierQueryEngine), not subject to transition/eject (isSecondary forces expire-only), and cleaned up by the sealed-chunk handoff (gastrolog-4xeh4).

Reuses existing RecordForwarder. Key difference from reverted approach: no chunk ID matching, no seal sync, no rotation coordination. Each secondary ChunkManager is autonomous. Rotation stays disabled on secondaries.

Key files: vault_ops.go (add forwarding after append), record_forwarder.go (re-add ForwardToTier), forward.go (re-add tier_id routing in streaming handler).

What NOT to do: no SetNextChunkID, no QueueSealForTier, no replCh, no seal ordering.

title: Orphaned active chunks after cluster restart
description:
On shutdown, the file ChunkManager closes files but does not seal the active chunk. On restart, a new active chunk is opened, leaving the previous one as an unsealed orphan that sits forever — never sealed, never compressed, never indexed, never transitioned by retention.

Fix: on startup, the file ChunkManager should seal any recovered unsealed chunk before opening a new one. This ensures every chunk from a previous run enters the normal lifecycle (compress → index → replicate → transition/expire).

Observed in the inspector as a stale 'active' chunk with a time range spanning hours or days, sitting below the real active chunk.

title: Stale tier data not cleaned up when node loses tier ownership
description:
When a node loses ownership of a tier (no longer primary or secondary after placement rebalancing), the tier instance and its chunk data remain on the node indefinitely. No cleanup path exists.

Scenario:
1. Node-3 is secondary for Tier X
2. Node-3 goes down, placement reassigns Tier X secondary to node-4
3. Node-3 comes back up, config shows it's no longer primary or secondary for Tier X
4. rebuildVaultIfTierMissing skips the tier (!isPrimary && !isSecondary) but doesn't remove the existing tier instance or its data
5. Stale chunks sit on disk forever

Fix: when a tier no longer belongs to a node, remove the tier instance from the vault and clean up its chunk/index data. Must be careful not to remove data that's still being transferred or in-flight.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Same cleanup gap applies when RF is reduced (e.g. RF=4 → RF=3). The evicted secondary still has the tier data. Any event that transitions a node from 'hosting this tier' to 'not hosting this tier' needs the same cleanup: node failure + rebalancing, RF reduction, manual reassignment.

title: JSONL sink tier type for end-to-end verification
description:
A new tier type (jsonl) that writes every record as a JSON line to a single file. No chunking, rotation, indexing, or replication — purely a verification sink.

Config: node selector + path (relative or absolute, same rules as storage areas).

Tracks: earliest timestamp, latest timestamp, running record count.

Use case: terminal tier in a chain. After a burst of scatterbox logs, compare the JSONL file against expected output to verify zero record loss through the entire tier pipeline.

title: Rotation/retention policy 'used by' shows tier type instead of meaningful name
description:
The 'used by' status on rotation and retention policies shows 'file, file, file, file...' because tier names default to their type string (set at creation: name: newTier.type). The UsedByStatus component calls tierRefsForRotationPolicy which maps t.name || t.id — and t.name is just 'file' or 'memory'.

Should show something identifiable like the vault name + tier position (e.g. 'my-vault/tier-1').

title: Back pressure handling for record forwarding
description:
The per-node forward buffer (1000 records) overflows during burst ingestion, silently dropping records. This defeats the purpose of ack-gated ingestion — the primary acks but secondaries lose data.

Need a general back pressure strategy:
- Should the forwarder block the ingester when the buffer is full (back pressure)?
- Should the buffer grow dynamically?
- Should there be a separate high-water/low-water mark with flow control?
- How does this interact with fire-and-forget vs ack-gated ingesters?

Currently: fire-and-forget drop on full buffer. Ack-gated ingesters should NOT drop — they need back pressure or the durability guarantee is meaningless.

title: Remove vestigial VaultsDir and resolveVaultDir
description:
Storage areas now provide absolute paths for file and cloud tiers. The VaultsDir field on Factories and the resolveVaultDir function are no longer needed by any tier type — file tiers get paths from storage areas, JSONL resolves relative to HomeDir, memory has no path.

Remove:
- resolveVaultDir() in reconfig_vaults.go
- Factories.VaultsDir field
- --vaults CLI flag and VaultsFlag in app config
- vaultsDir plumbing in app.go/buildFactories

Verify no edge cases still depend on relative dir resolution before removing.

title: General mechanism for routing frontend actions to the correct backend node
description:
TriggerIngester currently works via X-Target-Node header set by the frontend — the frontend has to know which node owns the ingester. This is backwards: the backend already knows.

Need a general routing strategy for actions that target a specific resource owner (ingester, tier, etc.) without the frontend needing to resolve the target node. The vault routing pattern (duck-typed GetVault() → VaultOwnerResolver) works well but only covers vaults.

Options:
- Add resource-type-specific resolvers (IngesterOwnerResolver) alongside VaultOwnerResolver
- Generic ResourceOwnerResolver that dispatches by procedure prefix
- Extend RouteTargeted to try multiple duck-typed getters (GetVault, GetId, etc.)

This blocks any future frontend→backend actions that target node-specific resources (trigger ingester, flush tier, reset counters, etc.).

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Many actions that should be direct signals are currently tunneled through the config system (Raft round-trip) because there's no lightweight way to reach the correct node. Examples: seal a vault, reindex, rotate. These don't mutate config — they're imperative actions. The routing mechanism should support both config mutations (RouteLeader) and direct node actions (RouteToResourceOwner) without forcing everything through Raft.

title: Config store lacks referential integrity — orphaned objects accumulate
description:
The Raft config store has no referential integrity enforcement. Deleting a vault leaves its tier configs behind. Deleting a tier doesn't clean up its rotation/retention policy references. Removing a node doesn't clean up ingesters, tiers, or storage areas assigned to it.

This is systemic: every entity that references another can become orphaned when the referenced entity is deleted. Without cascading deletes or a GC sweep, the config store accumulates garbage over time.

Symptoms observed:
- Rotation policy 'used by' shows raw UUIDs for tiers belonging to no vault
- Stale tier configs reference deleted vaults

Needs:
- Cascading deletes (delete vault → delete its tiers → clean up policy refs)
- Or: periodic GC sweep that identifies and removes unreferenced entities
- Or: referential integrity checks on mutation (reject delete if referenced, or cascade)

Applies to all entity relationships: vault→tier, tier→rotation policy, tier→retention policy, tier→node, ingester→node, ingester→vault, route→filter, route→vault, etc.

title: In-memory config store with referential integrity and dependency graph
description:
The current config store (config/memory.Store) is a collection of ad-hoc maps and slices with no relationship enforcement. As the system grows (multi-tenancy, route pipelines, lookup tables, cloud services, placement constraints), the lack of referential integrity creates real bugs: orphaned tiers from deleted vaults, dangling policy references, stale node assignments.

Replace the ad-hoc store with a structured in-memory store that:

1. **Declares entity relationships** — foreign keys between entity types (vault→tiers, tier→rotation policy, tier→retention policy, tier→node, ingester→node, ingester→vault, route→filter, route→vault destinations, cloud service→tiers, lookup→config, etc.)

2. **Enforces referential integrity on mutation** — reject PutTier with a nonexistent RotationPolicyID, reject DeleteRotationPolicy if any tier references it (or cascade), reject PutVault with tier IDs that don't exist

3. **Cascading deletes** — delete vault → delete its tiers. Configurable per-relationship: cascade, restrict (reject if referenced), or nullify (clear the FK)

4. **Orphan detection** — on any delete, walk the dependency graph and clean up unreachable entities

5. **Snapshot/restore** — same as today, the store serializes to a snapshot and rebuilds from it

The Raft log and FSM Apply pipeline stay the same — commands are still PutTier, DeleteVault, etc. The intelligence lives in the store layer between Apply and the maps. Every mutation goes through the store's integrity checks before committing.

This is foundational infrastructure. Multi-tenancy (gastrolog-5bm6o), route pipelines (gastrolog-5e85x), and the growing config surface all depend on the store not silently accumulating garbage.

title: Config Store Integrity
description: Foundational improvements to the in-memory config store: referential integrity, dependency graph, cascading deletes, orphan cleanup. Prerequisite for multi-tenancy and growing config surface.

title: Rename TestVault RPC to TestCloudService
description: TestVault is misleading — it tests cloud storage connections (S3 endpoint, credentials, bucket), not vaults. Rename across proto, Go backend, frontend, and add the missing Test Connection button to the cloud service settings form.

title: Remove active chunk class and cache class from cloud service config
description:
ActiveChunkClass and CacheClass exist on both CloudService and TierConfig. They're about local storage area selection, not the remote cloud service. The backend already reads them from TierConfig (buildTierParams line 696). Remove from:

- CloudService struct in config.go
- CloudService proto message
- Cloud service add form (StorageSettings.tsx)
- Cloud service card (CloudServiceCard.tsx)
- protoToCloudService / cloudServiceToProto conversions

Keep them on TierConfig where they belong.

title: Active chunk class and cache class should be storage class dropdowns
description:
On both the existing cloud tier edit view and the new cloud tier entry card, Active Chunk Class and Cache Class are raw number inputs. They should be storage class dropdowns (same as the file tier's storage class selector) since they reference the same storage area classes.

Both views already have storageClassOptions available — just need to swap NumberInput for SelectInput.
