2. **Tier Raft leadership divergence**: No longer causes retention failures. The accumulated fixes — FSM catchup at startup (921590ff), deferred tier rebuild in handleTierPut (8c262a7a), deferred PeerConns closes (0365fe8c), and the LeaderLoop + TierApplyForwarder infrastructure — collectively resolved the practical impact. Retention runs on the config placement leader and forwards applies to whichever node holds tier Raft leadership via TierApplyForwarder.

3. **Stale manifest deletes follower chunks**: Fixed by FSM.Ready() guard (bc00d425) which prevents reconciliation from running against an incomplete manifest after restart.

User confirms retention works correctly after restart in multi-node cluster testing. Closing.

title: Runtime log level switching
description:
No way to change log levels at runtime or per subsystem. Debugging cluster issues requires a restart, which changes the state being debugged.

## Requirements

### Backend: per-subsystem log level control
- The logging system already tags messages with subsystem/component names, but there is no mechanism to set log levels per subsystem — everything is global INFO.
- Add a startup flag (e.g. `--log-level chunk-manager=debug,orchestrator=warn`) to set initial per-subsystem levels.
- Add a runtime API (RPC endpoint) to change per-subsystem log levels on a running node without restart.
- The global default level should remain configurable as a baseline.

### Subsystem audit
- Audit the entire codebase to ensure subsystem names (the `component` slog attribute) are sensibly named, consistent, and cover the right granularity.
- Every major subsystem should have its own component tag: chunk manager, index manager, orchestrator, replication, tier raft, cluster, ingester (per type), query engine, config store, server/routing, etc.
- Identify any hot paths that log at debug level but lack a component tag, or components that are too coarse (e.g. one tag covering both ingestion and rotation).

### CLI
- `gastrolog config log-level list` — show current per-subsystem levels on a node.
- `gastrolog config log-level set <subsystem>=<level> [...]` — change levels at runtime.

### UI (Settings)
- Add a Log Levels section in the Service settings tab.
- Show current per-subsystem levels with dropdowns to adjust (debug/info/warn/error).
- Changes take effect immediately via the runtime API, no restart needed.

title: Cold tier re-downloads all cloud chunks on every restart to rebuild indexes
description:
On restart, loadExisting deletes 'leftover' chunk directories (1697 on node3), then RebuildMissingIndexes schedules index builds for every cloud-backed chunk. Each index build calls OpenCursor which downloads the full GLCB blob from S3. On the current test cluster this means 1697 S3 downloads and 3357 index rebuilds on every single restart.

The indexes should be persisted locally and survive restarts. The 'leftover directory' cleanup is too aggressive — it removes directories that contained valid index files for cloud-backed chunks.

title: Cloud-tier chunks always show 'no cloud badge' on follower nodes
description:
The inspector's cloud badge is rendered from a chunk's `CloudBacked` field, which is set per-node by `chunkMeta.cloudBacked`. By design (`backend/internal/orchestrator/reconfig_vaults.go:689`), tier-raft followers strip `sealed_backing` from their chunk-manager params so they keep local copies for fast queries — meaning their `CloudStore` is nil and `cloudBacked` is *never* set, even though the cluster has uploaded the chunk to S3.

## Symptom

When the inspector calls `ListChunks` against a vault, the response comes from whichever node served the request. With 4 nodes and 1 leader per cold tier, you have a 75% chance of hitting a follower → the chunk lists report `CloudBacked=false` for chunks that are *definitely* in the cloud.

## Verification

Empirically confirmed on a running 4-node cluster (2026-04-07):
- 82+ `.glcb` blobs in MinIO bucket `gastrolog/vault-019d6789-00d6-7766-b8d1-20e09a904de5/` and growing
- Every cold-tier chunk in the inspector shows no cloud badge regardless of which node serves the request
- On-disk distribution: leader (node4) holds ~62 local chunks (uploads-in-progress backlog), followers (node1/2/3) hold ~153 each — confirming the leader uploads + evicts while followers retain local copies

## Root cause

`backend/internal/server/vault_info.go:398-407` builds the `ChunkMeta` proto response from the local chunk manager's `meta.CloudBacked`. On followers this is always `false` because `sealed_backing` was stripped from their params. The cluster-wide truth lives in the tier FSM's `chunkEntry`, which is replicated via the Raft `MarshalUploadChunk` command to every member — but that knowledge isn't being plumbed back into the chunk-list response.

## Proposed fix

Source `CloudBacked` from the tier FSM (`backend/internal/tier/raftfsm/fsm.go`) instead of the per-node chunk manager's `metas` map. The FSM's `chunkEntry` is the cluster-wide ground truth for upload status; every node has it locally because it's replicated via Raft, so no extra network hops are needed.

Fix sites:
- `backend/internal/server/vault_info.go` — when building each `ChunkMeta`, look up the chunk in the tier FSM and override `CloudBacked` from the FSM entry
- Consider doing the same for `Archived` / `StorageClass` since they have the same per-node-vs-cluster-wide split

## Test coverage required

- **Single-node**: confirms FSM-sourced `CloudBacked` matches chunk-manager view when local node is the leader (regression check)
- **Multi-node**: a follower-served `ListChunks` returns the same `CloudBacked` as a leader-served one for the same chunk
- **Happy path**: chunk uploaded → all nodes report `CloudBacked=true`
- **Unhappy path**: chunk not yet uploaded → all nodes report `false`
- **Edge case**: chunk uploaded then deleted from S3 (suspect status) → behavior should be defined and asserted

## Architectural note

This is a symptom of a broader design tension: per-node truth (`chunk_manager.metas`) vs cluster-wide truth (tier FSM's `chunkEntry`). Multiple fields likely have the same problem (Archived, StorageClass, NumFrames). A clean fix should establish a clear rule for which fields are sourced from where.

title: Cluster data plane wedges silently when one follower is paused (SIGSTOP)
description:
A single voter follower paused via SIGSTOP causes the entire cluster's data plane to wedge for the duration of the pause, with **zero log entries**, **zero error messages**, and **zero visible signal** that anything is wrong.

## Reproduction (verified 2026-04-07 on branch gastrolog-427mh @ 0365fe8c)

4-node cluster: node1/2/3 voters, node4 voteless. chatterbox running steadily.

```
14:14:09  kill -STOP <node3 binary PID>
14:17:18  kill -CONT <node3 binary PID>   # 189 seconds later
```

| Window | Duration | Hot chunks created (each node) | New cluster.log lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-SIGSTOP | — | normal cadence | none (steady-state INFO is silent) |
| **SIGSTOP held** | 189 s | **0** | **0** |
| First 30s after SIGCONT | 30 s | 9 each | 16 (all from the SIGCONT moment) |

After SIGCONT, node3 immediately fired pre-vote requests for cold tier (`019d6789-0789-...`), warm tier (`019d6789-0510-...`), and config raft. node1/node2/node4 all replied with `rejecting pre-vote request since we have a leader` — the cluster never lost its leader and the other nodes were happy the entire time. node3 backed off, accepted node2's leadership (`019d6788-e239-723e-982e-f6bcab3d13f9`), and rejoined as a follower. Hot tier raw.log writes resumed within seconds.

## Why this is critical

- **Silent**: zero logs during the wedge means no operator visibility. From the outside, the cluster looks healthy.
- **Total**: every record produced during the pause is sitting in some upstream channel; not a single chunk lands on disk on any node.
- **Triggered by an unresponsive follower**, not by quorum loss: with 3 voters, losing 1 leaves quorum (2/3). hraft commits should still work. The wedge is in *our* code, not raft itself.
- **Defeats the fundamental promise of a 4-node cluster**: that you can lose one node and keep running.

## Hypothesised mechanism

`backend/internal/orchestrator/replication.go:replicateToFollower` fans sealed-chunk replication out to every follower individually via `chunk_transferrer.ReplicateSealedChunk` / `StreamToTier`. Under SIGSTOP, the paused process's TCP socket stays alive at the kernel level — the OS keeps acking packets even though user space is frozen. So `stream.SendMsg()` succeeds at the gRPC layer, but `stream.RecvMsg(resp)` for the ack hangs forever, because the application-level ack will never come.

If the post-seal pipeline waits synchronously on follower acks (or even joins on parallel goroutines via `errgroup`), one paused follower freezes the whole pipeline → backpressures rotation → backpressures append → backpressures ingest → entire cluster stops.

The smoking gun for the silent failure: **nothing logs because nothing has timed out yet.** Goroutines are blocked in `RecvMsg` with no context deadline. In `chunk_transferrer.go` several streaming RPCs accept `ctx context.Context` but the callers pass `context.Background()`, so the wait is infinite.

## Why the gRPC stale-conn fix (0365fe8c) doesn't help

That fix prevented one goroutine's failure from cascading into other goroutines using the same conn. It does nothing for "the conn is fine, but the remote process isn't processing." That's a *liveness* problem, not a *connection state* problem.

## Proposed fixes (defence in depth)

1. **Per-RPC timeouts on every cluster forwarder call.** Add `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)` (or shorter) to every `replicateToFollower`, `StreamToTier`, `ForwardSealTier`, `ForwardDeleteChunk`, etc. caller. Smallest blast radius.
2. **gRPC keepalive params** with `Time: 10s, Timeout: 5s, PermitWithoutStream: true` so HTTP/2 PINGs detect a paused server within 15s. The gRPC server's PING-handling loop is *also* paused under SIGSTOP, so the keepalive pong never comes back, and gRPC fails the conn.
3. **Best-effort sealed-chunk replication**: don't block the seal pipeline on follower acks. Replicate async via a per-follower retry queue. Failed replications log + alert. The leader's seal completes immediately and the pipeline stays moving.
4. **An always-on liveness check / alert**: if a node's last successful AppendEntries to a peer is older than N seconds, fire a Warning alert. This makes silent wedges visible from the operator console.

Of these, (1) is the smallest fix and would be a net improvement regardless of (2)/(3)/(4). (3) is the proper fix but is bigger. (4) is needed even after (1)-(3) because it's the only thing that makes silent failures visible.

## Test coverage required

- **Single-node**: not applicable (this is fundamentally a multi-node bug)
- **Multi-node happy path**: 4-node cluster, kill one process cleanly (SIGTERM), verify writes continue without delay
- **Multi-node SIGSTOP**: 4-node cluster, SIGSTOP one follower, verify writes continue (or verify they fail with a logged timeout within N seconds, never silently)
- **Multi-node SIGSTOP leader**: 4-node cluster, SIGSTOP the current tier raft leader, verify a new leader is elected within the heartbeat timeout and writes resume
- **Multi-node MinIO outage**: stop the MinIO container, verify cold-tier uploads fail with logged errors and alerts (not silent backpressure)
- **Edge case**: SIGSTOP a node for exactly the heartbeat timeout duration, verify behaviour at the boundary

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Update: leader-SIGSTOP test sharpens the diagnosis

Ran a 10-second SIGSTOP on node2 (the cluster leader at port :4576). Findings:

**All 4 raft groups elected new leaders within ~3 seconds of SIGSTOP:**

| Time after SIGSTOP | Raft group | Won by | Term |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~2.0 s | cold tier (0789) | node3 | 6 |
| ~2.4 s | config raft | node1 | 7 |
| ~3.0 s | hot tier (02a8) | node3 | 6 |
| ~3.1 s | warm tier (0510) | node1 | 6 |

**But ZERO chunks were created on any node for the remaining ~7 seconds of the pause, despite all raft groups having fully-elected new leaders.** Writes only resumed after SIGCONT.

This means **the wedge is NOT about leader election** — hraft handles leader loss correctly. The wedge is downstream, at the data plane / pipeline level.

## Mechanism (refined)

Most likely cause: **blocked forwarding goroutines are holding pipeline channel slots indefinitely**.

- chatterbox produces records → goes through ingestCh → digestCh → tier dispatcher
- tier dispatcher forwards to the hot tier raft leader (was node2 before SIGSTOP)
- forwarding uses `chunk_transferrer.go` with `stream.RecvMsg(resp)` against `context.Background()` — *no timeout*
- node2 gets paused → kernel keeps TCP socket alive → gRPC sees the conn as fine → `RecvMsg` blocks forever
- the goroutine is holding a channel slot
- more records pile up → channel fills → producer blocks → ingest stops

After leader election at t+3s, the *next* forward attempt would target the new leader, but the *previous* attempt is still parked in `RecvMsg` against node2's stale conn. Nothing kills it. The pipeline can't make progress because the in-flight slot never releases.

## Confirms the proposed fix #1 is necessary

`context.WithTimeout` on every cluster forwarder call. There's a clear pattern in `chunk_transferrer.go` (StreamToTier, ReplicateSealedChunk, TransferRecords, ForwardAppend, etc.) and `forward_rpc.go` of calls that accept `ctx context.Context` but get `context.Background()` from the caller. A 5-10s deadline at the call site would convert the silent forever-wait into a clean timeout error within seconds.

After fix: cluster would still wedge briefly during a SIGSTOP, but only for the timeout duration (5-10s), not the entire pause duration. After leader election (~3s) + timeout firing (~5-10s), the blocked goroutine returns an error, the pipeline retries against the new leader, and the cluster self-heals.

## Why fix #1 is necessary AND insufficient

`context.WithTimeout` covers the steady-state case but doesn't address:
- **Per-call retry against the new leader after timeout** — does the caller know to re-resolve who the leader is, or will it keep targeting node2?
- **Pre-existing channel backpressure** — once channels are full, draining them takes time even after the wedge clears
- **Operator visibility** — silent timeout errors are still pretty silent; we need an alert if forwarding to a peer fails repeatedly

So fix #1 is the foundation, but fixes #3 (async replication) and #4 (liveness alerts) are still needed.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Update: SIGKILL test definitively isolates the root cause

Followed up the SIGSTOP tests with a SIGKILL of node3 (clean process death). The contrast is conclusive:

| | SIGSTOP (zombie sockets) | SIGKILL (clean close) |
|---|---|---|
| Chunks created per surviving node (10-12s window) | **0** | **2** |
| New cluster.log lines during disruption | **0** | **~139** (errors, warns, elections) |
| Visible failure signal | none — completely silent | `EOF` within 0.7s, `connection refused` within 1s |
| Recovery model | only on SIGCONT | continuous, immediate |

When node3 dies cleanly (SIGKILL), the kernel immediately tears down its TCP sockets. Every peer's in-flight `RecvMsg` returns `EOF`, the dead conn gets invalidated via PeerConns, retries hit the new leader, the orchestrator logs `replication: failed to forward record to follower` cleanly, and writes continue on the surviving 3 nodes.

When node3 is paused (SIGSTOP), the kernel keeps its sockets alive — TCP heartbeats are handled in kernel space, ack'ing packets, advertising window sizes — but the user-space gRPC server never reads from the socket. From the *peer's* perspective the conn looks healthy. Every `RecvMsg` against an in-flight stream blocks forever waiting on an application-level response that will never come. The blocked goroutines hold pipeline channel slots indefinitely. Backpressure cascades up to ingest. Total wedge.

## Definitive fix priority

Fix #1 (per-RPC timeouts on cluster forwarder calls) is now clearly the *root cause fix*, not just a mitigation. With timeouts in place, SIGSTOP would be indistinguishable from SIGKILL from the application's perspective: blocked RPCs would time out within 5-10s, the goroutines would unwind, the dead conn would be invalidated, retries would hit the new leader. The cluster would degrade for ~10s instead of wedging silently for the duration of the pause.

Sites that need timeouts (caller passes context.Background() to a function that takes ctx and uses it for streaming):

- backend/internal/cluster/chunk_transferrer.go: `TransferRecords`, `ReplicateSealedChunk`, `StreamToTier`, `ForwardAppend`, `ForwardTierAppend`, `ForwardSealTier`, `ForwardDeleteChunk`, `WaitVaultReady`
- backend/internal/cluster/forward_rpc.go: any caller of `peers.Conn(...).Invoke(ctx, ...)` or `conn.NewStream(ctx, ...)` where ctx is bg
- Anywhere else in `backend/internal/cluster/` and `backend/internal/orchestrator/replication*.go` where forwarder calls accept ctx but receive bg

The deadline value should be derived from a config knob, default 10s for streaming, 5s for unary. Long enough to not flake under normal load, short enough to detect a wedge before it cascades.

title: Cold-tier S3/MinIO outages are silent at WARN/ERROR level
description:
Stopping the MinIO container that the cold tier is configured against produces **zero WARN or ERROR log entries about S3 unavailability**, even though the cold tier's `uploadToCloud` should be failing on every attempt.

## Reproduction (verified 2026-04-07)

```
14:27:03  docker stop gastrolog-minio
14:28:02  docker start gastrolog-minio   # ~60 seconds of outage
```

During the 60-second outage, the cluster log filled up with errors — but **all** of them were about the dead node3 (a separate disruption from an earlier test) and tier raft snapshot recovery. Zero entries mentioning S3, MinIO, the cloud store endpoint, upload failures, or `uploadToCloud`. The cold-tier upload code is at `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go:2444`:

```go
if m.cfg.CloudStore != nil {
    if err := m.uploadToCloud(id); err != nil {
        m.logger.Warn("cloud upload failed, keeping local", "chunk", id, "error", err)
    }
}
```

That `Warn` line should fire on every failed upload during a MinIO outage. It didn't appear once in the log capture.

## Possible explanations (need investigation)

1. **No upload attempts happened during the window**. Maybe the leader had no sealed chunks ready to upload during those 60 seconds. Unlikely given the chatterbox load.
2. **The Warn was logged but filtered/downgraded somewhere**. Worth checking if hclog adapters or slog routing is dropping it.
3. **The `Warn` was logged but the multirun --tee buffer ate it**. Unlikely — other Warns from the same components show up fine.
4. **`uploadToCloud` is succeeding against a stopped MinIO**. Worth checking if there's some bizarre fallback or if the gRPC/HTTP client is masking the error.

## Why this is high priority

The whole point of having a cloud tier is durability. If S3 becomes unreachable, the operator needs to know *immediately* — not via the absence of growing blob counts in S3, but via a proper alert and a stream of error logs. A silent upload failure means:

- The local node keeps accumulating sealed chunks because uploads never complete
- Disk usage grows unboundedly on the leader
- Followers also retain locals (they always do — see gastrolog-asg4l)
- Eventually the local disk fills up and *that's* when the operator finds out

The fix is similar to gastrolog-4rp6i: not just per-RPC timeouts but also liveness-style alerts. If `uploadToCloud` has failed N times in a row for a given tier, raise an Error-level alert via the alerting subsystem (the same one that fires for "chunk-suspect").

## Test coverage required

- **Multi-node**: 4-node cluster, stop S3, verify ERROR or WARN log entries appear within seconds
- **Multi-node**: stop S3, verify an `alert.Set` fires with sufficient context (which tier, which node, what error)
- **Multi-node**: restart S3, verify the alert clears and uploads resume
- **Edge case**: S3 returns 503 Slow Down (rate limit) repeatedly → verify retry/backoff logic logs and alerts appropriately

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Closing as wrongly reported — the Warn is already in place

Re-tested on a healthy cluster (post gastrolog-2mnv8 fix, MinIO running, chatterbox flowing). Stopped MinIO for 50 seconds, observed cluster.log:

```
[node4] 23:59:21.416 level=WARN msg="cloud upload failed, keeping local"
  vault=019d699f-eb7a-75cc-8373-6feda687bcb9
  tier=019d699f-f28b-7622-8565-f9b7e10517d2
  storage=019d699f-e02c-7da4-8fde-be1a6a72074d
  component=chunk-manager type=file
  chunk=06emjt61plq1t47dk8ff3ah1n4
  error="upload GLCB: operation error S3: PutObject, exceeded maximum
        number of attempts, 3, https response error StatusCode: 0,
        ...request send failed, Put http://localhost:9000/...:
        dial tcp [::1]:9000: connect: connection refused"
```

That's a proper WARN-level entry with structured fields, the chunk ID,
the vault/tier/storage triple, and the full error chain. Visibility is
correct. The Warn fires within ~10 seconds of MinIO going down (the
delay is the S3 client's retry-with-backoff before giving up).

The Warn is at `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go:2445` in
`PostSealProcess`:

```go
if m.cfg.CloudStore != nil {
    if err := m.uploadToCloud(id); err != nil {
        m.logger.Warn("cloud upload failed, keeping local", "chunk", id, "error", err)
    }
}
```

## Why my original report was wrong

I filed this issue earlier in the session after stopping MinIO during
a degraded-cluster test (node3 dead from a SIGKILL, snapshot install
loop active). I observed "no S3 warnings in cluster.log" and inferred
"S3 outages are silent." The inference was wrong because:

- The upload pipeline only fires when chunks reach seal → compress →
  upload, and the cluster was wedged on snapshot install during my
  test window
- No seals → no upload attempts → no Warns to fire
- I conflated "I didn't see X in this messy log" with "X cannot happen"

The correct test is a 50-second MinIO outage on a healthy cluster
where the upload pipeline is actively running. That test (just done)
shows the Warn is exactly where it should be.

## Optional follow-up (not filing, noting only)

The Warn is in place for log observability, but there's no alert in
the `alerts` subsystem (the one that powers the inspector UI) for
repeated upload failures. If product wants operators to see "S3 has
been unreachable for N attempts" in the inspector without grepping
logs, that's a feature request separate from this bug report. Not
filing speculatively — only worth doing if there's a real ux pull.

Closing this issue as "not a bug — original test methodology was wrong".

title: Catchup transfers FSM-retired chunks, then reconcile deletes them as orphans
description:
When a follower returns after being unreachable (SIGSTOP, SIGKILL, network partition), the leader's catchup mechanism transfers sealed chunks from its on-disk list to the follower. But the on-disk list can include chunks that have already been retired from the tier Raft FSM via retention — there's a window between FSM apply (DeleteChunk) and the leader's local file actually being unlinked. Catchup happily ships those orphaned files. The follower writes them to disk. The follower's reconcile loop then runs, sees them on disk but not in the FSM manifest, and deletes them as orphans.

End-to-end visible flow:

```
14:55:45  SIGSTOP node3 (paused, misses tier raft commits + retention deletes)
14:57:01  SIGCONT node3 (raft re-syncs FSM state — DeleteChunk commands replayed)
14:57:15  node1 catchup transfers chunk 06emg11bm9o074b9p5cne2sh94 to node3
14:58:00  node3 reconcile: "deleted orphaned chunk from follower" 06emg11bm9o074b9p5cne2sh94
```

The chunk that just got catchup-transferred is deleted ~45 seconds later by the receiver itself. Net result: catchup work is wasted, the chunk is permanently gone from the follower, and the cluster ends up under-replicated for any chunk that was in the leader's "FSM-deleted but disk-not-yet" window during the catchup pass.

## Root cause

`backend/internal/orchestrator/replication_catchup.go:66` builds the catchup list from the local file system:

```go
metas, err := tier.Chunks.List()
```

`tier.Chunks` is the local `chunk.ChunkManager`. Its `List()` returns whatever sealed chunk directories exist on disk. The leader's reconcile loop and FSM are independent — the FSM commits a delete, but the actual `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)` happens in a separate code path (OnDelete callback or post-FSM-apply work). Between those two events, the chunk is "FSM-deleted but disk-present", and catchup is racing this window.

`tier.ListManifest()` (defined in `tier_instance.go:52` as "the authoritative set of chunks that should exist") is the right source of truth. The reconcile loop already uses it (`retention.go:327`).

## Fix

In `catchupFollower`, intersect the on-disk chunk list with the FSM manifest. Only transfer chunks that are in BOTH:

```go
manifestSet := buildManifestSet(tier.ListManifest)
for _, m := range metas {
    if !m.Sealed { continue }
    if isFileTier && !m.Compressed { continue }
    if manifestSet != nil && !manifestSet[m.ID] {
        continue  // FSM has retired this — don't catchup what reconcile will delete
    }
    sealed = append(sealed, m)
}
```

This makes catchup symmetric with reconcile: both use the FSM manifest as ground truth. Anything not in the manifest is, by definition, not part of the cluster's view of the data.

## Test coverage required

- **Multi-node**: 4-node cluster, chatterbox running with short retention (1m), SIGSTOP a follower for >1 retention cycle, SIGCONT, verify no "deleted orphaned chunk from follower" entries appear for chunks the catchup just transferred
- **Multi-node**: 4-node cluster, kill a follower (SIGKILL), restart it, verify same: no orphan deletions of just-transferred chunks
- **Edge case**: chunk in FSM but missing from leader's disk → catchup should skip cleanly without error
- **Race**: chunk being retired during catchup pass → catchup shouldn't transfer a chunk that gets deleted from FSM mid-pass (acceptable race window — pre-fetch the manifest at the start)

## Discovery context

Surfaced while validating the gastrolog-4rp6i fix (per-call timeouts on cluster forwarders) on branch `gastrolog-4rp6i`. The silent-wedge fix made catchup actually run after a SIGCONT (instead of the cluster being wedged), which then exposed this orphan-deletion race. The two issues are sister bugs in the recovery-from-disruption family.

title: Startup skips empty vaults, breaking snapshot-restored nodes
description:
On startup, `initVault` (backend/internal/orchestrator/factory.go:165) skips registering any vault whose `buildTierInstances` returns an empty slice:

```go
// During ApplyConfig (startup), skip vaults with no local tiers.
// The filter set handles forwarding to the correct node.
// (The dispatch path in handleVaultPut registers zero-tier vaults
// so handleTierPut can add tiers incrementally.)
if len(tiers) == 0 {
    return nil
}
```

The comment justifies the skip by claiming `handleVaultPut` will register the vault later via the dispatch path. That's true when vaults are created at runtime (a fresh cluster being set up via config CLI) because `NotifyVaultPut` fires the dispatcher. **It is not true after a cluster restart from a snapshot** — the FSM is bulk-loaded from the snapshot, no notifications fire for the restored state, so `handleVaultPut` is never called for pre-existing vaults.

When node4 then receives `NotifyTierPut` notifications from post-snapshot raft log replay (or placement updates), the dispatcher walks through `handleTierPut` → `rebuildVaultIfTierMissing` → `AddTierToVault`, which fails hard with `vault not found`. Every subsequent `replication: failed to forward record to follower` then compounds because the target follower's state is broken.

## Smoking gun from a real 4-node cluster restart

```
15:16:02.277  [node4] loaded config ingesters=2 vaults=1
15:16:02.277  [node4] starting orchestrator vaults=0 ingesters=0   ← buildTierInstances returned []
15:16:02.578  [node4] ERROR dispatch: add tier to vault ... error="vault not found: 019d6800-d9ba-7aba-b382-2524a512d30a"
[× 6 — 3 tiers × 2 dispatch passes]
15:16:06.524  [node1] replication catchup: transfer failed ... error="vault not found: ..."
[× hundreds, spamming at multi-per-millisecond rates for the lifetime of the cluster]
```

`loaded config vaults=1` + `starting orchestrator vaults=0` is the before-and-after of initVault for this vault. The config store *has* the vault; the orchestrator silently doesn't.

Why does `buildTierInstances` return empty on node4? Because `node4` is voteless/non-member of the tier placements for this particular vault config, either due to a placement-assignment race or because `--voteless` on node4 interacts with placement assignment in a way that leaves it out.

Regardless of the underlying reason, **`initVault` should match `AddVault`'s behaviour**: register the empty vault anyway. `AddVault` (`reconfig_vaults.go:65`) explicitly does this with the comment "Register vault (even with zero tiers — tiers arrive incrementally via handleTierPut)". The inconsistency between startup and runtime is the bug.

## Fix

Delete the early-exit in `initVault`:

```go
-  // During ApplyConfig (startup), skip vaults with no local tiers.
-  // The filter set handles forwarding to the correct node.
-  // (The dispatch path in handleVaultPut registers zero-tier vaults
-  // so handleTierPut can add tiers incrementally.)
-  if len(tiers) == 0 {
-      return nil
-  }
```

After the fix, `initVault` registers empty vaults at startup the same way `AddVault` does at runtime. Subsequent `handleTierPut` calls then succeed in adding tiers incrementally.

## Test coverage required

- **Unit test**: ApplyConfig with a vault that has tiers, but none of which are placed on the local node → vault should be registered (with zero local tiers) so later `handleTierPut` can add them
- **Multi-node integration**: 4-node cluster init → ingest → cluster-kill → cluster-run → assert no `vault not found` errors in the log and no `reconcileVaultTiers` spam
- **Regression**: verify filter-based forwarding still works correctly when a vault is registered with zero local tiers (the comment's original justification was "the filter set handles forwarding to the correct node")

## Discovery context

Surfaced on 2026-04-07 while validating the per-call timeout fix (`gastrolog-4rp6i`) on branch `gastrolog-4rp6i`. After a cluster-kill + cluster-run, node4's log filled with `vault not found` errors at multi-per-millisecond rates, and node1's replication catchup spammed the same error trying to forward records to node4. Without this fix, cluster restarts on nodes with zero local tier placements (common for voteless nodes or nodes that aren't placement targets for a given vault) produce silently broken orchestrators.

title: Cursor read races writer: stale mmap size in chunk index path
description:
Multiple file-backed chunk-replication tests intermittently fail with errors like:

```
replication_test.go:640: cursor.Next: invalid idx.log entry:
  chunk 06emg8lmadrrp2j0pl327g91uk record 12:
  raw range [144:156] exceeds mmap size 151
```

The index entry says record 12 starts at byte offset 144 with a length that ends at 156, but the cursor's mmap of `raw.log` is only 151 bytes. The reader is using a stale mmap of the raw data file while the index has been updated to include records beyond what the mmap covers.

## Affected tests (observed flaking)

All in `backend/internal/orchestrator/replication_test.go`:

- `TestClusterReplicationSealSync` (line 590 — `cursor.Next: invalid attributes data`)
- `TestClusterReplicationDeletePropagation` (line 640 — `raw range exceeds mmap size`)
- `TestClusterReplicationSealedChunksArriveOnFollowers`

All three use the file-backed `setupCluster` harness and read sealed chunks via `cursorCountRecords` immediately after replication. Reproduction rate observed at ~3-7% under serial repetition (`-count=10`) and higher under multi-package parallel runs.

## Root cause (hypothesis)

The chunk file manager appears to update `idx.log` and `raw.log` independently, with the index entry committed before the mmap of the raw file is extended (or before the cursor's existing mmap is invalidated/grown). Any of these scenarios produces the symptom:

1. **Append-after-mmap**: cursor opens during a write, mmaps the file at its current length, then a subsequent append extends the file but the cursor still sees the old mmap.
2. **Seal-during-cursor-open**: cursor opens just before seal completes, sealing flushes more data but the cursor's mmap was already taken.
3. **Index-before-data ordering**: writer commits the index entry (visible to reader) before flushing the corresponding raw bytes (or extending the mmap).

The fact that the offsets are tiny (record 12, raw range 12 bytes) and match the test's small payloads (`del-prop-N`) confirms this is the test's actual data, not random corruption.

## Probable fix sites

- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` — wherever `OpenCursor` mmaps the raw file. The mmap size should be sourced atomically with the index size.
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/cursor.go` (or wherever the cursor lives) — when `Next()` reads an index entry whose raw range exceeds the current mmap size, it should either re-mmap (extending) or fail with a retryable error rather than the current panic-style "exceeds mmap size".
- The append path should commit raw bytes BEFORE the index entry, not after.

## Related historical failures

The error string "invalid attributes data" comes from the same family — `attr.log` is also mmap'd, also subject to the same race. The historical reference `gastrolog-4dd48` (`backend/internal/chunk/file/concurrent_append_test.go:13-16`) describes the same class of bug for `attr.log`. The current bug looks like the same race resurfaced for `raw.log` and/or `idx.log`.

## Test coverage required

- A focused stress test that exercises the exact race window: open a cursor on a chunk that's actively being appended, drive ~100 concurrent appends, ensure cursor reads either succeed (with current data) or fail with a retryable error — never with "exceeds mmap size".
- Repeat for `attr.log` to confirm gastrolog-4dd48 is still fixed.
- Run the existing `TestClusterReplication*` tests with `-count=100` and assert zero failures.

## Discovery context

Surfaced 2026-04-07 while validating fixes on branch `gastrolog-4rp6i`. The test failure is **not** caused by any of my recent changes (chunk_transferrer timeouts, replication_catchup manifest filter, factory.go empty-vault registration) — none of those touch the chunk file mmap/cursor layer. But the failure is consistent and reproducible under load, so it needs its own investigation and fix track.

title: Tier raft membership desync at startup + non-leader dispatcher trying to AddVoter
description:
Two related symptoms observed at cluster startup, both about tier raft group membership management:

## Symptom A: tier raft membership desync across nodes

After cluster restart, different nodes load different `initial configuration` for the *same* tier raft group from their local raft snapshots. Example from a real 4-node restart:

- node1's snapshot for tier `019d6800-db8c-71fb-a0a0-ff03d74eebf4` (hot tier) shows: `[node1 voter, node2 nonvoter, node4 voter, node3 voter]` (4 members)
- **node2's snapshot for the same tier shows: `[node2 voter]` (just 1 member, solo)**

The cluster runs and reconciles via raft membership exchange at runtime, but each node briefly has a different view until reconciliation completes. The persisted snapshots are written without coordination across peers.

Furthermore, **node2 is consistently a Nonvoter in the tier raft groups even though it's a Voter in the config raft and was not started with `--voteless`**. The asymmetry is structural, not from any flag.

## Symptom B: dispatcher tries to AddVoter from a non-leader node

At startup on `node1`:

```
[node1] level=INFO msg="dispatch: reconciling tier raft group on startup" component=dispatch tier=019d6800-e08c-7192-9c58-1e92c8d70c7c leader=019d6800-b101-755b-abaa-b1a9d384da66
[node1] level=WARN msg="dispatch: failed to add member to tier raft group" component=dispatch tier=019d6800-e08c-7192-9c58-1e92c8d70c7c node=019d6800-babf-738a-a242-fbe6bc0ed302 error="node is not the leader"
```

node1 is trying to *add* node3 as a member of the cold tier raft group (`019d6800-e08c-7192-9c58-1e92c8d70c7c`). It fails with `node is not the leader` — only the raft leader can call `AddVoter`. So either:

1. node1 has stale state about who the cold tier raft leader is
2. The dispatcher's "reconcile tier raft group on startup" path runs from every node but only the leader's reconcile is meaningful
3. The membership reconciliation should be gated on `IsRaftLeader()` for that specific tier group

Looking at the recent commits on this branch:

- `761102f3 refactor: remove placement-leader-side tier Raft membership reconcil...`
- `ea7d51b7 feat: per-tier leader loop reconciles tier Raft membership on the active node`

These suggest the membership reconciliation path was being moved from "the placement leader does it" (which is ambiguous on every node) to "the per-tier raft leader does it via a leader loop". Symptom B might be a leftover dispatcher-side reconciliation that the refactor missed, OR a residual entry point that fires before the leader loop takes over.

## Why these are likely the same bug

Both symptoms point at "tier raft membership management has multiple uncoordinated entry points". The desynced snapshots (Symptom A) are likely the long-term consequence of every node trying to reconcile membership independently — each one writes its own view to its local snapshot, and they drift. The dispatcher warning (Symptom B) is the *immediate* visible signal of the same problem: a non-leader node attempting membership changes via the wrong code path.

If the per-tier leader loop (`raftgroup/leader_loop.go`, `orchestrator/tier_leader_manager.go`) is the *intended* single source of truth for membership reconciliation, then:

- The dispatcher's startup-reconcile path (the one logging Symptom B) should be removed or gated on `IsRaftLeader()`.
- The persisted snapshots (Symptom A) should converge once the leader loop runs on whatever node holds tier raft leadership at that moment.

## Investigation plan

1. Find the dispatcher code path that logs `dispatch: reconciling tier raft group on startup` and `dispatch: failed to add member to tier raft group`.
2. Check whether it should still exist after the `761102f3` refactor or whether it's a leftover.
3. Trace `tier_leader_manager.go` to see what membership reconciliation it does and when.
4. Determine whether a single leader-side reconciliation pass would converge the desynced snapshots, or whether snapshot persistence itself needs to be coordinated.
5. Add a regression test that brings up a 4-node cluster, restarts all nodes, and asserts that all nodes' snapshots for each tier raft group converge to the same membership within N seconds.

## Discovery context

Surfaced 2026-04-07 during cluster restart validation after fixing the silent-wedge family (`gastrolog-4rp6i`) and the empty-vault startup bug (`gastrolog-264pk`). With those fixes in place, the cluster no longer wedges or spams "vault not found" — but these two warnings still appear. They're noise rather than errors, but they indicate an architectural seam in tier raft membership management that was partially-but-not-fully closed by the recent leader-loop refactor (`ea7d51b7`, `761102f3`).

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Investigation result: already fixed by gastrolog-427mh merge

The two symptoms were investigated against the post-merge code and the fix is already in place. Tracing:

**Symptom B** (dispatcher trying to AddVoter from non-leader): the code path that emitted `dispatch: failed to add member to tier raft group` no longer exists in `dispatch.go`. The relevant section is at `backend/internal/app/dispatch.go:409-414`:

```go
// Tier Raft group membership is handled by the per-group leader loop
// (see raftgroup.LeaderLoop). The placement leader does not push
// membership changes — the tier Raft leader (whoever currently holds
// leadership in the group) does, from inside its leader epoch after
// raft.Barrier() returns. This avoids the divergence problem where the
// placement leader and the tier Raft leader live on different nodes.
```

This is exactly the architectural fix needed: membership management was moved from "every dispatcher tries it (non-deterministically)" to "the actual tier raft leader does it from inside its leader epoch (deterministically)". Refactor commit: `761102f3 refactor: remove placement-leader-side tier Raft membership reconcil...`

**Symptom A** (snapshot membership desync): the new `tier_leader_manager.reconcile` (`backend/internal/orchestrator/tier_leader_manager.go:131`) runs from inside the leader epoch, computes the desired-vs-current diff, applies it via `Raft.AddVoter` / `Raft.RemoveServer` with a per-call `tierMembershipChangeTimeout`, and bails cleanly on lost-leadership errors. Once leadership is established for a tier raft group, exactly one node performs the reconciliation, and all nodes' raft state machines apply the resulting `AddVoter`/`RemoveServer` log entries identically. Snapshots taken after this convergence will agree.

## Why the warnings appeared anyway

The running cluster's binary was built from `gastrolog-4rp6i` *before* the merge that brought 427mh's leader-loop architecture into the codebase. The cluster restarted at `21:21:11`; the merge happened at `21:35-21:37`. The binary in memory still has the old dispatcher path that emits these warnings.

## Resolution

No code changes required for this issue. After the user restarts the cluster on a binary built from the post-merge state, both warnings should vanish:

1. The dispatcher no longer attempts membership changes, so `dispatch: failed to add member` cannot fire.
2. Once the leader loop has run a clean reconciliation pass, the persisted raft snapshots on all nodes will reflect the same membership.

Status moved to `in_review` pending cluster-restart validation.

If after restart the warnings *still* appear, that's a real follow-up bug — possibly because the leader loop isn't actually running for one or more tier groups (e.g., `SetDesiredMembers` wasn't called, or the leader epoch isn't firing reconcile). I'd want to investigate that fresh rather than assume.

title: Tier raft snapshot install loops on 'no such file or directory' for ~10 min after restart
description:
After a cluster restart, one tier raft group enters a snapshot install retry loop that runs for ~10 minutes before self-healing. During the loop the cluster spams ~500 ERROR/WARN log entries about the same snapshot install repeatedly failing. Eventually the loop breaks when a fresh snapshot at a higher term is generated, and the cluster recovers cleanly.

## Symptom

After cluster-kill + cluster-run, one tier raft group's leader (node2 in the observed case, group `019d6800-e08c-7192-9c58-1e92c8d70c7c` = cold tier) attempts to install a snapshot on a lagging follower (node3). Each attempt completes the network transfer successfully but immediately fails to open the just-created local snapshot:

```
[node2] installing snapshot on ... id=4-871-1775592079898 size=16506
[node3] snapshot network transfer progress ... percent-complete=100.00%
[node3] copied to local snapshot bytes=16506
[node3] failed to restore snapshot error="failed to open snapshot 4-871-1775592104204:
         open data/node3/raft/groups/019d6800-e08c-7192-9c58-1e92c8d70c7c/snapshots/4-871-1775592104204/meta.json:
         no such file or directory"
[node2] failed to install snapshot ... (same error from RPC response)
[node2] failed to send snapshot to ... (same error from RPC response)
```

Note the snapshot ID timestamp on the receiver side (`...104204`) differs from the sent ID (`...079898`). The receiver creates a NEW local timestamp via `FileSnapshotStore.Create(...)`, copies the bytes successfully, calls `sink.Close()` (which logs "copied to local snapshot"), then tries to `snapshots.Open(sink.ID())` and fails.

## Trace through hashicorp/raft v1.7.3

`raft.go:1810 installSnapshot()` flow:

1. `sink, _ := r.snapshots.Create(...)` — creates `<groupDir>/snapshots/<term>-<index>-<msec>.tmp/`
2. `n, _ := io.Copy(sink, rpc.Reader)` — writes bytes to sink
3. `sink.Close()` — `file_snapshot.go:397` finalizes:
   - `s.finalize()` closes file handles
   - `s.writeMeta()` writes `meta.json` to the temp dir
   - `os.Rename(s.dir, newPath)` renames `<id>.tmp` → `<id>`
   - `parentFH.Sync()` fsyncs parent dir
   - `s.store.ReapSnapshots()` removes snapshots beyond retain count
4. `r.logger.Info("copied to local snapshot", "bytes", n)` — log fires here
5. `restoreFuture{ID: sink.ID()}` sent to `r.fsmMutateCh`
6. FSM goroutine (`fsm.go:188 restore()`) calls `r.snapshots.Open(req.ID)` — **fails here**

Between step 3 and step 6, the just-finalized snapshot directory disappears. Possible causes (need verification):

- **`ReapSnapshots()` race**: with retain=2, getSnapshots() could list ID-with-newer-timestamp BEFORE the rename is visible, miscount the directory, and reap the just-finalized snapshot. Unlikely but worth checking.
- **Concurrent local snapshot**: hashicorp/raft can take periodic local snapshots in the background. If a concurrent snapshot fires `ReapSnapshots()` between the receiving Close() and the Open() call, it might see an older retention list and delete the receiver's snapshot. Plausible.
- **Filesystem visibility**: the rename in Close() might not be visible to the Open() call in another goroutine on macOS. parentFH.Sync() should make it visible — but only if the Sync actually propagates.
- **multiraft transport snapshot transfer interleaving**: if the multiraft groupTransport is somehow causing the receiver to handle multiple concurrent install_snapshot operations for the same group, they could clobber each other.

## Recovery

The loop self-heals after ~10 minutes when:
1. A leader election or term bump causes a *new* snapshot at higher term/index to be generated on the leader
2. That new snapshot installs successfully (specific code path differs?)
3. The follower catches up
4. Reconcile loop fires and removes the orphaned chunks the follower retained during the broken window

In the observed instance:
- 22:01:43 — first failure (term 4, snapshot 4-871)
- 22:12:15 — first success (term 5, snapshot 5-1313)
- 22:13:00 — reconcile pass deletes ~26 orphaned chunks on node3
- 22:13:00+ — cluster healthy and quiet

## Why this is critical

- **10 minutes of cluster spam during every restart** is unacceptable visibility burden on the operator
- **The cluster's lagging-follower recovery is broken** for at least the term=N snapshot path
- **Followers can lose chunks**: during the 10-minute broken window, the follower can't catch up on retention deletes either, leaving stale local data the leader has already retired
- **It's intermittent** — appears related to startup state (only the first snapshot at term=N fails, not subsequent ones at term=N+1)

## Diagnostic data points

Verified empirically on `gastrolog-4rp6i` after merging `gastrolog-427mh` into main. Build state: `35ca91aa Merge main: bring in tier raft architectural work from 427mh`. 4-node cluster, hot/warm/cold tiers, replication-factor 4, voteless node4. Cluster restart at `22:01:42`, snapshot loop active 22:01:43 → 22:12:15.

On-disk state confirms the receiver IS eventually creating snapshots successfully (snapshots dir contains `5-1785-...` and `5-1848-...` after recovery).

## Investigation plan

1. **Reproduce in a unit test**: stand up two `raftgroup.Group`s with file-backed boltdb + FileSnapshotStore, force a snapshot install via the multiraft transport, assert it succeeds the FIRST time.
2. **Race detector**: run the cluster_failure tests with -race; look for concurrent access to FileSnapshotStore.
3. **Add diagnostic logging** in groupmanager.go around snapshot store creation to dump path layout at startup.
4. **Compare to config raft**: config raft uses the same `NewFileSnapshotStore` but lives at `data/<node>/raft/` (not `data/<node>/raft/groups/<groupID>/`). Does the config raft snapshot install loop happen too, or only tier raft?
5. **Bisect**: which 427mh commit (or pre-existing) introduced this? Was there a snapshot path change in the multiraft → raftgroup refactor?

## Discovery context

Surfaced 2026-04-07 immediately after merging `gastrolog-427mh` (tier raft architectural work) into main. Earlier in the session this branch's restart was clean (only the empty-vault startup bug and a brief retention cleanup tail). The merge brought in 27 commits of tier raft work; one of them likely changed the snapshot path layout or introduced the race. Worth a `git bisect main..HEAD` once the test reproduction is in place.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Reproduction narrowed: only on pre-merge data dir + post-merge binary

Confirmed via fresh `cluster-init` immediately after the symptom run:

| | Pre-merge data dir + post-merge binary | Fresh init + post-merge binary |
|---|---|---|
| Log lines after restart | 1126 | 171 |
| ERROR/WARN total | 198+ | 5 (benign startup elections) |
| Snapshot install loop | Yes (10 minutes) | None |
| Cluster healthy? | After ~10 min self-heal | Immediately |

The post-merge code does NOT reproduce the bug on a fresh data dir. It only reproduces when the data dir was written by a binary built before the gastrolog-427mh merge (cc2c99f9).

## Refined hypothesis: snapshot path relocation across the merge

The 427mh merge brought in (among others):

- `ad064c1c refactor: move domain types out of multiraft transport package`
- `e10eff20 refactor: move tier state machine from chunk/raftfsm to tier/raftfsm`
- `945c4633 refactor: decouple tier Raft group creation from chunk loading`
- The `internal/multiraft → internal/raftgroup` package rename (groupmanager.go renamed)

If the pre-merge code persisted tier raft state under `data/<node>/raft/multiraft/<groupID>/` (or similar path), and the post-merge code's `raftgroup.GroupManager` uses `data/<node>/raft/groups/<groupID>/`, then on restart:

1. Post-merge `NewFileSnapshotStore("data/<node>/raft/groups/<groupID>", 2, ...)` runs
2. The constructor calls `os.MkdirAll(<base>/snapshots, ...)` — creates an EMPTY snapshots subdir
3. Raft tries to read pre-existing state from local snapshots — finds none
4. Leader sends snapshot via InstallSnapshot RPC
5. Receiver's `Create()` succeeds (new path), `Close()` succeeds
6. Receiver's `snapshots.Open(sink.ID())` fails with "no such file or directory" because... TBD

Step 6 is still not fully explained by path relocation alone. If the snapshot was just successfully created at `<new-path>/snapshots/<id>/` and immediately Open is called for the same ID, it should find it. Unless something else under the same goroutine is `RemoveAll()`-ing the new path before Open runs.

## Possible second mechanism: stale state cleanup at startup

Maybe the post-merge raftgroup creation path has a "clean stale state" step that does `os.RemoveAll(<path>/snapshots)` to ensure a clean slate, but races with the receiver's `Create()` write. That would also explain the symptom: receiver creates a snapshot, the cleanup goroutine removes the parent dir, Open() fails.

Worth checking `groupmanager.go:CreateGroup` and any startup hooks for `RemoveAll` / cleanup operations on the snapshots directory.

## Fix priorities

1. **Detect incompatibility at startup** — when loading a tier raft group with pre-existing on-disk state from a different layout, log a clear error and either (a) refuse to start with a "needs migration" message, or (b) auto-migrate the on-disk paths.
2. **Eliminate the 10-minute spam loop** — even if the underlying state is incompatible, the snapshot install loop should give up after N attempts with a clear error rather than retrying forever.
3. **Long term: backward-compatible snapshot loading** — for production deployments that can't `cluster-init`, the post-merge code should be able to read pre-merge snapshots, or there should be a one-time migration step at startup.

## Reduced severity but still critical for prod

- **Local dev**: workaround = `cluster-init` after major upgrades. Acceptable for development.
- **Production**: this is a real upgrade-time data-loss risk. Cluster operators upgrading across this commit boundary will hit the spam loop on first restart. They might either (a) wait it out and self-recover, OR (b) `cluster-init` and lose data.

Issue stays at priority 0 (critical) because of the production upgrade implication.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
## Investigation: code-level diffs across the 427mh merge eliminate the easy hypotheses

Compared the pre-merge (d425015d^) and post-merge (cc2c99f9) state of every
code path that touches tier raft snapshots / boltdb / paths. Findings:

### Identical (NOT the cause)

- **`hraft.NewFileSnapshotStore(groupDir, 2, io.Discard)`** — same call site,
  same args, same retain count, same logger discard
- **`raftboltdb.New(raftboltdb.Options{Path: filepath.Join(groupDir, "raft.db")})`**
  — same boltdb path
- **`groupDir := filepath.Join(m.baseDir, cfg.GroupID)`** — same on-disk layout
- **`m.baseDir = "<home>/raft/groups/"`** — same in pre and post merge
  (verified `git show ad064c1c^:backend/internal/multiraft/groupmanager.go`)
- **`newRaftConfig`** — same SnapshotThreshold (4), SnapshotInterval (30s),
  TrailingLogs (64), default config
- **FSM command byte format** — `38f3b210` and `e10eff20` were renames only,
  100% byte-identical command encoding (decodeSnapshot, encodeEntry, etc.)
- **multiraft transport InstallSnapshot handler** — last touched at
  `9caf902a` which is BEFORE the 427mh merge; transport is unchanged

### Behavioural change (suspected but probably not the cause)

`a9d0bf86 refactor: rename GroupConfig.Bootstrap → SeedMembers, use symmetric seeding`
changed how raft groups are seeded:

- **Pre-merge**: only the placement leader called `BootstrapCluster`. Other
  nodes had empty boltdb logs and joined via raft replication (AppendEntries
  from the leader).
- **Post-merge**: all assigned nodes call `seedGroup` which calls
  `BootstrapCluster` if `existing.Configuration().Servers` is empty.

This is supposed to be backward-compatible: on a node with existing pre-merge
state, `seedGroup` checks `existing.Configuration().Servers > 0` and skips
the BootstrapCluster call. Verified by reading the post-merge `seedGroup` at
`backend/internal/raftgroup/groupmanager.go:375`.

But there's a subtle pre-merge edge case: pre-merge follower nodes had
**empty boltdb logs at the moment of CreateGroup**. Their configuration was
learned later via AppendEntries replication from the bootstrap node. If the
post-merge code re-runs CreateGroup on a node whose boltdb log was populated
ONLY via replication (not via local bootstrap), the existing log might
behave differently than the post-merge code expects.

### What I haven't been able to verify without a reproducer

- Whether the post-merge `seedGroup` actually skips BootstrapCluster on a
  node whose log was populated via pre-merge replication
- Whether something during startup is calling `os.RemoveAll` on the snapshot
  directory between sink.Close() and snapshots.Open()
- Whether the issue is in `hraft.Raft.installSnapshot` itself when it
  receives a snapshot at a term that conflicts with an in-progress
  membership reconciliation by the new `tier_leader_manager` (which runs on
  the leader and could be racing with snapshot install on the follower)

### Reproducer infrastructure needed

To make further progress this needs:

1. A reliable reproducer — either:
   - A focused integration test that builds two binaries (pre-merge and
     post-merge) via build tags, runs one to populate state, then loads it
     with the other and asserts no snapshot install loop
   - Or a `git bisect` driven by the same pattern, checking out each commit
     in `cc2c99f9..d425015d` and running the upgrade scenario
2. A way to attach a debugger or strace to the snapshot install path on the
   receiver to capture the exact moment the directory disappears

Neither is small work — both are multi-hour investigations on their own.

### Pragmatic mitigation options (not fixes)

Since the cluster self-heals after ~10 minutes by generating a fresh snapshot
at a higher term, the operational impact is "10 minutes of log spam after
upgrade" rather than "permanent data loss". Workarounds:

1. **Document the upgrade path**: in release notes, instruct operators to
   either (a) wait out the 10-minute self-heal, or (b) `cluster-init` on a
   fresh data dir (loses chunks not yet replicated)
2. **Cap snapshot install retries** — needs upstream changes to hraft, not
   feasible from our wrappers without forking
3. **Detect the specific symptom and fire an alert** — wrap the FileSnapshotStore
   to log a single clear "snapshot install repeatedly failing for tier X"
   alert after N retries instead of relying on raw raft logs

### Status

Marking as `blocked` pending reproducer infrastructure. The cluster IS
operationally fine on fresh state (verified empirically); this is purely
an upgrade-path bug. Not blocking ongoing dev work.

title: Index format loaders use os.ReadFile, slurping entire index files into heap
description:
Ten production index format loaders across 5 packages all use `os.ReadFile`
to slurp entire index files into heap-allocated `[]byte`, violating the
"use mmap whenever possible" rule from the project's memory note.

## Affected sites

| File | Function | Decoder reads |
|---|---|---|
| `backend/internal/index/file/tsidx/format.go:208` | `LoadIngestIndex` | `[]Entry{TS, Pos}` (int64+uint32) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/tsidx/format.go:218` | `LoadSourceIndex` | `[]Entry{TS, Pos}` |
| `backend/internal/index/file/attr/format.go:112` | `LoadKeyIndex` | `[]AttrKeyIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/attr/format.go:121` | `LoadValueIndex` | `[]AttrValueIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/attr/format.go:130` | `LoadKVIndex` | `[]AttrKVIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/json/format.go:310` | `LoadIndex` | `[]JSONPathIndexEntry, []JSONPVIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/kv/format.go:188` | `LoadKeyIndex` | `[]KVKeyIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/kv/format.go:197` | `LoadValueIndex` | `[]KVValueIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/kv/format.go:206` | `LoadKVIndex` | `[]KVIndexEntry` (likely strings) |
| `backend/internal/index/file/token/format.go:104` | `LoadIndex` | `[]TokenIndexEntry` (likely strings) |

All follow the same pattern:

```go
func LoadXxxIndex(dir string, chunkID chunk.ChunkID) ([]Entry, error) {
    path := XxxIndexPath(dir, chunkID)
    data, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Clean(path))  // <-- slurps entire file
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    return decodeXxxIndex(data, ...)
}
```

## Why this matters

These index files are sealed/immutable once the chunk is sealed, so they're
prime mmap candidates. For each chunk, the loader allocates a heap `[]byte`
the size of the entire file. A query that reads N chunks allocates N × index
size of heap memory just for the raw bytes, on top of the decoded entry
slices. Index files for chunks with many records can be hundreds of KB or
MB-sized — that's serious GC pressure during query load.

The pattern was explicitly noted in MEMORY.md as a project-wide rule:

> NEVER use `os.ReadFile` to slurp entire files into heap memory. Use mmap
> for reads (especially for sealed/immutable data like chunk files and
> indexes) or stream in fixed-size chunks. Heap-allocated file reads cause
> massive GC pressure and RSS bloat.

## Fix complexity tiers

Some loaders are easier to fix than others depending on whether the decoder
retains references to the raw bytes:

**Tier 1 — easy**: decoders that copy primitive values out via
`binary.LittleEndian.Uint64(data[a:b])` etc. — no reference to the mmap
region survives the decode call. Safe to `mmap → decode → munmap`
immediately. `tsidx` is in this tier.

**Tier 2 — needs careful handling**: decoders that produce string fields
via zero-copy slicing of the data buffer. The returned entries would hold
references to the (now-released) mmap region. Two options:
  a. Copy strings during decode (allocates heap for the strings, but
     releases the much larger raw buffer)
  b. Keep the mmap alive for the entry lifetime (caller must call a
     Close method to release the mmap)

Option (a) is simpler. Option (b) is more memory-efficient but invasive.
Most likely the right choice is (a) for attr/kv/json/token loaders.

## Test coverage required

- Existing index decode tests should continue to pass after the fix
- New test: load an index via mmap, munmap, and verify the returned
  entries are still valid (catches accidental zero-copy slicing)
- Race-detector run on parallel loads of the same chunk index

## Discovery context

Found 2026-04-08 during a "look for known anti-patterns" sweep of the
codebase, after closing gastrolog-2mnv8 (the cursor mmap race) and
gastrolog-asg4l (the cloud badge). The codebase already has the right
mmap+stat-from-fd pattern in `chunk/file/record_reader.go:openDataFile`
(post the gastrolog-2mnv8 fix); the index loaders should match.

title: Fluent forward ingester gunzip is unbounded (gzip bomb / DoS)
description:
The Fluent Forward ingester reads a msgpack-encoded bin payload from the
network and, if marked as compressed, calls an unbounded gunzip helper:

```go
// backend/internal/ingester/fluentfwd/ingester.go:191
if isCompressed(option) {
    binData, err = gunzip(binData)
    ...
}
```

```go
// backend/internal/ingester/fluentfwd/ingester.go:468
func gunzip(data []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    r, err := gzip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data))
    ...
    return io.ReadAll(r)  // <-- unbounded
}
```

`io.ReadAll(r)` on a gzip stream has no upper bound. A small attacker-
controlled compressed payload can decompress to gigabytes. Combined with
the msgpack bin format's 4 GiB max-size header, an attacker who can reach
the fluent-forward port can:

1. Send a ~1 KiB gzipped payload that decompresses to several GiB
2. Cause a single goroutine to allocate the entire decompressed size on
   the heap
3. With multiple connections, multiply the attack across goroutines

The Go runtime will eventually OOM or trigger excessive GC pressure.

## Threat model

Fluent Forward is typically used as an internal log-shipping protocol
between trusted nodes (forwarder → aggregator). The threat model includes:

- **Trusted client misconfigured**: a legitimate forwarder configures
  compression with a large batch size and an unusual data shape that
  produces a high compression ratio. Memory spike, no malice. Realistic.
- **Compromised forwarder**: an attacker who has compromised one log
  source on the network can send crafted gzip bombs to the gastrolog
  ingester to OOM it. Plausible if the network has any
  internet-facing forwarders.
- **Hostile network**: if the fluent-forward port is exposed (even
  unintentionally), any internet attacker can send gzip bombs.
  Worst case.

Even for the "trusted internal" case, defensive bounds are good practice.

## Fix

Two complementary bounds:

1. **Cap the decompressed output**. Use `io.LimitReader` wrapping the
   gzip reader, with a reasonable max — say 100 MiB per packed-forward
   batch. If more than 100 MiB is received, return an error and drop the
   batch with a logged warning.

2. **Cap the input** (defense in depth). Reject any msgpack bin payload
   larger than, say, 10 MiB BEFORE decompression. Combined with the
   100:1 gzip ratio cap from #1, this gives a hard 100 MiB ceiling.

```go
const maxDecompressedBytes = 100 << 20 // 100 MiB

func gunzip(data []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    r, err := gzip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data))
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer func() { _ = r.Close() }()

    limited := io.LimitReader(r, maxDecompressedBytes+1)
    out, err := io.ReadAll(limited)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if int64(len(out)) > maxDecompressedBytes {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("fluentfwd: decompressed payload exceeds %d bytes", maxDecompressedBytes)
    }
    return out, nil
}
```

(The `+1` trick on the LimitReader is so we can distinguish "exactly at
the limit" from "exceeded the limit".)

## Test coverage required

- Unit test: gzip a 200 MiB byte slice, attempt to decode, assert error
- Unit test: gzip a 50 MiB byte slice, decode, assert success and
  correct content
- Unit test: malformed gzip → error, no panic, no hang
- Integration test: send a small gzip-bomb payload to a running
  fluentfwd ingester, assert it rejects with logged warning rather
  than OOMing

## Discovery context

Found 2026-04-08 during a "look for unfiled bugs" sweep of `io.ReadAll`
usage in production code paths. The other `io.ReadAll` sites in the ingester
package (HTTP and OTLP) all use `io.LimitReader` with a 10 MiB cap; only
fluentfwd is missing the equivalent bound.

Unrelated note: the same package's msgpack `dec.DecodeBytes()` at line 179
should ALSO have a bound on the bin size before it ever reaches gunzip.
The msgpack library may or may not enforce this; worth verifying.

title: Cloud storage operations use context.Background, no timeouts
description:
All cloud storage operations in chunk/file/manager.go pass
`context.Background()` to the CloudStore interface methods, which means:

1. No request-scoped timeout — a slow or unresponsive S3 can block the
   caller indefinitely
2. No cancellation on shutdown — the operation can't be interrupted
3. No deadline propagation from the caller's context

Affected call sites in `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go`:

| Line | Operation | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| 2083 | `CloudStore.DownloadRange` (`downloadTSIndex`) | query path |
| 2290 | `CloudStore.Delete` | chunk manager mu held |
| 2520 | `CloudStore.Download` (`downloadAndCacheCursor`) | query path (1st access) |
| 2853 | `CloudStore.Head` (`uploadToCloud` precheck) | post-seal pipeline |
| 2888 | `CloudStore.Upload` (`uploadToCloud`) | post-seal pipeline |
| 2961 | `CloudStore.DownloadRange` (`adoptCloudBlob`) | post-seal pipeline |
| 3109 | `CloudStore.Head` (`backfillTSOffsets`) | startup |
| 3113 | `CloudStore.DownloadRange` (`backfillTSOffsets`) | startup |
| 3147 | `CloudStore.List` (`loadCloudChunksFromStore`) | startup |

## Priority subset: the post-seal pipeline path

The highest-impact calls are the three in `uploadToCloud` and `adoptCloudBlob`:

```go
existing, err := m.cfg.CloudStore.Head(context.Background(), key)           // 2853
... m.cfg.CloudStore.Upload(context.Background(), key, ..., ...)            // 2888-2890
tocBuf, err := m.cfg.CloudStore.DownloadRange(context.Background(), ...)    // 2961
```

These run from `PostSealProcess`, which is called inline after each chunk
seal. If S3 is slow or unreachable, the post-seal pipeline backs up. With
chatterbox-rate ingestion (~1 chunk/second), a 30-second S3 stall means
30 queued post-seal work items. With a 5-minute S3 outage, it's a
significant pipeline stall.

The S3 client SDK has its own retry logic (we saw "exceeded maximum number
of attempts, 3" in the gastrolog-280gy test), but retries COMPOUND the
delay rather than cap it. A well-configured timeout at the call site would
bound the total wait.

## Fix (priority subset)

Add explicit per-call timeouts at the uploadToCloud/adoptCloudBlob call
sites. The tunings below are generous enough for slow networks and
realistic blob sizes:

- `Head` (metadata check, tiny roundtrip): **10 seconds**
- `DownloadRange` for TOC (48 bytes): **10 seconds**
- `Upload` for a chunk blob (up to ~10 MiB typical): **60 seconds**
- `Delete` for a chunk blob: **15 seconds**

All wrapped at the call site via `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx,
X); defer cancel()`.

## Follow-up work (separate commits)

The query-path and startup sites (downloadTSIndex, downloadAndCacheCursor,
backfillTSOffsets, loadCloudChunksFromStore) should propagate the caller's
context rather than use Background:

- Query path ops should inherit the query's request context so that a
  cancelled query actually cancels its cloud reads
- Startup ops should use the app's shutdown context so graceful shutdown
  can abort them

These are larger refactors because they require plumbing context through
the chunk manager interface. Not blocking this fix.

## Test coverage required

- Unit test: mock a CloudStore that blocks forever on Upload; call
  uploadToCloud; assert it returns with a timeout error within the
  configured window
- Same for Head, DownloadRange, Delete
- Integration: stop MinIO, attempt a seal+upload, assert the post-seal
  pipeline doesn't block for more than the upload timeout

## Discovery context

Found 2026-04-08 during a sweep for `context.Background()` usage in
production code, after fixing gastrolog-3rvws (index mmap) and
gastrolog-e3qug (gzip bomb). Pattern recognition: we already fixed the
same class of bug for the cluster forwarders (gastrolog-4rp6i per-call
timeouts). The cloud storage ops are the same shape of bug in a
different layer.

title: transitionChunk marks chunks unreadable on transient network errors
description:
In `backend/internal/orchestrator/transition.go:71`, `markUnreadable(id, streamErr)`
is called for ANY error from the cross-tier stream, including transient
network / timeout errors that have nothing to do with the source chunk
being readable:

```go
streamErr = r.orch.transferrer.StreamToTier(ctx, ..., chunk.CursorIterator(cursor))
...
if streamErr != nil {
    r.logger.Error("transition: stream failed", ...)
    r.markUnreadable(id, streamErr)   // <-- wrong for transient errors
    return
}
```

## Why this is wrong

`markUnreadable` adds the chunk to a per-runner in-memory map
(`retention.go:462`). The runner is cached per (tier, storage) in
`o.retention[key]` for the regular retention sweep path, so the mark
persists for the lifetime of the orchestrator process. Chunks marked
unreadable:

1. Are skipped on all subsequent retention sweeps for this node
2. Stay on disk until age-based retention deletes them (data lost
   if the transition never happens)
3. Fire an alert via `alert.Set("chunk-unreadable:<id>")`

Transient destination errors that can trigger this:

- Per-call timeout on the cluster forwarder (`gastrolog-4rp6i`) —
  the stream hits its 15-second cap against a SIGSTOPped peer
- Per-call timeout on cloud storage ops (`gastrolog-21xs8`) — if the
  transition goes through a cloud tier and S3 is slow
- gRPC `client connection is closing` race (`0365fe8c` workaround) —
  an unrelated goroutine's Invalidate() closed the conn mid-RPC
- Network blip, peer restart, `Unavailable` from a stopped follower

Every one of these would permanently retire a chunk from this node's
transition pipeline based on a transient blip that had nothing to do
with whether the chunk is actually readable.

## What "unreadable" SHOULD mean

The `OpenCursor` path at `transition.go:48` correctly marks unreadable
when the cursor open itself fails (ErrChunkSuspect is handled separately
as a special case). Cursor open failures genuinely mean the chunk is
unreadable — the file is missing, corrupt header, missing attr dict,
etc. That's the right place to mark unreadable.

The stream error path is different: the cursor DID open, and the
stream might fail for network reasons, peer reasons, or iterator
errors. Only the iterator-error subset should count as "chunk
unreadable" — and even that is questionable, because the iterator
could fail due to a transient file-system issue (unmounted disk
that comes back, etc.).

## Fix

Remove the `markUnreadable` call from the stream error path. If a
chunk is genuinely unreadable, the next retention sweep will try
again, hit the SAME error path, and eventually — if it's really
broken — the cursor.Next iterator errors will propagate. But for
transient errors, retrying is the right behavior.

A defensible compromise: distinguish between "source-side" errors
(cursor.Next / iterator) and "destination-side" errors (network,
gRPC, peer) by wrapping iterator errors in a sentinel at the
transferrer layer, then checking `errors.Is` in transitionChunk.
That keeps the safety net for genuinely corrupt chunks while
allowing transient errors to retry.

## Test coverage required

- Unit test: transitionChunk with a fake transferrer that returns
  a transient network error → chunk NOT marked unreadable, can
  be retried
- Unit test: transitionChunk with a fake transferrer that returns
  a source-side iterator error → chunk IS marked unreadable (if
  we keep the source-side subset logic)
- Regression: replay the scenario that originally bit us in
  gastrolog-4rp6i — SIGSTOP a peer mid-transition, verify chunks
  are not permanently retired

## Discovery context

Noted in a comment on gastrolog-4rp6i earlier in the session during
the silent SIGSTOP wedge investigation. Splitting it out as its own
issue now during the "find unfiled bugs" sweep because it's a
separate bug with a different fix.

title: HeaderBar cluster node list is unsorted
description:
HeaderBar.tsx renders the cluster-status tooltip node list directly from cluster?.nodes without sorting. The order comes from whatever order the backend returned and can change between polls, which violates the MANDATORY 'sort all user-facing lists' rule in CLAUDE.md.

Fix: apply .toSorted() at the hook-destructure site so all downstream StatPill tooltips render in stable alphabetical order.

Found during a sweep audit for sorted-list rule violations across the frontend. Only real violation found — other suspicious sites (InspectorDialog.tsx node list) were already sorted with a local-node-first ordering policy.

title: RebuildMissingIndexes spams cloud-backed chunks at startup
description:
On startup, RebuildMissingIndexes() in orchestrator/lifecycle.go iterates every sealed chunk and calls IndexesComplete(id). For cloud-backed chunks, this is guaranteed to return false because uploadToCloud() in chunk/file/manager.go does os.RemoveAll(chunkDir(id)) — every local file (raw, attr, idx, AND all 10 index files) is gone after a successful upload.

## Cause

chunk/file/manager.go:608 List() returns BOTH local and cloud-backed chunks. After cloud upload, the chunk is moved from m.metas → m.cloudIdx, marked CloudBacked: true, Sealed: true, and the local chunk dir is removed at line 2941. The chunk still appears in cm.List() via the cloudListCache merge.

orchestrator/lifecycle.go:336-353 rebuildTierIndexes guards against !meta.Sealed but does NOT guard against meta.CloudBacked. So:

1. Chunk gets ingested, post-seal pipeline builds 10 index files, uploads to cloud, deletes local dir.
2. Chunk is still in List() with Sealed=true, CloudBacked=true, no local files anywhere.
3. On restart, rebuildTierIndexes loops over the chunk, IndexesComplete() returns false (10 os.Stat calls all return ENOENT), 'rebuilding missing indexes' is logged, BuildIndexes is scheduled.
4. BuildIndexes fires, tries to open source chunk data → ENOENT (data file was deleted on upload too), build fails or no-ops.
5. Repeat for every cloud-backed chunk on the node.

## Symptoms

User observed 'a million rebuilding missing indexes messages from node4 on restart'. Node4 is the voteless node in a 4-node cluster with hot/warm/cold tiers; cold tier is cloud-backed. Every cloud chunk on every node will trigger this — but is more visible on quieter nodes.

## Why this is wasteful

- Log spam: one INFO line per cloud chunk + N WARN lines per failed indexer.
- Scheduler slots: each chunk gets a queued RunOnce job that's pure waste.
- Filesystem syscalls: 10 os.Stat + 10 glob calls per cloud chunk during the rebuild scan.
- Hides legitimate index rebuild signals among the noise.

## Fix

Add CloudBacked guard to rebuildTierIndexes:

  if !meta.Sealed || meta.CloudBacked {
      continue
  }

Cloud chunks don't have local indexes by design — their queries go through the cloud-aware OpenCursor → openCloudCursor path, not through the local index manager. There's nothing to rebuild.

title: Cluster shutdown: drain components in order, no timeouts as the primary mechanism
description:
Today's shutdown produces ~184 lines of WARN/ERROR spam (~75% of the entire shutdown trail) and two of the four nodes take exactly 5 seconds longer than the others to terminate, because the gRPC server's GracefulStop fallback timeout fires. Both symptoms have the same root cause: the shutdown sequence relies on timeouts rather than draining components in a deliberate order.

Per project principle: 'we do it properly. shutdowns should be graceful and predictable, and not rely on timeouts as the first step.'

## Current symptoms (observed 2026-04-08, 4-node cluster with chatterbox steady-state ingest)

| Phase | Lines | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 'replication: failed to forward record to follower' x 127 | 70% of spam | fireAndForgetRemote keeps fanning out new ingest records to peers that are dead/dying during the orchestrator shutdown window |
| 'failed to make requestVote RPC' x 28 + 'Election timeout' x 8 + 'entering candidate state' x 14 | 27% | tier raft groups try to elect a new leader against unreachable peers during the 5-second teardown window |
| 'chunk metadata announce failed (raft is already shutdown)' x 3 | <2% | orchestrator background goroutines fire apply-to-Raft after the local raft instance has been shut down |
| 'failed to pipeline appendEntries' x 3 | <2% | multiraft transport sees peer EOFs |

Time anomaly: node4 takes 5.008s, node3 takes 5.688s, node2 finishes in 62ms, node1 in 2ms. The 5-second figure exactly matches the GracefulStop fallback in cluster/cluster.go:466. The gRPC server is waiting for active server-side handlers to drain, and they don't drain — most likely because they're blocked in unary forwarder calls to dead peers (also 5-second timeout — not a coincidence).

## Root principle the fix must follow

**Drain, don't timeout.** Every shutdown step must block on a real 'I'm done' signal (channel close, sync.WaitGroup, raft future), not on a wall-clock deadline. Timeouts may exist as outer-level safety nets (e.g. the multirun script) but must NEVER be the primary mechanism that lets a step proceed.

## Required sequence

1. **Signal phase change**. A single atomic ShutdownPhase (Running -> Stopping -> Stopped) visible to all components.
2. **Ingester drain**. Cancel each ingester's context, then wait for the ingester goroutines to exit. No new records enter the orchestrator after this point.
3. **Inbound RPC drain**. A gRPC interceptor returns Unavailable for any NEW request once Phase >= Stopping. Existing handlers keep running until they finish naturally. cluster.Server.Stop() waits on a sync.WaitGroup of active handlers, not a 5-second timer.
