- Any FSM or raft-level changes (EventID is purely record-tier metadata)
- Cross-node dedup strategy beyond "EventID is now unique"

title: Stale ingester alive state persists after crash or config edit while down
description:
## Problem

`SetIngesterAlive(id, nodeID, true)` is written to the Raft-replicated store whenever `runIngester` starts a local ingester, and `false` when it exits via the graceful path. Two cases leave a stale `true` behind:

1. Process crashes / SIGKILL / power loss — `runIngester` never reaches the `setIngesterAlive(false)` line.
2. Config edited while node is down — operator removes this node from the ingester's `NodeIDs`. On reboot, `applyIngester` / `handleIngesterPut` silently decline to run it and never touch the alive state. The pre-crash `true` persists in Raft.

Symptom: UI `IngesterCard` badge shows `3/4 alive` when only 3 nodes are actually running, because the fourth node's stale `true` inflates the count.

## Fix

At every point where a node decides NOT to run an ingester it knows about, proactively `SetIngesterAlive(id, localNode, false)`. Idempotent — no-op when already false, corrects the stale-true after crash or down-time config edit.

Decision sites:
- `orchestrator.applyIngester` ([factory.go](backend/internal/orchestrator/factory.go)) — boot path, early returns when this node isn't selected or isn't the singleton assignee.
- `configDispatcher.handleIngesterPut` ([dispatch.go](backend/internal/app/dispatch.go)) — FSM notification path, early returns via `!shouldRunIngester`.
- `configDispatcher.handleIngesterAssignment` ([dispatch.go](backend/internal/app/dispatch.go)) — singleton reassignment path, already calls `RemoveIngester` which covers the running case but not the "never started locally" case.

## Tests

- Unit: `setIngesterAlive(false)` is called when `shouldRunIngester` returns false and the ingester isn't running locally.
- Unit: `setIngesterAlive(false)` is called at boot for configured ingesters this node doesn't run.

## Out of scope

No config schema changes, no Raft command changes — just extra `SetIngesterAlive` writes on paths that previously did nothing.

title: Split PutSettings into one RPC per settings page
description:
PutSettings is the single RPC behind every "server settings" save in
the UI. Entity pages (Vaults, Tiers, Ingesters, Users, Nodes,
Certificates, Storage, Filters, Rotation/Retention Policies, Routes)
each already have their own RPCs — this issue brings the remaining
four UI surfaces in line with that pattern.

Current PutSettings callers:
- Cluster/Service settings page (Auth, TLS, Scheduler, Query, Cluster)
- Lookups page (Http, Csv, Json, Yaml, Mmdb, Static)
- MaxMind card on the Files page
- Setup wizard

All four emit a single coarse notification key ("server") so
dispatcher handlers can't tell what actually changed. This surfaced in
gastrolog-3y4b3: every lookup save triggered a full scheduler
rebuild, which caused gocron Shutdown timeouts under load.

Split into one RPC per page:
- PutServiceSettings  — Auth, TLS, Scheduler, Query, Cluster
- PutLookupSettings   — Http, Csv, Json, Yaml, Mmdb, Static
- PutMaxMindSettings  — MaxMind auto-download config
- PutSetupSettings    — (or fold into the above; decide in impl)

Each RPC:
- Validates only its subsystem.
- Emits a dedicated notification key — dispatcher handlers subscribe
  to their own key, no more fan-out.
- Maps to the save mutation of exactly one settings page.

Scope: proto, backend handlers, dispatcher, frontend hooks, UI call
sites, tests. Single atomic change per the "rename through the entire
stack" rule. Likely audit to find any page I missed in the initial
enumeration.
close_reason: Implemented and verified: PutServiceSettings, PutLookupSettings, PutMaxMindSettings, PutSetupSettings with per-subsystem validation and notify keys; proto/backend/dispatcher/frontend/tests updated. Residual client ergonomics (empty mutation bodies, refetch/flicker) tracked in gastrolog-1bkcg.

title: Remove /metrics Prometheus endpoint
description:
The /metrics endpoint in server/metrics.go exists to serve Prometheus
scrapers, but nothing in the gastrolog stack consumes it: the UI reads
from the internal PeerState / StatsCollector aggregation pipeline, not
from Prometheus. The endpoint also serves only the local node's view,
which is a cluster-first violation — scraping node A and node B give
different answers for metrics that conceptually belong to the whole
cluster.

Rather than fix the aggregation (separate proposal), remove the
endpoint entirely. If external Prometheus scraping becomes a demand
later, it can be re-added with cluster-first semantics from the start.

Scope:
- Delete server/metrics.go (the writer + providers).
- Unwire registerMetrics and any mux.HandleFunc("/metrics", …) hookups.
- Remove BroadcastMetricsProvider and PeerReceivedAtProvider interfaces
  if they have no other consumers.
- Remove the Broadcaster.MetricsSnapshot() method (and the sent/errored
  in-memory maps) if nothing else reads them.
- Update docs or help topics mentioning /metrics.
- Tests: remove /metrics-specific tests; keep the rest.

~270 LOC removal plus dependency sweep.

title: Retention-evicted cloud chunks flood logs AND UI alert panel
description:
When chunks get evicted from the last (cloud) tier, the logs flood
with paired WARN lines per evicted chunk:

  chunk-manager: "cache: download-and-cache failed, falling back to
    range requests" error="blob not found: …/<chunk>.glcb"
  orchestrator:  "reconcile: chunk not found, marking suspect"

These also land in the UI alert/log panel, drowning out every other
message during a retention sweep. Dozens of warnings per second for
every chunk retention just evicted.

Root cause (suspected):
- Retention on the cloud tier deletes the blob.
- A reconcile / cache-warm sweep still holds a reference to the
  (now-deleted) chunk — either the local cloud index entry outlives
  the blob delete, or the sweep snapshotted the index before the
  deletes fired.
- The sweep attempts to download, gets "blob not found", falls back
  to range requests (which also fail), emits both warnings, and marks
  suspect.

None of this is wrong per se — a just-evicted chunk IS missing and
the system correctly notices. But:
- A chunk WE just deleted via our own retention isn't "suspect".
- WARN-level logging of a normal lifecycle event is wrong — should be
  Debug at most.
- The UI alert/log panel surfaces these as if they were real
  incidents, which hides real incidents.

Work:
- Suppress cache-download-and-cache WARN when the chunk has a recent
  delete / tombstone. Debug-log it.
- Reconcile: distinguish "retention just evicted it" from "should
  exist but doesn't". Only the latter warrants a suspect mark AND a
  WARN.
- Ideally the local index drop happens atomically with (or before)
  the blob delete so the sweep doesn't observe the stale reference.

Affects:
- backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go (cache code path)
- backend/internal/orchestrator/*.go (reconcile sweep)

Reproducer: multi-node cloud-backed tier with short retention; watch
server logs + UI alert/log panel during the first retention sweep
after eviction threshold.

title: Stale placement view: RPCs sent to nodes that no longer own the vault/tier
description:
A node's cached view of "which peers host which vault/tier" drifts from
reality, so it forwards RPCs and replication work to peers that have
already disclaimed ownership. The peer correctly returns "vault not
found" / "tier not found in vault", but the calling node treats it as
an error and floods the logs (and UI alert panel).

Observed warnings, all targeting the same peer and vault:

  vault-server:  "ListChunks: remote node failed"
    error="forward list chunks to <peer>:
      rpc error: code = Internal desc = list chunks: vault not found"

  orchestrator:  "replication: sealed chunk failed"
    error="follower rejected command: import failed:
      vault not found: tier <tier> in vault <vault>"

Root cause (suspected): the calling node's placement resolver still
lists the peer as an owner (via cached Raft-config, stale NodeStats, or
a local map that outlives the placement change) after the peer's
handleTierPut / handleVaultDeleted removed the local registration.

Work:
- Audit the placement-lookup call sites feeding these RPCs:
  - ListChunks forwarder (backend/internal/server/*.go, vault-server)
  - Sealed-chunk replicator (backend/internal/orchestrator/replication.go)
- Ensure they read the current tier placements (not a snapshot) or
  subscribe to placement-change notifications and drop stale targets.
- Translate "vault/tier not found" responses from the peer into a
  benign signal: skip / log at Debug and request a placement refresh.
  Don't treat it as a remote failure.

Affects:
- backend/internal/server/ (vault-server forward path)
- backend/internal/orchestrator/replication.go
- wherever placement is resolved for those paths

Reproducer: bring up a multi-node cluster, assign a vault to a subset
of nodes, remove the vault from one of those nodes, observe log
warnings as the remaining nodes still RPC to the removed one.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Concrete symptom: in a 4-node cluster with RF=4, every chunk in every tier shows only 3 replicas. One specific peer (node that keeps returning 'vault not found') is consistently missing from the replica set. Confirms the calling node's placement view drifted — it lists the peer as a target but the peer has disclaimed ownership.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Operator hypothesis: the 'missing one replica' display in the vault/tier view may be the inspector counting peer-only (excluding the currently-viewed node from its own replica count), in which case the N-1 number is a display bug not a real replica gap. Worth verifying against the placement code before treating the count as evidence of 5z607 itself; the 'vault not found' RPC failures remain the authoritative signal of stale placement.

title: Chunk inspector: per-node badges showing replica status for each replica target
description:
The chunk detail pane currently renders the replica set as a comma-
separated string: "3/4  node-1, node-4, node-3, node-2". You can't tell
which specific node is missing the replica.

Replace with per-node badges, one per replica target, each colored by
its individual replica status:

- info (green) — this node has the replica and is live
- warn (yellow) — this node is live but missing the replica (catching
                  up / transient)
- error (red)  — this node is not live (dead / disclaimed ownership)

Hovering shows the node ID / name. At a glance the operator sees
exactly which node is degraded, matching the per-entry visual grain
of the ingester inspector.

Proposed placement: the same row that today prints the plain list —
replace the text with a horizontal badge strip. Total count (3/4)
can stay as a small prefix or drop it entirely since the colored
strip makes the count obvious.

Affects:
- frontend chunk detail view in the inspector
- reuses the Badge component (info/warn/error variants)

Non-goals: no backend change — the data already flows via ListChunks
(replica set) + NodeStats live-peer list.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Concrete inconsistency to resolve during this work: observed REPLICAS reading '5/4  node-1, node-4, node-3, node-2' — four named nodes but count says five. Under the 1:1:1 tier/node/storage rule, impossible. Either the count source (probably the same chunk meta field the list reads) is double-counting or the list source dedupes while the tally doesn't. Fold the fix into the badge rework: same render pass should derive both from a single deduped set of (node, state) pairs, so the count falls out of .length.

title: GLID shortener should middle-ellipsize to fit available width, not fixed char counts
description:
Today's GLID shortener collapses IDs to a fixed "prefix…suffix"
pattern with hardcoded character widths. Output in the same list is
inconsistent ("06ep…xxxxx" vs "0…xxxxx") AND unrelated to how much
room the container actually has: wide column wastes it on nothing,
narrow column truncates too hard.

The right approach is width-driven:
- Measure the available container width (ResizeObserver on the
  parent, or CSS container queries).
- Measure the font's glyph widths (Canvas 2D context.measureText on
  the computed font, or a cached fractional char-width from a sample).
- Produce middle-ellipsis text that uses exactly the space available:
  as many leading chars + ellipsis + as many trailing chars as fit.
  If the full ID fits, show the full ID.

Practical shape:
- A small React hook: useMiddleEllipsis(text, ref) → displayed string
  that updates on resize.
- OR a styled component: <GLID value={id} /> that handles its own
  measurement + ellipsis.
- Always preserve the full ID as a title attribute so hover reveals
  the original.

Non-goals:
- Common-prefix collapsing across siblings (separate idea — can
  layer on later).
- Font-metrics precision beyond "fits comfortably"; a small safety
  margin is fine.

title: Retention transition retries corrupted chunks forever, flooding ERROR logs
description:
When a sealed chunk has genuinely corrupt idx.log / attr.log data,
the retention transition sweep picks it up every minute, tries to
stream records to the next tier, hits the same read error, logs an
ERROR, and starts the whole cycle again at the next sweep. Observed:

  transition: stream failed
    error="read source chunk: invalid idx.log entry: chunk <id>
      record 83: attr range [3246:3288] exceeds mmap size 3270"
  transition: stream failed
    error="read source chunk: invalid attributes data"

Same two chunk IDs, once per minute, indefinitely.

Root cause: in transition.go, markUnreadable only fires when the
stream error satisfies errors.Is(streamErr, cluster.ErrSourceRead).
The read-side errors returned from streamLocal — produced by the
cursor's record iterator — are plain fmt.Errorf("read source
chunk: %w", err) and carry no ErrSourceRead sentinel, so the check
is always false. The chunk never transitions to an unreadable state,
the retention sweep keeps retrying.

Fix sketch:
- At the streamLocal boundary (or at the transition-scope err
  wrapping), classify read errors from the source cursor and wrap
  them as ErrSourceRead. Then the existing markUnreadable path
  fires and the chunk is retired to the "unreadable" set so future
  sweeps skip it.
- Keep transient destination errors (network, gRPC Unavailable,
  peer timeout) OUT of that classification — per the existing
  comment in transition.go, those must remain retryable.

Test:
- A corrupted-chunk integration test: inject a chunk whose idx
  records point past attr.log size; invoke TransitionChunk; assert
  it's marked unreadable after one attempt and that subsequent
  retention sweeps don't touch it.

Separate question: how did the idx/attr sizes get out of sync in
the first place? Likely its own issue — data-integrity on the write
path — but the retry-loop fix should land independently because
the retry loop is harmful even for chunks corrupted for innocuous
reasons (e.g. underlying storage corruption).

title: Histogram double-counts records during tier transition, then drops below real count after
description:
With a 3-minute tier rotation, the histogram shows a sustained bump
coinciding with transition cadence, then a sharp drop after. Observed
counts: 2,957 records in one window, 618 records in the adjacent
window for the same time range — roughly 5× difference.

Two failure modes, both probably present:

(a) Double-counting during the transition window. The source chunk is
still on disk (streamed/awaiting receipt, not yet expired) while the
destination chunk is already queryable. The histogram aggregator walks
both tiers and sums records without deduping. With 3 tiers in the
chain, a record mid-flight can be counted up to 3× simultaneously.

(b) Under-counting once source chunks are deleted. If the destination
tier is on a different node and the histogram query isn't fanning out
to that node (or the dest is cloud and its records aren't counted the
same way), the count drops from inflated to below-real once transition
completes.

Fixes to consider:
- Histogram aggregation must exclude chunks in the "transition
  streamed" state. The tier FSM's transitionStreamed set already
  tracks these; the aggregator needs to consult it.
- OR: histogram counts only chunks NOT marked unreadable/streamed
  AND filters out records whose canonical tier is elsewhere.
- Query fan-out: ensure the histogram RPC walks every node that owns
  a tier in the vault chain, cluster-first style (similar pattern to
  the Search/Explain/GetFields fix that was covered in CLAUDE.md).

This is a correctness regression: operators can't trust the histogram
to reflect reality during or around retention transitions. Pri 1.

Affects:
- backend histogram RPC
- orchestrator query fan-out
- tier FSM transition state consultation

Reproducer: multi-node cluster, vault with a 3-tier chain on a short
(1-3 min) rotation interval, sustained ingest; watch the histogram
across a transition window.

title: Benchmarking Program: Cross-Platform Performance Baselines
description:
Establish a durable, repeatable benchmarking program for GastroLog across operating systems, hardware classes, storage backends, and cluster/network conditions.

Why:
- We need empirical performance evidence that is comparable across environments.
- Customer ingest rates are unknown and variable, so benchmarks must be environment-aware and reproducible.
- We need trendable baseline data tied to exact code revisions for regression detection.

Scope:
- Build benchmark framework and schema for result capture.
- Add benchmark suites for ingest, forwarding, query paths, and transitions.
- Define reporting artifacts suitable for CI + local runs.

Out of scope:
- Product-level SLO commitments.
- One-off ad hoc perf experiments without captured metadata.

title: Build benchmark framework with full environment provenance
description:
Create a benchmarking framework that produces reproducible, comparable results across multiple platforms and deployment topologies.

The framework must capture complete run provenance so each result can be interpreted and compared correctly.

Required provenance metadata:
- Git commit SHA and dirty/clean repo state
- Benchmark binary/build info (Go version, build flags)
- OS and kernel version
- CPU model, core/thread count, architecture
- Memory size
- Storage type(s): NVMe/SATA/SSD/HDD/ephemeral/cloud volume, filesystem, mount options where available

- Benchmark config knobs: dataset shape, chunk rotation settings, query parameters, concurrency, warmup and iteration counts

Acceptance criteria:

- Two runs from different hosts can be compared programmatically without manual normalization
- Existing and new benchmark suites can plug into the framework consistently
- Framework supports single-node and multi-node benchmark execution modes

title: Network inspector sparklines should be backend-owned, not UI-cold-started
description:
The Network section in the node inspector currently derives tx/rx rates and sparkline history in the frontend by differencing cumulative per-peer counters from NodeStats.peer_bytes. This causes a cold-start UX every time the inspector view mounts: rows start blank and fill only after multiple broadcast ticks.

Why this is a problem:
- Operators cannot rely on immediate historical context when opening the inspector.
- UI-local rate history is ephemeral and not reusable for backend telemetry/logging.
- Backend already owns the source counters; trend windows should be computed there and shipped as part of status payloads.

Current behavior (confirmed):
- backend/internal/cluster/peer_bytes.go tracks monotonic cumulative bytes_sent/bytes_received per peer since process start.
- frontend/src/components/inspector/PeerBytesSection.tsx computes rates/sparklines client-side from consecutive samples.
- backend/internal/ingester/metrics/ingester.go does not emit these per-peer transport counters/rates.

Required fix:
- Move per-peer rate-window/sparkline history computation to backend state.
- Expose backend-computed current rates + recent sparkline points in inspector-facing payloads (NodeStats or adjacent message).
- Update frontend to render backend-provided series directly (no local warm-up logic).

Acceptance criteria:
1) Opening inspector shows non-empty sparkline/rate data immediately when node has prior traffic (no 100s warm-up).
2) Backend is source of truth for rate windows and sparkline points.
3) Frontend no longer computes sparkline history by local differencing of cumulative counters.
4) Add tests for backend rate-window logic and frontend rendering of backend-provided series.
5) Verify behavior in single-node and multi-node setups via existing WatchSystemStatus flow.
close_reason: Fixed

title: Window operators/functions for time-series and counter analytics
description:
Add first-class windowed analytics to the query language so operators can compute rates/deltas and rolling statistics directly in queries.

Why:
- We currently have stats/timechart but no robust counter/window math (rate/delta/derivative, lag, moving windows).
- This blocks core observability workflows on monotonic counters (network bytes, forwarded records, queue counters) unless users export and post-process externally.
- Needed for telemetry analysis and for backend-emitted metrics streams to be genuinely useful in-query.

Must-have (v1):
1) Windowing primitives
   - tumbling window by duration (e.g. 1m, 5m)
   - sliding window by duration and step
   - partitioning keys (per series/group)

2) Counter/time-series math
   - delta(x): current - previous sample
   - rate(x): per-second normalized delta over window
   - increase(x): positive cumulative increase over window
   - derivative(x): slope over time for gauges

3) Row-relative functions
   - lag(x, n=1), lead(x, n=1)
   - difference(x) shorthand for x - lag(x)

4) Rolling aggregations
   - moving_avg(x, window)
   - moving_sum(x, window)
   - moving_min/moving_max(x, window)

5) Counter correctness behavior
   - reset handling for monotonic counters (ignore negative jumps or configurable reset policy)
   - sparse/missing sample handling with explicit policy (drop/fill/zero)

6) Execution constraints
   - bounded-memory streaming implementation where possible
   - deterministic behavior in distributed/multi-node merge paths

Nice-to-have (follow-ups):
- ewma(x, alpha) / exponential smoothing
- rolling_percentile(x, p, window)
- stddev/variance over window
- anomaly helpers (zscore over rolling window)
- session windows and event-count windows (N rows)
- interpolation/fill options (ffill/bfill/linear)
- calendar-aware windows (hour/day boundaries, timezone-aware)

Acceptance criteria:
- Query language syntax and AST updated for window operators/functions.
- Parser + validator tests for all must-have forms.
- Engine execution tests for single-node and multi-node correctness.
- Explicit docs with examples for counter analysis (rate/increase/delta).
- Performance tests demonstrating bounded memory and acceptable latency under large streams.

title: Preserve leader WriteTS when importing sealed chunks on tier replicas
description:
Sealed-chunk tier replication sends decoded records (TierReplication ImportSealed → Orchestrator.ImportToTierStorage → ChunkManager.ImportRecords). Both file and memory ImportRecords paths currently overwrite each record's WriteTS with the local clock (writeRecord / memory import loop), even though RecordToExport / ExportToRecord carry the leader's WriteTS over the wire.

That makes follower chunks diverge from the leader for any behavior keyed off WriteTS (e.g. Follow sorts pending by WriteTS, SearchThenFollow uses firstMatchTS from WriteTS, pipeline/aggregate write_ts output, chunk meta writeStart/writeEnd derived from stored WriteTS). Default search merge order uses IngestTS/SourceTS and is unaffected.

Preserve wire WriteTS on import (or only skip overwrite when replicating—pick the smallest consistent rule), update the ImportRecords docstring to match behavior, and add tests covering import from replicated records so follower WriteTS and chunk write bounds match the leader.
acceptance: Follower sealed chunk built from replicated records has the same per-record WriteTS and chunk writeStart/writeEnd as the leader for the same payload; ImportRecords documentation matches implementation; tests prevent regression.

title: Add help recipes for edge ingress (SNMP traps and similar)
description: GastroLog intentionally has no SNMP trap listener; operators use snmptrapd, Telegraf, OpenNMS, etc., then forward syslog/HTTP/OTLP into existing ingesters. Same pattern applies to other niche protocols. Add focused recipes under frontend/src/help/ (Recipes in topics.ts) when we decide to document them — not a product gap for core Gastrolog.
acceptance: New or updated recipe markdown under frontend/src/help/; each recipe links sender config + matching GastroLog ingester; SNMP recipe states no native trap support and points to syslog/HTTP paths; topic registered in topics.ts under Recipes; ingester help pages link new recipes where relevant.

title: Align settings mutations with authoritative API responses (naming + empty Put bodies)
description:
The Connect API surface is inconsistent in ways that force extra client round-trips and confuse anyone used to normal REST/GraphQL ergonomics: many config Put/Delete RPCs already return GetSystemResponse (e.g. PutFilter, PutVault, PutRoute), but the settings split left PutServiceSettings, PutLookupSettings, PutMaxMindSettings, PutSetupSettings, PutPreferences, etc. with empty responses. The UI then invalidates or depends on WatchSystem + refetch to learn state, which looks amateurish (duplicate GetSystem/GetSettings, ListVaults/GetStats on trivial edits) and is easy to get wrong across followers/watch ordering.

Naming is also uneven (wire vs proto field names, RPC names vs returned aggregates), which increases cognitive load when wiring clients.

We should treat mutations as "you changed this resource; here is the new canonical view" wherever feasible—either the same message GetX would return, or a deliberately narrower snapshot if payload size matters—then update handlers and regenerate clients. Frontend should prefer setQueryData from mutation responses (existing useSystemMutation pattern) and narrow invalidation instead of blanket refetch storms.
acceptance:
- Put* / Delete* for server settings, lookup, maxmind, setup, preferences (and any similar empty responses) return the same read-model types clients already use (e.g. GetSettingsResponse for lookup/maxmind paths, GetSystemResponse when raft system view changes), or a documented minimal alternative—not empty {}.
- Handlers reuse the same load/build path as GetSettings / GetSystem so responses cannot drift from GET.
- Regenerate buf/connect stubs; frontend mutations update React Query cache from response and avoid redundant Get* when the response is authoritative.
- Audit RPC/message naming for consistency (document renames in proto CHANGELOG or one-shot migration note if any wire breaks).
- Add or extend tests so a mutation response matches GET semantics (version fields included).
close_reason: User-verified fix complete

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: User verified fix in runtime testing; instrumentation removed; issue closure confirmed in chat.

title: WatchSystem: push full config snapshots, not version-only (avoid push-then-pull GETs)
description:
Today WatchSystem only streams system_version (Raft config index). The frontend has no authoritative payload, so it invalidates React Query keys and refetches GetSystem / GetSettings / etc.—push-then-pull.

Mutations already return GetSystemResponse (and settings mutations echo); the gap is remote/cross-tab updates that only hit the watch stream.

Extend WatchSystemResponse (proto) with optional snapshots built on the server when the config signal fires—e.g. GetSystemResponse system (required for parity with GetSystem), and optionally GetSettingsResponse settings with include_secrets=false for parity with normal UI reads. Update SystemServer.WatchSystem to call the same builders as GET handlers.

Frontend: useWatchSystem should setQueryData + setSystemVersion from the message when snapshots are present, and skip invalidateQueries for those keys. Keep version-only behavior as fallback for older clients only if we care; otherwise drop invalidation path.

Related: complements mutation echo work (e.g. gastrolog-1bkcg); removes redundant GETs after config bumps that are not from the local mutation.
acceptance: WatchSystem messages carry enough data to refresh system (and settings if in scope) without mandatory GetSystem/GetSettings refetch; network panel shows no follow-up GETs for those keys when only the stream notifies.

title: Volume histogram: tier-transition double counting and inflated cloud bars
description:
## Background

The search volume histogram shows incorrect record counts in three related ways during tier transitions and across the cloud tier. All three stem from the same area of code: the histogram pipeline in `backend/internal/server/query.go` (`searchDirect`, `computeDedupHistogram`) and `backend/internal/query/histogram.go` (`timechartCloudCounts`, `timechartChunkByIngestTS`).

This issue tracks the work already done plus the remaining cloud-bar issue.

## Sub-bugs

### 1. Warm-tier records double-counted during tier transitions (FIXED)

**Symptom:** When a chunk transitioned from one warm tier to the next, its records were counted in both the source and the destination tier in the histogram until the retention sweeper removed the source. Bars roughly doubled in width every transition window.

**Root cause (two parts):**
- `searchDirect` only ran EventID-based dedup when `multiNodeVault` was true, so single-node multi-tier setups never deduped at all.
- `importState.writeRecord` in `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` was calling `EncodeIdxEntry` without `IngestSeq`, `IngesterID`, `NodeID`, so records imported via `ImportRecords` (i.e. tier transitions) had zero EventID fields. Even when dedup ran, it couldn't dedup these.

**Fix:**
- Removed the `multiNodeVault` gate from the dedup branch in `searchDirect`; runs whenever `transform == nil && hasRange`.
- Added the missing `EventID` fields to the `EncodeIdxEntry` call in `importState.writeRecord`.
- Strengthened the dedup gate in `streamedHistogramBuilder.add` to require `!rec.EventID.IngesterID.IsZero()` instead of any non-zero `EventID` (which was triggering on `IngestTS` alone and falsely deduping synthetic test records).

### 2. Dedup pass downloaded cloud blobs from S3 (FIXED)

**Symptom:** None visible to the user, but every histogram refresh (~5s) would range-fetch every cloud-backed chunk in the query window from S3 — locally and on every remote node — purely to feed counts. The legacy histogram path was carefully designed to use cached TS-index lookups for the same numbers without any blob fetches.

**Root cause:** `computeDedupHistogram` called `eng.Search` and `s.collectRemote` without `SkipCloud=true`. `q.SkipCloud` was also not in `ForwardSearchRequest`, so it couldn't propagate to remote nodes.

**Fix:**
- Set `qHist.SkipCloud = true` in `computeDedupHistogram`.
- Added `bool skip_cloud = 4` to `ForwardSearchRequest` in `backend/api/proto/gastrolog/v1/cluster.proto`. Honored by `newSearchExecutor` in `backend/internal/app/executors.go` and the test stub in `backend/internal/server/multinode_test.go`.
- New helper `mergeCloudCountsIntoDedupHistogram` in `backend/internal/server/query_remote.go` folds the legacy histogram's `CloudCount` per bucket back into the deduped (warm-only) result.
- `mergeHistogramBuckets` now also sums `CloudCount` and ORs `HasCloudData` across nodes; previously it only summed `Count`, dropping remote cloud counts.

### 3. Cloud histogram bars are wildly inflated and uneven (IN PROGRESS)

**Symptom:** With the above fixes in place, cloud-tier bars (rendered as hatched purple bars in the UI) are much taller than warm bars and vary dramatically bucket-to-bucket. Manifests should give exact per-chunk record counts via the cached TS index, so cloud bars should be smooth and predictable. Current investigation hypotheses:

- H1: per-tier double-counting on the same node (same cloud chunk listed under multiple tier-vaults by `PrimaryTierQueryEngine`)
- H2: cross-node duplication (same cloud chunk surfaced by multiple nodes in `mergeHistogramBuckets`)
- H3: stale/accumulated cloud chunks not pruned by retention
- H4: `timechartChunkByIndex` over-attributing records to buckets at boundaries
- H5: `mergeCloudCountsIntoDedupHistogram` adds cloud counts on top of a deduped value that already includes cloud (i.e. `SkipCloud` not actually suppressing)

Instrumentation is in place in `backend/internal/query/histogram.go:timechartCloudCounts` (per-vault and per-chunk) and in `backend/internal/server/query.go:searchDirect` (legacy local vs remote vs merged sums; dedup-merge in vs out). Awaiting a reproduction run to see which hypotheses hold.

## Repro for sub-bug 3

1. `just cluster-init && just cluster-run`
2. Wait until a few warm→cloud transitions have happened (at least one cloud chunk in tier 3)
3. Open the search UI, run `last=15m reverse=true`
4. Observe hatched cloud bars at the older end of the histogram

Expected: cloud bar heights roughly proportional to the cloud chunks' `RecordCount` distributed across their `IngestStart`-`IngestEnd` range.
Observed: cloud bars are tall and uneven, dwarfing warm bars at the newer end.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Warm-tier transitions no longer double the histogram (sub-bug 1 — already verified by user)
- [ ] No S3 blob fetches triggered by histogram refresh (sub-bug 2 — verified by ghost/hatched bars showing up without download spikes)
- [ ] Cloud-tier bars match expected per-bucket distribution from chunk manifests (sub-bug 3 — pending)
- [ ] All existing tests in `backend/internal/server`, `backend/internal/cluster`, `backend/internal/query`, `backend/internal/orchestrator` still pass
- [ ] Debug instrumentation removed once the cloud-bar fix is verified

## Files touched so far

- `backend/api/proto/gastrolog/v1/cluster.proto` (+ regenerated `cluster.pb.go`)
- `backend/internal/app/executors.go`
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go`
- `backend/internal/cluster/forward.go`
- `backend/internal/query/histogram.go`
- `backend/internal/server/multinode_test.go`
- `backend/internal/server/query.go`
- `backend/internal/server/query_remote.go`

Plus instrumentation files (to be removed):
- `backend/internal/query/debug_526fda.go`
- `backend/internal/server/debug_526fda.go`

title: Cluster-wide data destruction cascade triggered by transient peer EOF (tier-loss wipe + retention storm)
description:
## Symptom

A transient record-forwarder EOF between two nodes triggers a cascade that
destroys data **across the entire cluster**, not just the unreachable node.
Observed effects:

- The histogram for last=15m goes completely blank (no chunks within the
  recent window survive), then refills with new ingest.
- A flood of WARN/ERROR log lines: "tier removed from vault", "FSM onDelete:
  DeleteSilent failed ... manager is closed", "retention: failed to forward
  chunk deletion to follower ... vault not found".

## Root cause (proven via raft WAL inspection)

`Orchestrator.sealAndDeleteAllChunks` (`backend/internal/orchestrator/reconfig_vaults.go:332`)
and `Orchestrator.ForceRemoveVault` both invoke `tier.Chunks.Delete(meta.ID)`
in a loop over every locally-known chunk. `Manager.Delete` fires
`Announcer.AnnounceDelete`, which submits `CmdDeleteChunk` to the **tier
Raft group**. Raft replicates the command to every voter, where
`FSM.applyDelete` runs `OnDelete`, which physically removes the chunk file
on every node.

So a node losing placement of a tier (e.g. because of a transient EOF on the
record forwarder) and trying to clean up its own local copies turns into "every
node deletes every chunk in this tier."

The `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce` / `chunk.SilentDeleter` interface exists for
exactly this case ("LOCAL cleanup paths ... that must not propagate the delete
via tier Raft" — see `backend/internal/chunk/announcer.go:43`). It was used by
`replaceForwardedChunk` and `deleteFromFollowers` but missed by
`sealAndDeleteAllChunks` and `ForceRemoveVault`.

### WAL evidence (vault `06eqgeran5pqj0vdm58rcrte7o`, single incident, term 9)

Decoded from `data/node*/raft/wal/wal-*.log` via `cmd/walinspect`:

```
tier   group ID                    RetentionPending(@9)  CmdDeleteChunk(@9)  excess (cascade-induced)
hot    06eqgerc65s8v9rj42b22ijfbk  238                   434                 196
warm   06eqgere9lpv78rc0dercmv8t4  417                   693                 276
cold   06eqgerg9hpth7b4trpugp61l8    0                   240                 240
                                                                            ───
                                                                            712 chunks wiped clusterwide
```

Cold has no retention rule, so its 240 deletes (all at term 9, packed into
consecutive raft indices 2804, 2806, 2812, 2815, …) cannot be retention. Each
hot/warm tier shows excess deletes far above their `RetentionPending` count.
The "burst over 30 minutes" interpretation in the previous bug body was wrong:
the deletes hit the WAL in one tight burst (term 9, contiguous indices) and
then the leader spent the next half hour failing to forward those replicated
deletes to node3 (whose chunk manager was closed), producing the WARN flood
that *looked* like a retention storm.

## Trigger trace (cluster.log, 2026-04-20 incident)

```
03:16:06.279  node1  forwarder gets EOF on stream to node3 (transient unreachability)
03:16:06.315  placement: hot   placements=3 (reassigned off node3)
03:16:06.523  placement: warm/cold placements=3 (reassigned off node3)
03:16:07.855  node3  "tier removed from vault" hot  remaining_tiers=2
                      -> dispatch.go:230 calls RemoveTierFromVault
                      -> sealAndDeleteAllChunks loops cm.Delete(...) for every chunk
                      -> AnnounceDelete -> CmdDeleteChunk -> raft -> ALL VOTERS DELETE
03:16:09.648  node3  "tier removed from vault" warm remaining_tiers=1 (same)
03:16:27.659  node3  "tier removed from vault" cold remaining_tiers=0 (same)
03:16:27.659  node3  "vault removed (no remaining tiers)"

03:21-03:40   leader's retention forward retries to node3 (whose manager is
              closed) generate "follower rejected command: vault not found"
              warnings at the 1-min sweep cadence. These are the *symptoms* of
              the wipe, not its cause.
```

## Fix

In `backend/internal/orchestrator/reconfig_vaults.go`:

- `sealAndDeleteAllChunks`: replace `tier.Chunks.Delete(m.ID)` with
  `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce(tier.Chunks, m.ID)`.
- `ForceRemoveVault`: replace `cm.Delete(meta.ID)` with
  `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce(cm, meta.ID)`.

Both call sites are local-only cleanup. Cluster-wide effect (when the user
actually wants the vault/tier gone everywhere, e.g. admin teardown) comes
from each node independently running its own teardown when the config change
propagates — not from per-chunk delete announcements out of one node.

## Acceptance / regression test

1. Reproduce the cascade by suspending a node's record forwarder (or simply
   killing one node) on a multi-vault cluster with tiers spread across all
   nodes. Once placement reassigns tiers off the failing node, the failing
   node's WAL must contain at most a small number of `CmdDeleteChunk` for
   chunks that were *actually* expired (matching `CmdRetentionPending`), not
   one per local chunk on the tier.
2. Add an orchestrator-level test that wires a real-ish chunk manager with an
   `Announcer` and calls `RemoveTierFromVault` / `ForceRemoveVault`, asserting
   that `Announcer.AnnounceDelete` is *not* called.
3. Recheck that the existing `replaceForwardedChunk` / `deleteFromFollowers`
   paths (already correct) still use `DeleteNoAnnounce` — no regression there.

## Related

- `backend/internal/chunk/announcer.go:30` `SilentDeleter` interface.
- `backend/internal/chunk/announcer.go:43` `DeleteNoAnnounce` helper, with the
  exact comment explaining why it exists.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go:622-625` `replaceForwardedChunk`
  comment: "It must NOT propagate the delete via tier Raft."

title: CLI inspect parity with web inspector
description:
The gastrolog CLI inspect command only surfaces a subset of what operators see in the web inspector (e.g. vaults, tiers, chunks). The UI inspector exposes substantially more runtime and placement detail (ingesters, per-node status, placement health, and related system views). That gap forces ad-hoc RPC helpers or raw API use for incidents—e.g. debugging ingester alive maps vs local logs.

Close this gap later by extending the CLI (new subcommands, flags, or inspect sections) and/or documenting intentional non-parity so CLI and UI stay aligned for on-call workflows.
acceptance: Operators can answer the same high-level questions from the CLI that the web inspector answers today, without one-off programs; or the docs explicitly scope what the CLI will not cover and why.

title: GetFields returns invalid UTF-8 in FieldValue.value — proto marshal fails
description:
## Symptom

Frontend gets this on GetFields responses:

\`\`\`
{"code":"internal","message":"marshal message: proto: field gastrolog.v1.FieldValue.value contains invalid UTF-8"}
\`\`\`

Proto3 strings must be valid UTF-8, so Connect/proto-go refuses to marshal \`apiv1.FieldValue.Value\` (or \`FieldInfo.Key\`) when the extracted value contains arbitrary bytes.

## Root cause

\`server/query_fields.go::GetFields\` runs \`tokenizer.CombinedExtract(rec.Raw, extractors)\` against raw log bodies. Log records can contain arbitrary bytes (binary payloads in stdout, partial UTF-8 at buffer boundaries, escape sequences, etc). Extracted \`kv.Key\`/\`kv.Value\` strings can therefore be non-UTF-8, but we pipe them straight into \`apiv1.FieldValue.Value\` / \`apiv1.FieldInfo.Key\` (proto3 string fields).

Also applies to \`rec.Attrs\` values — structured attrs from ingesters are usually clean but not guaranteed.

## Fix

Sanitize all strings at the proto boundary in \`query_fields.go::toProto()\`:
- \`fi.Key\` (field info key)
- \`FieldValue.Value\` (top-value strings)

Use \`strings.ToValidUTF8(s, \"\\uFFFD\")\` — lossless for valid UTF-8, replaces invalid byte sequences with the Unicode replacement character (\`�\`). Shown-as-display is acceptable (this is a field discovery surface; users see what was extracted).

Also audit other RPCs that carry extracted-from-raw strings into proto:
- \`Explain\` (ExplainResponse attrs)
- \`Histogram\` (bucket labels from field values)
- Any \`TableResult\` cell that comes from raw extraction

## Acceptance

- GetFields never produces invalid-UTF-8 marshal errors even for records with arbitrary-byte bodies.
- Regression test with a record whose body contains a byte sequence invalid as UTF-8; GetFields response marshals cleanly and the value shows \`�\` where the bytes were.
- Quick grep audit of other proto-boundary surfaces for similar patterns.

## Files
- \`backend/internal/server/query_fields.go:115\` (toProto)
- \`backend/internal/server/query_fields.go:105\` (add — also apply to key)

title: Paused peer causes cluster-wide stall — sync RPC head-of-line blocking
description:
## Symptom

On a 4-node cluster, SIGSTOPing a single follower node (node3) caused:
1. node3 to go offline (expected)
2. **node2 (cluster Raft leader) to *also* go offline** (unexpected)
3. Searches on node1 to stop responding for several minutes
4. Immediate recovery when node3 was unpaused: node2 came back instantly, node3 came back a few seconds later

Observed via imux pause/continue while the user's cluster was running.

## Why this is wrong

4 nodes with 1 paused = 3 live = quorum is met. Writes and reads should continue on the remaining 3. Pausing one peer must never cascade to another.

The instantaneous recovery on unpause is the smoking gun: node2 was **blocked waiting on an RPC to node3**, not crashed. Once node3 responded, node2's pending call completed and everything unwound.

## Hypothesis: head-of-line blocking via sync peer RPC with no deadline

SIGSTOPed peers are the worst failure mode: TCP socket stays open, writes succeed, response never comes. Any caller that does \`client.Method(req)\` without \`context.WithTimeout\` blocks forever.

If such a call lives on a critical loop (heartbeats, broadcasts, ingester-alive sync, config stream renewal, peer health probes), the whole loop stalls.

## Suspect list — places to audit for missing per-call deadlines

Grep these paths for peer RPCs without \`context.WithTimeout\`:
- \`backend/internal/cluster/broadcaster.go\` — fanouts to all peers
- \`backend/internal/cluster/peer_conns.go\` — connection-level RPCs
- \`backend/internal/cluster/forward_rpc.go\` / \`forward.go\`
- \`backend/internal/cluster/forward_append.go\` — record forwarding (ack-gated path is suspicious)
- \`backend/internal/cluster/tier_apply_forwarder.go\`, \`vault_apply_forwarder.go\`
- Peer-reachability / health checks — grep for any goroutine that probes all peers
- WatchConfig / WatchJobs / WatchIngesterStatus server-side fanouts
- SetIngesterAlive / peer stats collection
- The multiraft.Transport heartbeat batch if it has a coalesce-and-wait loop

## Repro

1. Start a 4-node cluster (\`just backend cluster-run\` against 4 homes)
2. Identify any non-leader node (or a follower)
3. Pause its process with SIGSTOP: \`kill -STOP <pid>\`
4. Observe other nodes' status via the inspector or \`gastrolog cluster\`
5. Expected: paused node shows offline, others remain healthy, searches continue
6. Actual: another node (often the leader) also shows offline; searches hang

## Acceptance

- Pausing any single node in a 4+ node cluster does NOT mark other nodes offline
- Searches on healthy nodes continue uninterrupted during the pause
- Ingestion on healthy nodes continues uninterrupted (may need ack-gated path exception documented)
- Unpausing the stopped node recovers it cleanly without further disruption
- Regression test: a reliability matrix scenario that simulates SIGSTOP via a slow/hung transport wrapper, with assertions that the rest of the cluster continues to commit and serve reads
- Audit log of every peer-facing RPC path with a confirmed deadline shape; any call without a context deadline must be documented as intentionally unbounded (and moved off the critical path)

## Priority

Priority 0 (ship-blocker). A pause of one node taking out the cluster is a reliability showstopper: real-world events that resemble SIGSTOP include GC pauses, disk freezes, hypervisor pauses, kernel stalls, and overloaded nodes. Any of these would reproduce this.

## Reliability matrix connection

gastrolog-5ff7z (in progress on branch gastrolog-5ff7z) builds a reliability matrix but currently simulates failures via clean \`stopNode()\` which shuts down the WAL and closes connections. That does NOT reproduce SIGSTOP semantics (sockets open, no response). A "paused peer" scenario needs a slow/null transport wrapper that accepts sends but never delivers responses. Adding that scenario is part of this issue's acceptance.
close_reason: Paused peer no longer cascades. Root cause: ingest() held o.mu.RLock across fireAndForgetRemote (which waits for per-follower RPCs). Fixes landed over 5 commits: multiraft per-RPC deadlines (AppendEntries/BatchHeartbeat/RequestVote/etc); Broadcaster.Send fire-and-forget (push semantics, no wg.Wait); Forwarder.Forward bounded by ReplicationTimeout; PeerState TTL 5s→20s (4× broadcast interval); ingest() releases o.mu.RLock before calling fireAndForgetRemote + TierReplicator.send honors ctx via runWithCtx helper. pipelineIdleTimeout addition was a bad fix that caused placement cascade; reverted. Verified via pprof goroutine dump showing the exact stuck call chain. Cluster now tolerates SIGSTOPed peer: local ops unaffected, circuit breaker backs off unreachable peer, unpause triggers automatic catchup replication.

title: Fast paused-node detection via 1s heartbeat broadcast
description:
## Symptom

Paused-node detection currently takes ~15-20s. A node that goes silent (paused, frozen, dead) keeps showing as alive in the UI / `PeerState.IsAlive` for up to 4 missed broadcasts before the TTL trips. Operators expect this to be near-instant.

## Root cause

After gastrolog-5oofa, the cadence is:

- Stats broadcast interval: **5s** (`StatsCollector.broadcast`, default `Interval = 5s` in `statscollector.go`)
- `PeerState` TTL: **20s** (`app.go`: `cluster.NewPeerState(20 * time.Second)`)

The 4× safety factor was the 5oofa fix to stop a tighter TTL from flapping healthy peers under jitter. But "4× a slow heartbeat" is the wrong knob — the knob that actually controls detection latency is the **heartbeat cadence**, not the TTL multiplier. The current cadence is slow because the existing broadcast carries a bulky payload (jobs, route stats, version, addresses) that doesn't want to fly every second.

## Proposed fix

Split the cadence in the existing self-broadcast + TTL machinery — no new probing protocol, no per-peer ticker, no quadratic regression beyond what the existing fan-out already is.

- New lightweight proto:
  ```proto
  message Heartbeat {
    bytes node_id = 1;
    google.protobuf.Timestamp ts = 2;
  }
  rpc BroadcastHeartbeat(BroadcastHeartbeatRequest) returns (google.protobuf.Empty);
  ```
- New ticker in `StatsCollector` at `HeartbeatInterval` (default **1s**) — pulls `node_id + now`, fans out via the same `Broadcaster` infrastructure as the existing stats broadcast.
- Existing 5s stats ticker stays unchanged. Heavy payload doesn't get faster.
- `PeerState.HandleHeartbeat(hb)` sets `lastSeen` for `hb.node_id` — same liveness signal as `HandleBroadcast`, just without the rest of the state to merge.
- `PeerState` TTL drops to **4s** (4× the new 1s heartbeat — same safety factor, faster detection).
- New `HeartbeatInterval` field in `system.Cluster` config + proto, alongside `BroadcastInterval`.

## Cost

Per node: +N small RPCs/sec where N is the number of peers. Payload is ~32 bytes + gRPC framing per message. On a 4-node cluster: ~12 RPCs/sec total cluster-wide. Negligible compared to the existing 5s broadcasts.

## Follow-up (not in this issue)

hraft's per-peer last-contact (`Raft.Stats()`) is another live signal already on the wire — vault-ctl Raft heartbeats run every 1s. Could feed that into PeerState as a third input alongside heartbeat + stats broadcast, removing the need for the new heartbeat once enough Raft groups exist on every pair of nodes. Out of scope here — solve the cadence first, optimize later.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `Heartbeat` proto + RPC + broadcaster path + `PeerState.HandleHeartbeat` landed.
- [ ] `HeartbeatInterval` configurable via `system.Cluster` (default 1s).
- [ ] `PeerState` TTL is configurable; default 4× heartbeat interval.
- [ ] **Detection latency ≤ 2s in existing pause-test scenarios** (currently 15-20s). Specifically: in a multi-node test, pause node B at t=0; node A's `peerState.IsAlive(B)` returns false by t=2s.
- [ ] No regression in healthy-peer flicker: existing pause/restart scenarios where the peer recovers must not show it as offline during normal jitter.
- [ ] Unit tests: `HandleHeartbeat` updates lastSeen; TTL expiry flips `IsAlive`; rehab via subsequent heartbeat or stats broadcast.
- [ ] Multi-node integration test asserts the <2s detection bound.

title: Parallelize chunk compression with bounded encoder pool
description:
## Goal

Parallelize chunk compression to use multiple cores per `chunk/file/Manager`. Currently compression is serialized per Manager via a single `zstd.Encoder` + `zstdEncMu` mutex; under retention bursts (many sealed chunks queued for compression after a tier rotation) this is the bottleneck.

## Hard constraints (lessons from prior incidents)

**Do NOT re-trigger gastrolog-4r8s** ("Zstd encoder accumulates unbounded history buffers", commit `7727b160`):

> The shared zstd encoder uses default concurrency, causing klauspost/compress to maintain a pool of internal encoder instances (each with ~8MB history buffer) that are never released. With concurrent CompressChunk jobs, this accumulated 112MB of live memory in `ensureHist`.

Specifically:

1. **Do NOT change `WithEncoderConcurrency(1)`.** That setting is load-bearing — it disables klauspost's internal worker-encoder pool that grew unboundedly. A higher value re-creates the bug exactly as before.
2. **Do NOT use `sync.Pool` for encoders.** Go's `sync.Pool` has no hard cap; under burst it can hold many entries between GC cycles. The 4r8s incident's root cause was *unbounded* growth of an encoder pool — `sync.Pool` reproduces the same shape (different mechanism) under heavy load.

## Proposed design

**Fixed-capacity channel-based encoder pool** (semaphore pattern):

```go
type encoderPool struct {
    encoders chan *zstd.Encoder
}

func newEncoderPool(size int) (*encoderPool, error) {
    p := &encoderPool{encoders: make(chan *zstd.Encoder, size)}
    for i := 0; i < size; i++ {
        enc, err := zstd.NewWriter(nil,
            zstd.WithEncoderLevel(zstd.SpeedDefault),
            zstd.WithEncoderConcurrency(1),  // load-bearing — see gastrolog-4r8s
        )
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        p.encoders <- enc
    }
    return p, nil
}

func (p *encoderPool) Acquire(ctx context.Context) (*zstd.Encoder, error) { ... }
func (p *encoderPool) Release(enc *zstd.Encoder) { p.encoders <- enc }
func (p *encoderPool) Close() error { ... }
```

- Pool size N (default 4, configurable via `system.Cluster` settings or chunk-tier params). Memory ceiling: N × ~8MB = 32MB per Manager at default.
- `CompressChunk` acquires one encoder, hands it to `compressFile` for raw.log, releases, acquires again for attr.log, releases. (Or, with two acquires: raw + attr in parallel within one call.)
- `Manager.Close()` closes all encoders in the pool.

**raw.log + attr.log in parallel within a single CompressChunk call**: dispatch two goroutines, each acquires an encoder, runs `compressFile`, releases. ~2× per-call speedup.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Pool implementation with fixed channel capacity (NOT `sync.Pool`).
- [ ] `WithEncoderConcurrency(1)` preserved on every encoder created in the pool. Add a code comment citing gastrolog-4r8s right at the encoder construction site to prevent future agents from "fixing" it.
- [ ] N configurable, sane default (4).
- [ ] raw.log + attr.log compressed concurrently within a single CompressChunk call.
- [ ] All existing reliability tests pass — particularly anything in gastrolog-5ff7z's matrix that exercises seal → compress → search interleaving, plus the historical race fixes around compression:
  - bdda4633 — compression scheduler / manager lifecycle races
  - 2215e153 — double-compression TOCTOU race
  - 421d4f7e — cursor/compress mmap race
  - dde301b8 — openDataFile mmap-during-rename race
- [ ] Memory ceiling holds under load. Run a tier-rotation burst (force ~50 simultaneous CompressChunk calls), verify RSS ceiling stays at expected `BaselineRSS + N × ~8MB`.
- [ ] pprof goroutine + heap profiles before and after to confirm: contention on the pool stays bounded; no `ensureHist` accumulation; no leaked encoders.
- [ ] Throughput regression test: time to compress N chunks before vs after, with N concurrent invocations. Should drop roughly proportional to pool size on a multi-core machine.

## Out of scope

- Frame-level parallelism within a single chunk (would require forking or replacing the seekable zstd library).
- Cross-Manager / cross-tier parallelism — already exists (independent encoders per Manager).
- Bumping `WithEncoderConcurrency` — explicitly forbidden; see above.

## Investigation step before implementation

Capture pprof on a node under retention pressure to confirm the bottleneck actually is `zstdEncMu`. If goroutines are parked elsewhere (disk I/O, FSM apply, replication), the pool buys little. The fix should follow the data, not the theory.

title: Research: chunk-local indexing & compression approaches (FST, Roaring, CLP, columnar)
description:
Research the following indexing and compression approaches as used in production log management and search systems. For each, produce a concise technical summary covering: (1) core data structures and encoding, (2) compression characteristics and known tradeoffs, (3) query performance implications, and (4) availability of mature Go libraries.

## Approaches (starting set, NOT exhaustive)

1. **Finite State Transducers (FSTs)** for term/string dictionaries — as used in Lucene, ClickHouse, and Bleve; compare against hash maps and B-trees for this use case.

2. **Roaring Bitmaps** for posting lists and positional/offset indexes — adaptive container selection (array/bitset/RLE), rank/select performance, behavior on sorted time-ordered data.

3. **CLP-style log type extraction** — separating static message templates from variable parts at ingest time, column-oriented storage of the variable streams, and how this enables compression and search on the encoded form without a traditional index.

4. **Columnar index layout (struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs)** — how field-column separation interacts with general-purpose block compressors like zstd.

**Do NOT limit the research to only the four approaches above.** They are a starting point, not a closed list. If a better, newer, or more applicable approach exists in the literature or in production systems (e.g. tantivy/Tantivy-rs's tradeoffs vs Lucene, succinct data structures, learned indexes, ANN/embedding-based search, segment trees with delta encoding, FM-indexes / wavelet trees, anything from VictoriaLogs / Quickwit / Loki / Splunk / Datadog Husky / Honeycomb's storage layer), include it. The goal is the best chunk-local search story, not a defense of the listed four.

## Constraints

- All approaches **must be applicable chunk-locally** — no global index across chunks. Each chunk must be self-contained for index purposes.
- Any approach **requiring full decompression before search is a non-starter**. Search must work directly on the encoded/compressed form, or via decompression of the smallest necessary unit (e.g. one frame).
- Flag approaches that are **synergistic** with each other (e.g. FST + Roaring is a known Lucene combination).

## Deliverable

Produce a research document at **`docs/advanced_indexing.md`** as the canonical artifact for this research. The document MUST contain:

1. **Executive summary** — 1–2 paragraphs naming the recommended approach (or short-list of synergistic approaches) and the rationale, before getting into the comparison.
2. **Per-approach assessment** — 1–2 paragraphs each covering the four listed approaches plus any additional approaches the research surfaces. Each assessment covers (1) core data structures and encoding, (2) compression characteristics and tradeoffs, (3) query performance implications, (4) Go library options with concrete repo URLs, last-commit recency, and maintenance status.
3. **Synergy matrix** — a table or short bullets identifying which approaches compose well (e.g. FST term dictionary + Roaring posting list + columnar variable streams), and which are mutually exclusive or redundant.
4. **Constraint compliance check** — for each approach, an explicit yes/no on the chunk-local constraint and the no-full-decompression constraint, with one-line justification.
5. **Recommended path forward** — concrete next-step issues to file for the chosen approach, including any prototyping work, benchmarks against the current scan-based search, and integration points with the GLCB chunk format (gastrolog-2n697).

The document is the primary review artifact — link to it from any follow-up implementation issues. Comments on this issue should reference sections of the document, not duplicate them.

## Why now

The current GLCB chunk format (gastrolog-2n697) has TS indexes embedded but no field-level inverted indexes — every keyword/field search scans the records. As cluster sizes grow, scan-based search becomes the bottleneck. The right indexing approach for chunk-local search isn't obvious; this issue scopes the research before any code is written.

title: JSON indexer Build path SIGBUS: mmap-during-mutation race with compression/retention
description:
## Symptom

Node4 in a long-running 4-node cluster crashed at **2026-04-28T05:10:02** with `fatal error: fault` (SIGBUS) and `exit status 2`. Other nodes survived. Cluster had been running since 2026-04-27T01:32; ~28 hours of steady ingest before the crash.

```
2026-04-28T05:10:02.204823 unexpected fault address 0x151435166
2026-04-28T05:10:02.204827 fatal error: fault
2026-04-28T05:10:02.209393 [signal SIGBUS: bus error code=0x1 addr=0x151435166 pc=0x1043134a8]

goroutine 412955441 [running]:
runtime.sigpanic()
encoding/binary.littleEndian.Uint64(...)              binary.go:117
gastrolog/internal/chunk/file.DecodeIdxEntry          record.go:97
gastrolog/internal/chunk/file.(*mmapCursor).readRecord record_reader.go:213
gastrolog/internal/chunk/file.(*mmapCursor).Next      record_reader.go:172
gastrolog/internal/index/file/json.(*Indexer).pass1   indexer.go:182
gastrolog/internal/index/file/json.(*Indexer).Build   indexer.go:483
gastrolog/internal/index.(*BuildHelper).Build.func1.1 build.go:37
golang.org/x/sync/errgroup.(*Group).Go.func1
```

The faulting address `0x151435166` is a virtual address inside an mmap'd region of the chunk's idx.log. SIGBUS on macOS/ARM64 specifically indicates a previously-mapped region that has been unmapped or the underlying file truncated — i.e. **the chunk's idx.log was mutated underneath the cursor that the JSON indexer was holding**.

## Root cause

`backend/internal/index/file/json/indexer.go:171` opens a cursor via `idx.manager.OpenCursor(chunkID)` and iterates `cursor.Next()` to scan records for indexing. The cursor wraps `chunk/file.(*mmapCursor)`, which mmaps the chunk's data files and decodes idx entries inline at `record.go:97` via `binary.littleEndian.Uint64`.

If between cursor open and any subsequent `Next()`, another goroutine on the same node:
1. **Compresses** the chunk (atomic temp-file → `os.Rename` swap; the original mmap'd FD remains open but the rename invalidates the mapping under macOS — SIGBUS on next read), OR
2. **Deletes** the chunk via retention (`os.Remove` → mapping unmap), OR
3. **Replaces** the chunk via cloud upload / decompress on read,

then the cursor's next `mmapCursor.readRecord` faults.

Historical fixes for the same family of races covered the **cursor path itself**:
- `dde301b8` "fix: close openDataFile race that mmaps compressed bytes as uncompressed"
- `421d4f7e` / **gastrolog-2mnv8** "cursor/compress mmap race"
- `2215e153` "double-compression TOCTOU race in file chunk manager"

Those work for live record reads through the cursor. The **JSON indexer Build** at `indexer.go:171-189` opens its own cursor as part of post-seal index construction and **does not appear to share the lifecycle guards** that protect the cursor path. Same race surface, different caller.

## Suggestive context from the log

- Spike of `level=WARN msg="kv index capped due to hard cap"` (with the `MaxValuesPerKey=1000` that motivated the FST research in gastrolog-4dh5i) on chunks `06et43mvr5ohb35c79g2vqlje8`, `06et43n1btrld5e9hn5il3mo5g`, `06et43u14toh35ivd6tue2kdio`, etc. throughout `05:09:01` – `05:09:43` — indexer activity was concurrent with retention/compression activity on the same vault and tier IDs.
- `2026-04-28T05:10:00.355421 level=WARN msg="reconcile: failed to delete orphaned chunk" component=orchestrator tier=06eso8pdbpqfj2bj91qseena68 chunk=06et430n6hsm5djbkuui62p6h0 error="chunk not found"` — **1.85 s before the panic**, retention was reconciling and finding chunks already gone. Strong indicator of concurrent file lifecycle activity on the same tier.

The chunk that triggered the SIGBUS is not directly identifiable from the goroutine stack (the chunk ID is encoded in registers but not logged), but the chunk-IDs in the indexer warnings give a list of plausible candidates active in that window.

## Fix shape

The JSON indexer's `Build` path needs the same lifecycle protection as the cursor path. Concrete options, in increasing rigor:

1. **Refcount the mmap region** against deletion/truncation. The chunk manager's `OpenCursor` should pin the underlying file mapping until `Close()` is called; compression's atomic rename and retention's `os.Remove` should wait for the refcount to drop to zero. This is the most general fix and aligns with how historical mmap-race fixes were structured.

2. **Serialize Build against compression/retention** at the chunk-manager level — a per-chunk RWMutex where Build/cursor reads take the read lock and compression/delete take the write lock. Simpler than refcounting but less concurrent.

3. **Defensive: `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` + recovery on SIGBUS**. Don't do this — masking a memory-corruption signal is worse than crashing.

The "right" answer is (1), and probably already exists for the cursor path; the audit is to find why it's not effective for the JSON indexer's cursor. Likely candidates:
- The JSON indexer opens its own cursor through the manager but the manager's lifecycle guards only protect existing-cursor lookups, not new-cursor opens during compression.
- The compression path renames the file *first* and only then takes a lock that the indexer respects, leaving an unprotected window where new cursors can be opened against an already-renamed file.

## Acceptance

- [ ] A reproducer test that races JSON index Build against compression of the same chunk, verifies no SIGBUS / no panic, and verifies that one operation either completes correctly or reports a clean `ErrChunkBusy`-style error to the caller.
- [ ] Same race tested against retention deletion of the same chunk during Build.
- [ ] All historical compress/cursor race fixes (`dde301b8`, `421d4f7e`, `2215e153`) still pass — no regression in their tests.
- [ ] Audit other indexer Build paths (KV, TS, etc.) for the same race surface; either share the fix or file companion bugs.

## Severity & containment

- P1 — **node-killing crash** in a long-running cluster. Has happened once observed; the conditions (compression + indexer + retention all active on the same vault at once) are normal steady-state operation, so this can recur on any node, on any deployment.
- Workaround: there isn't one short of disabling JSON indexing or compression. Restart the affected node; the cluster's vault-ctl Raft will catch up the missing replica via the gastrolog-2kio8 heartbeat / placement machinery.

## Files implicated

- `backend/internal/index/file/json/indexer.go:171-189` (Build → cursor open + iterate)
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/record.go:97` (DecodeIdxEntry — the actual SIGBUS site)
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/record_reader.go:172, 213` (mmapCursor.Next, readRecord)
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` (chunk lifecycle, OpenCursor, CompressChunk, retention deletion)

## Out of scope

- The `kv index capped` warnings co-occurring with this crash are unrelated — they're the existing 1000-value cap that gastrolog-4dh5i scopes. Tracked separately; do not roll into this fix.
- Improving SIGBUS error messages (the runtime panic dump is plenty; a defer-recover would mask the bug we want to fix).

title: Local chunk manager appends to FSM-sealed chunk after crash recovery
description:
## Symptom

After a node crash and restart, the local chunk manager on the recovered node
treats a chunk as active that the cluster's vault-ctl Raft FSM has already
marked sealed. The local manager keeps appending records to that chunk —
past the rotation policy's row cap — even though every node in the cluster
(including the recovered one's own FSM lookup) reports the chunk as
`sealed=true`.

Discovered live on node4 after the SIGBUS crash tracked in
gastrolog-26zu1.

## Concrete evidence

Cluster: 4 nodes, 3 tiers (hot/warm/cold), RF=4, ~10K-row rotation policy.
Crash: node4 SIGBUS at 2026-04-28T05:10:02 (gastrolog-26zu1). Restart:
2026-04-29T09:30:12. Anomaly observed: 2026-04-29T~09:40.

Chunk `06et43ubmlusv7ts57675vd374` in tier `06eso8pf8putddq75ph0trci0g`
(cloud / "cold").

**FSM view, identical from node1 and from node4:**
```
sealed         = true
cloud_backed   = false
compressed     = false
replica_count  = 1
record_count   = 53,084  ← still rising at observation time
```

**On disk under node4** (`data/node4/storage/disk-1/vaults/<vault>/<cloud-tier-id>/06et43ubmlusv7ts57675vd374/`):
```
attr_dict.log   Apr 28 05:10   ← frozen at crash time
source.idx      Apr 28 05:10   ← frozen at crash time
ingest.bt       Apr 29 09:30   ← rewritten on restart open
source.bt       Apr 29 09:30   ← rewritten on restart open
raw.log         Apr 29 09:40   ← actively being written
idx.log         Apr 29 09:40   ← actively being written
attr.log        Apr 29 09:40   ← actively being written
```

The `.bt` files (in-memory IngestTS / SourceTS B-trees) being rebuilt on
restart-open at 09:30 prove the chunk was reopened **as the active chunk** —
that codepath rebuilds the btree from `idx.log` so subsequent appends can
find ingest positions in O(log n). A reopen for read-only access of a sealed
chunk doesn't write `.bt` files.

The `raw.log` / `idx.log` / `attr.log` mtimes at 09:40 prove appends are
actively landing.

**Rotation cap is being violated:** policy is 10K rows; chunk is at 53K and
climbing. So the rotation trigger isn't firing either — likely because the
rotation policy doesn't gate on FSM-sealed state, only on "is this our
active pointer? has it hit its limit?" — and the active pointer on node4 is
this chunk, which seems to have been sealed by the FSM with a row count it
no longer holds.

## Root cause sketch

Two distinct defects entangled:

**A. Chunk-manager restart doesn't reconcile sealed state with FSM.** On
restart, `chunk/file/Manager` enumerates the chunk directories under its
storage root, picks the most recent unsealed one as its active pointer,
and reopens the in-memory btree from `idx.log`. It does NOT consult the
tier FSM (`vaultraft.FSM.TierFSM(tierID).Get(chunkID)`) to ask whether
the cluster has since marked this chunk sealed. Pre-crash, the chunk was
node4's active cloud-tier chunk. While node4 was offline, the rest of
the cluster's vault-ctl Raft applied a CmdSealChunk(vd374) (probably as
part of post-failover cleanup or a lingering retention/transition flow).
On restart, FSM catchup brings in the seal, but the local manager has
already chosen the chunk as its active pointer and won't relinquish it.

**B. Append path doesn't gate on FSM-sealed status.** Even if defect A is
fixed for fresh starts, this defect would still allow a race: a chunk
gets sealed via Raft mid-append (e.g. a leader switches and the new
leader seals the in-flight chunk to take ownership). Records currently
in flight from the active-chunk forwarder still land on the file. The
sealed status is FSM-side metadata; the local Append path doesn't
re-check it before writing.

The combination: the local manager has stale "active" state, FSM has
authoritative "sealed" state, and the append path uses the local state
unconditionally.

## Reconcile doesn't catch this — by design

`reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` (`backend/internal/orchestrator/retention.go:420`)
only deletes chunks **not in the FSM manifest**. `vd374` IS in the manifest
(the FSM has a row for it, just marked sealed). So reconcile correctly
leaves it alone — it's not an orphan. We need a separate reconciliation pass
that detects FSM-sealed-but-locally-active chunks and forces the local
state to match.

## Why this is P1

- **Silent data divergence.** node4 has 53K+ records in a chunk the rest of
  the cluster considers sealed at whatever count it had pre-seal.
  `replica_count=1` means no other node has a copy of the post-restart
  appended records.
- **Permanent data loss risk.** If anything triggers a rebuild from FSM
  (snapshot install, full wipe + rejoin, retention drop of an
  FSM-orphaned chunk on another node) the divergent records on node4
  will be lost without notice.
- **Rotation policy is silently violated.** A 10K-row chunk holding 53K
  rows breaks invariants downstream code may assume (e.g. cloud-blob
  size budgeting, transition planning, search-time bucket sizing).
- **Recurs on every crash.** The recovery path is the only crash recovery
  path; any time a node crashes mid-active-chunk and the cluster seals
  in its absence, this happens. With gastrolog-26zu1 still open, crashes
  are not hypothetical.

## Fix shape

Both A and B need to land. Suggested shapes, in order of how I'd sequence:

1. **Append-side gate (defect B), as the immediate stop-the-bleeding fix.**
   Before `Manager.Append` writes a record, consult the tier FSM for the
   chunk it's about to write to and reject the append if `sealed=true` in
   the FSM. The error should be `ErrChunkSealed` so callers (record
   forwarder, replication) can roll over to a fresh active chunk.
   This needs a `tier FSM` reference threaded into the Manager — gastrolog-554s3
   put the wiring scaffolding in place, the index/file Manager just needs
   a FSM-readable callback added to its Config.

2. **Restart reconciliation (defect A).** On Manager open, after the chunk
   directories are enumerated, walk each chunk and ask the tier FSM:
   - If the FSM has the chunk and it's sealed → mark the local meta sealed,
     do NOT reopen as active, do NOT rebuild `.bt` files for active
     append.
   - If the FSM has the chunk and it's active → reopen as active (current
     behavior).
   - If the FSM doesn't have the chunk → orphan; let
     `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` clean it up after the
     `orphanReconcileMinAge` buffer.

3. **One-shot recovery for `vd374` (and any siblings)** in production: on
   the next retention sweep after both fixes land, identify chunks where
   `local_active=true && fsm_sealed=true`, freeze appends, decide
   authoritatively whether the post-restart appends are recoverable
   (probably not — they were never replicated, never went through the
   leader's CmdAppendRecord) and wipe the divergent records. Or, more
   conservatively, ingest them into a fresh active chunk on a still-RF=N
   node before wiping. Operator decision.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Append rejected with `ErrChunkSealed` when the FSM has the target
  chunk marked sealed, even if the local Manager's active pointer is
  pointing at it.
- [ ] On Manager open, sealed-in-FSM chunks are NOT chosen as the active
  pointer and do NOT have their `.bt` files rebuilt.
- [ ] Regression test: spin up a 4-node cluster harness (orchRel /
  multinode), simulate a follower crash mid-write, advance vault-ctl
  Raft on the surviving nodes to seal the chunk in absence of the
  follower, restart the follower, assert (a) the chunk is recognized as
  sealed locally, (b) no further appends land on it, (c) the cluster
  reaches a consistent record count where node4's post-seal-pre-restart
  contributions are accounted for or explicitly dropped.
- [ ] All of gastrolog-5ff7z's existing reliability tests still pass.

## Files implicated

- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` — Manager.Open, Manager.Append,
  the active-pointer selection on restart, the rotation policy hook.
- `backend/internal/vaultraft/fsm.go` (tier FSM lookup the Manager would
  call into).
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/retention.go` —
  `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` is fine as-is for orphans; a new
  reconcile pass for FSM-sealed-vs-local-active divergence belongs
  here or adjacent to the Manager.

## Out of scope

- The SIGBUS crash that put node4 in this state — gastrolog-26zu1.
- Increasing the KV index 1000-key cap that flooded the WARN logs in
  the same window — gastrolog-4dh5i.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text: Subsumed by gastrolog-51gme. The proposed fixes here (append-time FSM-sealed gate, restart-time FSM↔local reconciliation) both become emergent properties of the unified TierLifecycleReconciler — specifically the missing FSM CmdSealChunk callback that 51gme requires landing first. Keeping this issue open as a regression-test target: when 51gme is verified, the steady-state scenario described here (FSM seals a chunk while node is offline, node restarts, no further appends land on the sealed chunk) becomes one of the reliability harness assertions.

title: Vault inspector wraps chunk IDs to two lines instead of single-line truncation
description:
## Symptom

In the vault inspector's chunk list (Tier panel), each chunk-ID cell renders as TWO LINES when the column is narrow enough:

```
06etgsu...
rgv9g
```

instead of the intended single-line middle-truncation:

```
06etgsu...rgv9g
```

Visible across the full column on every chunk row when the inspector pane is at typical width. Reproduced on the cloud / file tier views in the screenshot attached to the comment thread.

## Where

`frontend/src/components/inspector/VaultCard.tsx` ~line 395:

```tsx
<MiddleTruncate
  className={`font-mono ${c("text-text-muted", "text-light-text-muted")}`}
  title={encode(chunk.id)}
>
  {encode(chunk.id)}
</MiddleTruncate>
```

The `MiddleTruncate` component (from `@re-dev/react-truncate`) is doing its best — it computes `06etgsu...rgv9g` from the full ID — but the cell's containing `<span>` and `<td>` lack the layout constraints that would force the truncation to fit on one line. The neighboring time-range cell at line 405 has `whitespace-nowrap`; the chunk-id cell does not.

## Fix shape

Three options, in increasing rigor:

1. **Add `whitespace-nowrap` + `overflow-hidden`** to the chunk-id cell. Lets `MiddleTruncate` measure correctly and produce a single-line result.
2. **Set a fixed-width column** on the chunk-id `<th>`/`<td>` (e.g. `w-[24ch]` or `min-w-[20ch] max-w-[28ch]`). Stops the table layout algorithm from giving the column whatever the longest neighbor needs.
3. **Both.** Belt-and-suspenders.

Option 1 alone usually does it for `MiddleTruncate`. Option 2 also fixes the secondary issue that the time-range column dominates the row width, leaving the chunk-id column narrow.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Chunk IDs render on a single line at all reasonable inspector widths.
- [ ] Truncation point shows enough leading/trailing characters to disambiguate adjacent chunks (i.e. don't truncate so aggressively that two visible chunk rows look identical).
- [ ] No regression on time-range / status / records / size column readability.
- [ ] Hover tooltip still shows the full ID via the existing `title={encode(chunk.id)}` attribute.

## Notes

- `MiddleTruncate` reads container width to decide how many chars to keep. The wrapping symptom usually means the container has `display: block` or no `whitespace-nowrap` and is letting the truncated ellipsis text break at the `...`.
- The component renders fine in the routes view and other places — the failure is local to the chunk-ID column in `VaultCard.tsx`. Cross-check those other usages for the missing CSS.

title: Unify chunk lifecycle / dead-chunk cleanup behind a single reconciler
description:
## Why

Cleaning up dead chunks is currently spread across at least **eight distinct
