2. `onPruneNode` (L505) — proposes `CmdFinalizeDelete` for each chunk in the `finalizable` slice (chunks whose `ExpectedFrom` was drained by the prune).

Same disease, same cure, same fold target (the apply handler that triggered the callback). Folding both lands in one commit because the FSM-handler change is the same pattern applied twice.

After the fold:
- `applyAckDelete` finalizes when its mutation drains `ExpectedFrom` (single chunk).
- `applyPruneNode` finalizes each chunk in its existing `finalizable` slice (zero new computation — the slice is already computed).
- `onAckDelete` and `onPruneNode` callbacks become audit-only (no `go Apply(...)`).
- `CmdFinalizeDelete` stays in the protocol for explicit external triggers; the leak-prone "natural finalize" path is gone.
- Zero leader-only callbacks remain in the reconciler that propose downstream Raft commands.

title: active-chunk reconcile at seal: per-chunk EventID hash chain + record-level divergence resolution
description:
## Problem

Active chunks accept appends on the leader and replicate to followers via `AppendRecords`. If something happens mid-replication — leader transfer, transient network blip, retry races — follower copies can silently diverge from the leader copy. When the leader seals, only the leader's record sequence is canonical. Records that landed on a follower but not the leader (or vice versa) are silently dropped at seal time.

The chunk seal is a natural cluster-wide synchronization point — replicas have to coordinate the seal anyway. Reusing that coordination to detect and reconcile divergence costs no new round-trips in the happy path.

## Design

### Per-chunk running hash

- Each replica maintains a single `xxh3` running hash per active chunk, updated on every `AppendRecords` apply.
- Combiner: `running = xxh3(running || event_id_bytes)`. Order-sensitive (sequential fold). Deterministic across replicas because every replica sees the same `EventID` for each record (EventID is minted at ingest time as `(IngesterID, NodeID, IngestTS, IngestSeq)` — see `chunk/types.go:229`).
- 8 bytes per active chunk stored alongside `RecordCount` / `Bytes` in the FSM's manifest entry. NOT per-record; just the running fold value.
- Content corruption with EventID intact is a separate bug class and out of scope here. This protocol detects "different set of records OR same set in different order."

### Happy-path seal

- Leader proposes `CmdSealChunk` carrying its final hash.
- Each follower's `applySealChunk` compares its own running hash against the leader's.
- Match → normal seal, ack.
- Mismatch → trigger the divergence-resolution sub-protocol below.

### Divergence resolution

When hashes mismatch on apply:

1. Leader collects the full ordered `EventID` list from every replica (one round trip; ~4 KB per 1k records).
2. Leader computes the union of EventIDs, sorts lexicographically by EventID tuple (`IngestTS, IngesterID, NodeID, IngestSeq` — naturally ordered by ingest time with the other fields disambiguating sub-clock-precision collisions).
3. Leader proposes `CmdReconcileSeal` carrying the canonical ordered EventID sequence.
4. Each replica applies it: walks its local records, keeps those whose EventID is in the canonical list, requests any missing records from peers via the record-level extension of gastrolog-19241's `RequestReplicaCatchup`.
5. When the replica's local sealed chunk matches the canonical list, it acks the seal.

Dedup is implicit: each EventID appears once in the canonical list. Records with identical EventIDs across replicas are the same record by construction.

## Why this composition works

- Per-record state cost: zero (no new per-record fields). EventID already exists; the running hash is one accumulated value per chunk.
- Happy-path overhead: `xxh3` update per append (a few nanoseconds), one fixed-size value compared at seal time.
- Divergence path: ~3 MB transferred for a 50k-record chunk in the worst case. Rare by assumption.
- Reuses existing primitives:
  - `EventID` for identity (already canonical, already used by the query `dedup` operator).
  - `IngestTS`-ordered storage + indexes for natural ordering.
  - `RequestReplicaCatchup` / `CatchupSelectedChunks` (gastrolog-19241) for the peer fetch — just at record granularity instead of chunk granularity. Both protocols become symmetric: chunk-level "we agree this chunk should exist; bring it to me" and record-level "we agree these records should be in this chunk; bring me the ones I'm missing."

## Acceptance

- Every active chunk carries a running hash updated on each apply.
- Seal-time hash mismatch triggers reconcile; matching hashes seal without extra work.
- After a forced divergence (test harness drops some `AppendRecords` to one replica then triggers seal), the sealed chunk on every replica is byte-identical and contains the union of all records that any replica saw.
- Steady-state append throughput regresses by no more than ~1% from the hash update (measured at the ingest rate where seal cadence matters).

## Related

- gastrolog-19241 (peer-to-peer catchup): the chunk-level half of the symmetric protocol; this issue is the record-level half.
- gastrolog-2eclw (orphan active chunk after leader transfer): closely adjacent. If 2eclw's cure is "transiently multiple actives, drain to one by routing new records to the existing one," then those records eventually need to flow through reconcile-at-seal anyway. This protocol is the safety net under that cure.
- gastrolog-15fm8 (finalize leak): unrelated mechanism, same general "leader-only post-apply callback" disease family.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Don't implement straight from the description — poke holes first.**

The protocol above is a sketch from one design session and reaches for a few attractive properties (single hash in header, EventID-keyed dedup, reuse of gastrolog-19241's catchup at finer granularity). Worth a deliberate round of adversarial review before any code lands, looking for at least:

- **Hash determinism under concurrent appends.** `running = xxh3(running || event_id_bytes)` assumes a strict serial order of `AppendRecords` apply on each replica. The vault-ctl Raft apply IS serial per group, so this should hold — but it's worth confirming there's no fast-path that bypasses the apply (e.g. local-append on the leader before the AppendRecords RPC fires) which would mean the leader's running hash and the followers' running hash are folded over different orderings.

- **What happens when the divergence-resolution protocol itself partially fails.** A replica that can't reach any peer for some missing record during reconcile — does it block the seal forever, or seal a degraded chunk and rely on a later catchup? Both have failure modes.

- **Record reordering across the active→seal boundary.** If reconcile-resorts records by EventID lex order, but the active chunk was being appended in arrival order (which may not equal EventID order — e.g. records from two ingesters interleave by arrival, not by `IngestTS`), the sealed chunk's record order changes from the active's. Anything downstream that assumes "sealed order == append order" breaks. Specifically: the ingest_ts index already imposes a sorted view, so query-side this is fine. But cursor-based readers (live tail) might see records reordered at the seal moment if they cached the active layout.

- **Tombstones and the unioned-EventID list.** If one replica deleted a record locally (corruption recovery, manual operator action) and another still has it, the EventID is in the latter's list. Reconcile would resurrect the deleted record on the cleaned replica. We probably want a tombstone mechanism at record granularity, or accept that the canonical list is "ever-recorded EventIDs" and tombstones don't exist at this layer.

- **Active-chunk concurrent writers under the gastrolog-2eclw cure.** If "transiently multiple actives" lets new records flow to the orphan-active until rotation, and the orphan-active had a running hash that the new leader (g-3) doesn't have because g-3 isn't a replica of the orphan, then the new leader can't validate the seal. Interaction between this protocol and 2eclw's cure needs to be made explicit.

- **Cost of the EventID list exchange in the unhappy path.** ~3 MB per 50k-record chunk seems negligible at one seal. At cluster-wide-divergence-storm scale (say, post-network-partition with thousands of in-flight seals), it might not be. Worth a back-of-envelope on the worst case.

If any of these holes are load-bearing, the design changes meaningfully. Don't pre-commit to xxh3-streaming or the single-hash-in-header shape until they're closed.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Hole #7: late-arriving replica with a still-active chunk.**

Scenario: nodes A, B, C in placement; C goes offline with records 1-50 of chunk X locally (FSM still says X is active for C). While C is offline, A and B receive records 51-100 via `AppendRecords` (not Raft-replicated — best-effort fire-and-forget). A proposes `CmdSealChunk` with the canonical hash; A and B apply, hashes match, they seal. C reconnects, vault-ctl Raft replays the log, C reaches `CmdSealChunk` apply. C's running hash (over 50 records) doesn't match the canonical (over 100). What now?

The protocol-as-sketched broke here:
- Reconcile needs network I/O to peers; Raft applies must be fast/synchronous.
- Once the local chunk manager is told to seal, the chunk is immutable — you can't post-hoc append 51-100.
- If C also has records 51-X that A/B never saw (partition-split-brain case), those records aren't in the canonical EventID list and need to be discarded as an un-replicated-write loss.

**Refinement — two-stage commit at the chunk-manager level:**

Stage 1 (Raft apply, synchronous): `applySealChunk` records the canonical hash in the FSM and marks the chunk `sealed`. If `local_running_hash == canonical_hash`, also tell the local chunk manager to finalize. Otherwise mark the local chunk as `sealed-pending-reconcile` — the chunk manager keeps records mutable until reconcile completes.

Stage 2 (background, post-apply, via the existing catchup sweep): walk chunks in `sealed-pending-reconcile`; fetch canonical EventID list from any peer; drop local records not in the list; request missing records via gastrolog-19241's record-level peer fetch; recompute hash; finalize the local seal when it matches.

Worth checking whether the existing `pendingDeletes` / `tombstones` split in the receipt protocol can be reused directly — that's already a "FSM says it's gone, local manager catches up via background work" pattern. Don't invent parallel state if the existing primitive fits.

**Data-loss alert.** Records on C that aren't in the canonical EventID list get discarded at reconcile time. That's standard Raft durability (un-replicated writes are not committed), but it needs to surface loudly: alert + log the discarded EventIDs so an operator can investigate. Quiet data loss is the worst class.

**Promoting this from "hole to poke" to "design requirement":** the two-stage commit isn't optional — it's the only way the protocol composes with realistic operational scenarios where replicas miss seal events. Update the design body when the holes are otherwise resolved.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Design-session update (shower thought) — pre-req nailed down, ack contract clarified.**

Three things converged in conversation:

## 1. Hole #1 (hash determinism) closed by a pre-req: FIFO-per-stream dispatch on the leader

The protocol's rolling-hash assumes every replica folds records in the same order. Vault-ctl Raft apply is serial per group, but the **leader-side replication dispatch is not** today:

- Fire-and-forget records: `fireAndForgetRemote` does `wg.Wait()` per record → ordering preserved per (vault, follower). Holds.
- Ack-gated records (RELP, HTTP X-Wait-Ack): `ackAfterReplication` runs in its own goroutine, parallel with the next record's dispatch. Per-target mutex in `chunk_replicator.send` serializes wire-send but is not FIFO. Two concurrent ack-gated dispatches can race on the lock and land in either order on the wire.

Pre-req fix: every `(vault, follower)` pair gets a **single writer goroutine** draining a FIFO queue. Append paths enqueue, the drainer dequeues and sends in order. Wire order = enqueue order = leader append order. Holds for both ack-gated and fire-and-forget paths after the unification described below.

## 2. Ack contract simplification — collapse the two paths

Followup observation: WE define the ack contract. If a successful append ack means **"durably written at least once on the leader"** (not "durable on N replicas"), then per-record follower→leader acks are unnecessary — the rolling-hash + reconcile-at-seal protocol IS the cross-replica durability proof.

Dies:
- `Record.WaitForReplica` field
- `pendingAcks` / `replicationTask` / `forwardTask` plumbing
- `ackAfterReplication` goroutine path
- `fireAndForgetRemote` vs ack-gated branching at `AppendToVault`
- The `wg.Wait()` per-record workaround in `fireAndForgetRemote`
- The bidirectional shape of the replication stream (server-streams half no longer needed)
- RELP / HTTP X-Wait-Ack code paths setting `WaitForReplica`

Lives, simpler:
- `cm.Append` succeeds locally → ingester gets ack. Single durability point.
- Enqueue command into each follower's per-(vault, follower) outbound stream. Stream's writer goroutine drains FIFO. Order on wire = enqueue order.
- Stream is purely outbound; no return channel for per-record acks.

Two replication mechanisms working in concert:
1. **Real-time fire-and-forget** — dominant path. Records reach followers within milliseconds. Best-effort.
2. **Reconcile-at-seal** — safety net. Catches whatever the fire-and-forget path missed. Repairs before seal completes.

## 3. SEAL ordering invariant (key for the hash protocol)

The leader must enqueue commands to each follower stream in strict order matching its local lifecycle decisions:

```
... record_{k-1}   (chunk N)
    record_k       (chunk N — last before seal)
    SEAL N
    record_{k+1}   (chunk N+1 — first after rotate)
...
```

Enforcement is purely enqueue-order discipline on the leader:
1. Append path enqueues record_k to all follower streams.
2. Local rotation triggers → rotate locally, get new active chunk N+1.
3. Enqueue SEAL N to all follower streams **before returning** from the rotate path.
4. Next record enqueues into chunk N+1 on each follower.

With single-writer FIFO drains on each stream, wire order matches enqueue order, follower applies in wire order, chunk N's rolling hash on the follower closes at the same record set the leader closed it on. Hash match becomes a real proof of identity, not a scheduling lottery.

## 4. Overflow / backpressure / unreachable followers

The simplified shape needs no per-record overflow policy. Backpressure + existing circuit breaker cover it:

- **Healthy follower, queue room** → enqueue, drain.
- **Healthy follower, queue full** → enqueue blocks → rotate/append blocks → ingest backpressures naturally.
- **Unhealthy follower** (timeouts, errors) → `bumpReplicaBackoff` marks it; leader's enqueue path skips that follower's stream entirely until `skipUntil` expires. No unbounded queue growth.
- **Reconnect** → chunk-level catchup ([gastrolog-19241](dcat://gastrolog-19241)) pulls missed sealed chunks; the record-level reconcile-at-seal protocol closes any active-chunk divergence at next seal.

## 5. Documentation contract that ships with this

> A successful append acknowledgment from gastrolog means the record has been durably written to the vault leader's local storage. The record is then fire-and-forget streamed to placement followers' active chunks as soon as possible — best-effort, no per-record acknowledgment. At chunk seal time the reconcile-at-seal protocol verifies that all replicas hold the same set of records via a rolling EventID hash; any divergence (dropped record, reordering, missed write during a transient outage) is detected and repaired before the sealed chunk is committed cluster-wide. If at-multiple-replica durability before-ack is required for your workload, gastrolog is not the right system.

## Holes from comments 1 & 2 — current status

- C1.1 (hash determinism under concurrent appends) → **closed by the FIFO-stream pre-req above**.
- C1.2 (partial divergence-resolution failure) — still open. Need policy: block seal vs seal-degraded.
- C1.3 (record reordering across active→seal boundary) — still open. Cursor-based readers (live tail) need an answer.
- C1.4 (tombstones in unioned EventID list) → **withdrawn** as invented. There's no record-granularity delete; if a record is reachable on any replica during reconcile, it exists by definition.
- C1.5 (interaction with gastrolog-2eclw orphan-active cure) — still open.
- C1.6 (EventID list cost in storm scenarios) — still open. Worst-case bound math needed.
- C2.7 (late-arriving replica with stale hash on CmdSealChunk apply) — still open. The gnarly one.

## Implementation order

1. **First**: FIFO-per-stream dispatch + drop the bidi return half + remove WaitForReplica machinery. Standalone refactor, no protocol change yet. Verifies the ordering invariant by construction.
2. **Then**: per-chunk rolling xxh3 in active-chunk state; fold on AppendRecords apply; ship in CmdSealChunk payload.
3. **Then**: follower-side hash compare on `applySeal`; mismatch path stubbed (log + fail safely).
4. **Then**: divergence-resolution sub-protocol (CmdReconcileSeal, EventID list exchange, record-level catchup via gastrolog-19241 extension).
5. **Then**: address remaining holes (C1.2, C1.3, C1.5, C1.6, C2.7) before any of this is considered done.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Refinements from adversarial review of c3.**

### 1. "Drop the bidi return half" was overstated — need stream-level error signaling

c3 said "Stream is purely outbound; no return channel needed." That's wrong as written.

The current `send()` does `SendMsg(cmd)` then `RecvMsg(ack)` per command. The recv is what produces the `send: %w` / `recv ack: %w` errors that drive `closeStream()` and `bumpReplicaBackoff()`. Without ANY return signal, a dead follower looks identical to a healthy one until the next `SendMsg` blocks long enough to hit a deadline. Backpressure-through-blocking only works if we're confident the underlying TCP/gRPC stream noticed the death.

Refined shape:

- Stream stays **bidirectional in shape**, but the server-stream half changes role: it carries **protocol-level errors only** (malformed command, out-of-sequence apply, follower-side I/O failure, follower-side seal-hash mismatch returned async after `applySeal` runs).
- The leader's writer goroutine does NOT block per-record waiting for a return frame. It enqueues, sends, moves on.
- A **separate reader goroutine** per stream consumes whatever the follower sends back. On any received protocol error or stream EOF, it triggers `closeStream` + `bumpReplicaBackoff`.
- gRPC-level keepalives (already enabled for cluster RPCs) handle "TCP died but no application traffic" detection.

Net effect: still no per-record ack on the hot path; the FIFO drainer is fire-and-forget at the application layer. But the leader does learn quickly when a follower dies — either by RecvMsg error in the reader goroutine or by gRPC keepalive failure.

### 2. Divergence resolution — spell out the set-difference protocol explicitly

c3 said "filter/fetch missing records" without spelling it out. Concretely:

When `applySealChunk` on a follower observes its rolling hash ≠ the leader's hash carried in `CmdSealChunk`:

1. Follower does NOT seal locally yet. Local state: an active chunk with some records, unknown gaps.
2. Leader runs the divergence sub-protocol: collects an ordered EventID list from every replica that holds this chunk. Each replica's list is its complete local EventID sequence (chunk-scoped; small — 16 bytes per record).
3. Leader computes the canonical list = union of all collected EventIDs, sorted by EventID tuple `(IngestTS, IngesterID, NodeID, IngestSeq)`.
4. Leader proposes `CmdReconcileSeal` carrying the canonical ordered EventID list.
5. On apply, each replica:
   a. Walks its own local chunk's EventIDs into a set `local`.
   b. Walks the canonical list. For each canonical EventID `e`:
      - If `e ∈ local`: keep the local record at the new position implied by canonical order.
      - If `e ∉ local`: enqueue a record-level fetch from a replica that DOES have `e` (round-robin among the replicas whose collected list included `e`).
   c. For each `e ∈ local \ canonical`: this can only happen if `e` was contributed by THIS replica only and the canonical list excludes it — impossible since canonical is the union. So this set is always empty. (Sanity check: if it's ever non-empty, that's a protocol bug.)
   d. Rebuild local chunk to canonical order using kept records + fetched records.
6. After rebuild, recompute the local rolling hash; should now match the canonical hash recomputed from the canonical list. Replica `CmdAckReconcileSeal`.
7. Once all replicas ack, the leader proposes `CmdSealChunk` again (or a `CmdFinalizeReconcileSeal`); applySeal now finds matching hashes.

Record-level fetch reuses the existing replication stream from step 1 — leader doesn't need new RPCs; the same FIFO-per-stream carries `RequestSpecificRecord(eventID)` commands and the response flows back on the now-meaningful server-stream half.

### 3. Slow-follower latency-blocked-ingest — NEW HOLE

The agent's critique landed: `replicaBackoff` trips on errors only, not latency. A follower that responds slowly but successfully (high RTT, paged-out disk, slow GC) doesn't trip the circuit. With FIFO-per-stream, the leader's writer goroutine waits for queue room — slow follower caps cluster ingest throughput.

Three options, none yet chosen — adding as **open hole #8**:

a. **Bounded queue + drop-with-tombstone**: queue has a max length. On full enqueue, drop the record's enqueue for that target, record a per-chunk "skipped enqueues count". At seal time, the follower's hash will diverge; reconcile catches up. Pro: ingest never blocks on slow follower. Con: reconcile-at-seal becomes the normal path under sustained slowness, defeating the "rare" assumption.

b. **Latency-based circuit breaker**: track per-stream EWMA of enqueue-to-ack latency (or enqueue-to-drain latency in the no-ack design). Trip backoff when EWMA exceeds threshold. Pro: keeps `replicaBackoff` as the single operational lever. Con: needs careful tuning to avoid flapping.

c. **Operator force-detach RPC**: explicit cluster admin command to mark a follower as "ignore for vault X". The follower gets pulled out of placement, reconciles back in via the existing cluster-wide protocols. Pro: no automatic policy, predictable. Con: requires human action; not a self-healing protocol.

Likely (b) for the steady state with (c) as the emergency lever, but worth a separate design discussion.

### 4. Implementation order — the agent misread

c3 stated the order explicitly: **FIFO-per-stream refactor is step 1; rolling hash is step 2**. Reviewer claimed step 1 is "deploying the rolling hash in FSM state before the FIFO dispatch fix" — that's the reverse of what c3 said. Step 1 stands as written. The hazard the reviewer flagged (spurious hash mismatches if hash deployed before FIFO) is real and is exactly why FIFO comes first.

### 5. Hash-fold single-path invariant — NEW INVARIANT, must be enforced

Reviewer's strongest point. The xxh3 fold is order-sensitive. The leader's fold happens at local-append time (NOT at AppendRecords-apply time, since the leader doesn't apply its own outbound RPCs). For the leader's hash to match every follower's hash, EVERY leader-side append into the active chunk MUST go through the single canonical append path that also folds the hash.

Audit candidates that must be checked (or refactored to converge through the canonical path):

- `cm.Append` — the normal record-stream path. Canonical.
- `ImportRecords` — creates a fresh sealed chunk (not the active one), so the hash fold doesn't apply here. Safe.
- Drain queue replay on startup — currently writes records back via `cm.Append`? Or some other path? Audit.
- Retention transition source-read — should NOT append to an active chunk on the destination; it imports as sealed via `ImportRecords`. But verify.
- The `gastrolog-2eclw` orphan-active cure (whatever its final shape) interacts here. Any "transient multiple actives" path that takes appends needs to either fold the hash on the orphan too, or seal the orphan without a hash compare (treating it as legacy).

Add to acceptance criteria: **"every code path that appends to an active chunk's record sequence must go through the canonical append-and-fold path. A lint rule or runtime panic catches violations."**

### Revised implementation order

1. **FIFO-per-(vault, follower) stream refactor**. One writer goroutine + one reader goroutine per stream. Reader handles only protocol errors and stream-EOF. Drop the per-record bidi ack on the hot path. Drop `Record.WaitForReplica`, `pendingAcks`, `ackAfterReplication`. **No protocol change yet** — just the dispatch refactor and the ack-contract simplification documented for users.
2. **Single-path append invariant**: audit all paths that append to an active chunk's record sequence, force them through the canonical append-and-fold path. Add a runtime check / lint rule.
3. **Rolling xxh3 hash in active-chunk state**: fold on canonical-append. Ship in `CmdSealChunk` payload. Followers compare on apply; **mismatch is a fatal log + drop-into-reconcile-stub** — does not seal yet, just stalls.
4. **Reconcile-at-seal sub-protocol**: `CmdReconcileSeal`, canonical EventID list, record-level fetch via the existing replication stream, set-difference rebuild on each replica.
5. **Latency-based backoff** (or whichever option from hole #8 wins): so slow followers don't cap ingest.
6. **Address remaining holes** (C1.2, C1.3, C1.5, C1.6, C2.7) — none of these block prior steps but all must be closed before this is considered "done."

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Further sharpening from c4 — kills ImportSealedChunk entirely + makes reconcile state-driven.**

Two consequences of the c4 protocol that weren't drawn out explicitly. Both follow from the same core insight: every replica has the same input records (via the FIFO-disciplined real-time stream) and the rolling hash is durable in the FSM. That makes the protocol fully symmetric — no "leader is the data authority" role at seal time or after.

## 1. `ImportSealedChunk` dies in both paths

c4 implied this but didn't say it. Spelling it out:

**Happy path (hashes match at seal):**
- Every replica's active-form already holds the same record sequence in the same order (FIFO + same applied sequence).
- Each replica runs `sealToGLCB` locally against its own active-form files.
- No records cross the wire post-seal. No leader→follower transfer at all.

**Unhappy path (hash mismatch at seal):**
- Each replica independently runs the chunk-scoped k-way merge against its peers via existing cross-replica cursor reads (the same RPC the query engine uses for cross-node search).
- Each replica writes the merged record sequence to its own fresh sealed chunk, computes the rolling hash as it writes, and on completion compares against the canonical hash.
- Still no leader→follower record transfer. The leader's role is just to propose `CmdReconcileSeal`; everyone reconciles independently against the same set of peer chunks and arrives at the same answer because EventID-sorted union with dedup is deterministic.

**Net code that dies:**
- `ImportSealedChunk` RPC + handler
- `scheduleReplication`, `replicateSealedChunk`, `replicateToTarget`
- The "buffer-the-whole-chunk-in-memory" path that hit the gRPC 128MB limit
- `ChunkReplicator.ImportSealedChunk` + the legacy `DeleteChunk`-via-stream path

**Net code that lives in a simpler shape:**
- Real-time `AppendRecords` stream (now FIFO-disciplined)
- Cross-replica cursor reads (already exist for query — now also a reconcile primitive)
- `RequestReplicaCatchup` (now extends from chunk-granularity to record-granularity, but the transport is the same)

## 2. Reconcile becomes state-driven, not seal-time

The rolling hash is durable in FSM (same lifetime as `RecordCount`/`Bytes`). That turns reconciliation into a chunk-state property rather than a seal-time event:

**C2.7 collapses entirely.** Late-arriving replica applies `CmdSealChunk` optimistically: record canonical hash + state=Sealed in the FSM. On apply, if its local rolling hash doesn't match canonical, the chunk transitions to a "needs-reconcile" sub-state and a background trigger schedules the merge. Same code path as seal-time reconcile, just runs async-post-apply instead of in-apply. No separate handling for late-arriving replicas. No apply-time network I/O. Removes the gnarliest open hole.

**Silent corruption gets caught for free.** A periodic integrity sweep recomputes the rolling hash over a sampled (or systematically-walked) sealed chunk and compares against the canonical hash. Mismatch → schedule reconcile. Disk rot, partial-write recovery gaps, bit flips — all caught by the same mechanism.

**Operator-triggered reconcile becomes a one-liner.** "Cluster doesn't trust this chunk anymore" or "I just restored this from backup, verify it" → propose `CmdReconcileSeal`. Every replica reruns the merge. Useful for: post-incident repair, audit-driven re-verification, restore validation.

**Cross-cluster bootstrap / restore.** A new replica joins and locally hydrates chunks from some external source. The FSM holds canonical hashes; the replica computes hashes over its hydrated copies; mismatches trigger automatic reconcile against existing healthy replicas. No special bootstrap-from-snapshot path.

**Implementation collapses to one `Reconcile(chunkID)` operation** called from:
- `applySealChunk` on hash mismatch (seal-time case)
- Late-applied seal whose hash doesn't match local (C2.7 — same code path)
- Background integrity sweep
- Operator RPC

One implementation, four trigger sources.

## Updated implementation order

1. **FIFO-per-(vault, follower) stream refactor + ack-contract simplification** (c4 step 1).
2. **Single-path append invariant audit** (c4 step 2).
3. **Rolling xxh3 hash, durable in FSM for active and sealed chunks** — stored, persisted across snapshots, recomputable on demand from the chunk's record sequence.
4. **Generic `Reconcile(chunkID)` operation** — the k-way merge + cross-replica fetch + local rebuild. One implementation.
5. **Wire the four triggers**: seal-time mismatch, late-apply mismatch, background integrity sweep, operator RPC.
6. **Kill ImportSealedChunk + the sealed-chunk replication subsystem** — once 1-5 are in place, post-seal transfers are unreachable.
7. **Latency-based slow-follower handling** (hole #8).
8. **Address remaining open holes**: C1.2, C1.3, C1.5.

## Updated open decisions

- **C2.7** → **closed** by the state-driven reconcile shape above.
- **C1.6** (EventID list cost under storms) → **closed**. There's no canonical EventID list anymore; the k-way merge consumes records as a stream, no manifest payload required.
- **Hole #8** (slow-follower policy) — still open. Three options on the table (drop-with-tombstone / latency-EWMA-breaker / operator-force-detach). Default lean: latency-EWMA-breaker for steady state + operator-force-detach as the emergency lever.
- **C1.3** (cursor reordering when reconcile rebuilds a sealed chunk) — slightly bigger surface now that reconcile can fire any time. Live-tail readers may need to be paused across reconcile windows. Open.
- **C1.5** (2eclw orphan-cure interaction) — open but lower stakes. The orphan-active cure currently seals via `AnnounceSeal` without a hash payload; the rolling-hash protocol can grandfather "swept" seals (skip hash check for chunks sealed via the orphan-handling path) or force them through reconcile (more uniform but more I/O on already-quiescent chunks). Spell out before merge.
- **C1.2** (partial reconcile failure) — open. Easier to handle now since reconcile is state-driven: "stalled reconcile keeps the chunk in needs-reconcile state, next sweep retries." Failure isn't fatal, just persistent until the partition heals.

## Properties that fall out

- **No leader has chunk-data authority post-seal.** Replicas are symmetric. Leader's role narrows to triggering protocol transitions.
- **Sealed chunks are integrity-verifiable any time.** Durable hash + recompute-and-compare is the primitive.
- **Reuses existing infrastructure**: cross-replica cursor reads (query engine), EventID-sorted merge (query merge), dedup-by-EventID (query operator), the per-(vault, follower) stream (c4 refactor).
- **The hot path is faster**: no record buffering on the leader at seal time, no gRPC-message-size limits, no record-set retransmission. Each replica just runs its own local seal.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Hole #8 closes + late-arrival case already handled by existing tombstone mechanism.**

## Hole #8 — slow-follower policy: drop on overflow

reconSEALiation produces complete chunks regardless of what the real-time fire-and-forget stream missed. That makes slow-follower drops structurally identical to any other transient miss — divergence detected at seal, repaired by the k-way merge. No special handling needed.

Policy: each per-(vault, follower) outbound stream has a **bounded enqueue queue**. On full enqueue, drop the record's enqueue for that target, log at info, increment a per-stream skipped-enqueue counter. Healthy followers keep up; slow followers fall behind silently; the follower's hash diverges from the leader's hash at chunk seal; reconSEALiation fires and produces the complete chunk on every replica via the symmetric k-way merge.

Net properties:
- Ingest never blocks on a slow follower.
- No latency-based circuit breaker needed (would be a second mechanism doing the same job).
- The existing error-based `replicaBackoff` still applies for genuinely-unreachable followers (skip the stream entirely until backoff expires).
- Operators get a per-stream "drop rate" metric that's a clean health signal: 0 in steady state, non-zero during slow-follower episodes, paired with reconcile activity at seal time.

Hole #8 closed.

## Late-arrival case is already covered by `f.tombstones`

Late node rejoins the cluster carrying a chunk that retention deleted while the node was offline. Existing mechanism handles this end-to-end without changes:

- **`f.tombstones`** in vault-ctl FSM (`backend/internal/vaultraft/vaultctlfsm/fsm.go`) — `map[chunk.ChunkID]time.Time`. Durable, Raft-replicated, survives snapshot install.
- **Tombstone is written** atomically in `applyAckDelete` (when ExpectedFrom drains via the gastrolog-15fm8 fold-finalize) OR in `applyFinalizeDelete` (explicit-finalize path). Tombstone presence = positive proof every node in placement at the time of deletion acknowledged the chunk is gone.
- **Late node's snapshot install** brings `f.tombstones` forward to current cluster state.
- **`SweepLocalOrphans`** (`backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_lifecycle_reconciler.go:614`) walks the local chunk manager's chunks. For each: if no FSM manifest entry, no pendingDelete, AND tombstone exists → `deleteLocalCopy` runs. Files gone.

So a late node with an aged-out local chunk:
1. Snapshot install pulls in the tombstone.
2. `SweepLocalOrphans` sees `tombstoned == true` for the local file.
3. Local files swept silently.

No special reconSEALiation logic needed for this case. The tombstone IS the protocol's answer.

Unwitnessed-writes accepted loss: records the late node had that no current replica observed AND that the cluster collectively retired via retention — those records are gone. Consistent with the documented durability contract from c4: "ack = durably written at least once on the leader; cross-replica durability is provided by the protocol up to retention." A node partitioned off through a full retention cycle loses unwitnessed writes; that's the durability/availability tradeoff being made.

## Adjacent edge: late node with `ExpectedFrom` obligation that never finalized

If the cluster's receipt protocol was waiting on the offline node when retention fired, no tombstone exists (ExpectedFrom never drained). This is the case `44590d7a` already handles via `SweepStalePendingDeleteAcks` on the vault-ctl leader: stale placement-membership entries get pruned out of ExpectedFrom, the receipt finalizes naturally, the tombstone is written. Late-rejoining node then arrives to a world that already has the tombstone.

## Updated implementation order

No change from c5. Hole #8 is now closed; the implementation just needs to honor "drop on overflow" rather than "block on overflow" in step 1 (FIFO-per-stream refactor).

## Updated open decisions

- ~~Hole #8~~ → **closed** with drop-on-overflow policy.
- **C1.3** (cursor reordering when reconcile rebuilds) — open.
- **C1.5** (2eclw orphan-cure interaction with rolling-hash protocol) — open.
- **C1.2** (partial reconcile failure semantics) — open, but lower stakes now that reconcile is state-driven (just stays in needs-reconcile state, next sweep retries; reconcile doesn't have to complete synchronously with anything).

Three remaining; none block first cut.

comments.author: kluzz@radical.org
comments.text:
**Remaining three open holes closed.**

## C1.2 — Partial reconcile failure semantics

**Resolved**: reconcile that can't complete (peer unreachable, peer's own copy in needs-reconcile state, network partition mid-merge) **stalls in the chunk's `needs-reconcile` FSM state**. The next sweep tick retries. No special semantics, no degraded-seal marker, no synchronous block on the whole cluster.

Why this works given the state-driven shape from c5:
- Reconcile is no longer a one-shot at seal — it's a state that gets driven to completion over time.
- Stalled chunks remain readable on whichever replicas already have a consistent version. The chunk's lifecycle just doesn't fully close.
- Permanent partitions get resolved via the same mechanism that handled today's `44590d7a` stale-ExpectedFrom case: when a node drops out of placement, `SweepStalePendingDeleteAcks` (or its reconcile-equivalent) prunes it from per-chunk obligations and the remaining replicas converge.
- Failure is not fatal; it's persistent until either the partition heals or the node falls out of placement.

## C1.3 — Cursor reordering when reconcile rebuilds a chunk

**Resolved**: no special handling; document the rule and call it done.

C1.3 was overstated in c1. The actual reasoning:
- **Normal seal preserves arrival order** — record at position N in active is at position N when sealed.
- **Reconcile rebuilds in EventID-sorted order** — which may differ from arrival order if records arrived non-monotonic across ingesters.
- **But reconcile only fires on divergence**, and divergence means **the replicas already disagreed on the position-to-record mapping**. Replica A had `[r1, r2, r3]` at positions 0-2; replica B had `[r1, r3, r4]`. Position-to-record was already non-portable across replicas. Reconcile makes it consistent — a strengthening, not a weakening.

The "perfect storm" for C1.3 to bite:
1. Hash mismatch at seal (rare).
2. Merge produces a different position-order than what the divergent replica had (only when arrival order on that replica differs from EventID-sort order).
3. A consumer holds a `RecordRef{ChunkID, Pos}`.
4. The consumer fetches via that ref AFTER reconcile rebuilds the chunk.
5. The consumer assumes position-stability across reconcile.

Window between "ref handed out" and "reconcile completes" is bounded by reconcile duration (k-way merge over peer chunks — seconds at typical chunk sizes). Outside that window, ref→record mapping is stable. Inside, only consumers caching refs across the gap notice anything.

Clients that need stable cross-time identity: use `EventID`. Globally unique, cluster-wide, immutable across reconcile. Position is implementation detail.

**Documentation contract that ships with this:**

> Record positions within a chunk are not stable identifiers. They may change if reconSEALiation rebuilds the chunk (happens at seal-time hash mismatch or background integrity check). Consumers that need stable cross-time record identity should use `EventID`. The `RecordRef{ChunkID, Pos}` references returned in query results are valid until reconcile fires on the referenced chunk.

Live-tail / follow readers are unaffected (don't cache positions across active→sealed transition). Sealed cursors are unaffected (handled by existing chunk-lifecycle / mmap invalidation paths the same way as chunk deletion).

## C1.5 — Interaction with gastrolog-2eclw orphan-active cure

**Resolved**: orphan-swept seals **carry a sentinel hash (e.g., all-zeros)** that tells `applySealChunk` to skip the hash compare. Grandfather path.

Reasoning:
- `SweepIdleActiveChunks` (today's `c1c6fd80`) seals stranded active chunks via direct `AnnounceSeal` with locally-fetched metadata. There's no rolling hash to ship because the chunk was orphaned — by definition no live record-stream was flowing, so no replica was folding a hash over it.
- An orphan is **already corruption recovery, not steady-state correctness**. Replicas with copies of an orphan are by definition divergent in content (one of them is the chunk's leader at orphan-creation time; others may have partial records via long-since-stopped streams).
- Forcing orphans through reconcile would: (a) waste I/O on chunks that are by nature already half-rotten; (b) potentially produce worse outcomes than accepting the stranded-state content (the merge sources include divergent peers, no canonical truth exists).
- Best to accept what's there, seal it, let retention age it out.

`AnnounceSeal` from `SweepIdleActiveChunks` carries hash = 0 (all-zeros sentinel). `applySealChunk` interprets hash = 0 as "skip verification; this is a recovery seal." Records the orphan-swept flag in the FSM for audit visibility. Reconcile triggers (background integrity sweep, operator-RPC) treat orphan-swept chunks as out-of-scope (skip them).

A code-level lint or runtime check ensures **only the orphan-sweep path** can produce hash = 0; every normal seal must produce a real hash. Otherwise an accidentally-zero hash would silently disable verification cluster-wide.

## All open decisions now closed

| Hole | Resolution |
|---|---|
| C1.1 | Closed in c4. FIFO-per-stream dispatch enforces deterministic apply order. |
| C1.2 | Stall in needs-reconcile state; sweep retries; partitions heal via placement changes. |
| C1.3 | No special handling. Document that position is non-stable; clients use `EventID` for cross-time identity. |
| C1.4 | Withdrawn in c4. No record-granularity deletion exists; concern was invented. |
| C1.5 | Grandfather: orphan-swept seals carry hash=0 sentinel; verification skipped; reconcile skips orphan-swept chunks. |
| C1.6 | Closed in c5. No canonical EventID list; k-way merge consumes records as a stream. |
| C2.7 | Closed in c5. State-driven reconcile means late-applying replicas just transition into needs-reconcile and run the merge async. |
| #8 | Closed in c6. Drop-on-overflow policy for slow followers; reconSEALiation produces complete chunks regardless. |

## Implementation order (unchanged from c5)

1. **FIFO-per-(vault, follower) stream refactor** + ack-contract simplification.
2. **Single-path append invariant audit** (lint or runtime check).
3. **Rolling xxh3 hash** in active and sealed chunk FSM state. Durable, recomputable.
4. **Generic `Reconcile(chunkID)` operation** — k-way merge against peers, dedup by EventID, local rebuild.
5. **Wire the four reconcile triggers**: seal-time hash mismatch, late-apply hash mismatch (C2.7), background integrity sweep, operator RPC.
6. **Kill `ImportSealedChunk`** and the sealed-chunk record-shipping subsystem.
7. **Document the rules**: ack contract (c4), position-non-stability (C1.3), partial-failure semantics (C1.2).

Acceptance criteria from the original issue stand. With the resolutions above, the protocol is fully specified and ready to be turned into code.

title: chunk-state convergence under cluster topology changes
description:
## Theme

GastroLog's chunk-state machine assumes leader-only post-apply work converges silently — every Raft apply that needs follow-up (propose finalize, seal the orphan active, request the missing replica) runs as an inline callback on the *current* leader. When leadership transfers during the window between apply and callback — the routine case under K8s rolling redeploys, scale-out, eviction — the follow-up work is dropped, and the cluster ends up with stranded FSM state at various points in the chunk lifecycle.

This epic captures the design direction for closing those gaps coherently rather than stacking one new periodic sweep per failure mode.

## Disease

**Leader-only inline post-apply callbacks without atomic guarantees.** The pattern recurs throughout `vault_lifecycle_reconciler.go`:

```go
func (r *VaultLifecycleReconciler) onAckDelete(chunkID, ackingNodeID) {
    if !r.vaultInst.IsRaftLeader() { return }
    // ... check FSM state ...
    go r.vaultInst.ApplyRaftFinalizeDelete(chunkID)
}
```

Three failure modes share this shape:
- Leadership transfers between the apply that triggered the callback and the callback's `go ... Apply(...)` reaching the new leader. The new leader didn't fire `onAckDelete` (the apply already happened in its predecessor's epoch); the followup never lands.
- The leader's goroutine dies (pod cycled mid-flight).
- The followup `Apply` itself fails (network blip) with no retry.

Each manifestation gets a different child issue. The reflex was to add a new periodic sweep per failure mode (the codebase already has `SweepPendingObligations`, `SweepLocalOrphans`, `SweepMissingReplicas`, `SweepStaleLeaderFSMEntries`); each new sweep is polling at the Raft-apply level — the same anti-pattern as `refetchInterval` is at the event-stream level.

## Cure principles

1. **Fold FSM-local state transitions INTO the apply handler.** When the follow-up work is pure FSM mutation (delete map entry, set flag, tombstone), the apply handler that triggered it can do it atomically. No second Raft round trip; every node's apply produces identical state by construction. `applyAckDelete` should remove the `pendingDeletes` entry when `ExpectedFrom` drains to empty, not defer that to `onAckDelete` (gastrolog-15fm8).

2. **Trigger non-FSM-local work from leadership-change events at apply time.** When the follow-up needs network or local-FS work (seal an active chunk that has records, fetch missing records from a peer), the trigger should be "the apply that observed me becoming leader" rather than a periodic sweep. Each leadership change is one event; the work fires once and is retried on failure via a sweep — but the sweep is the safety net, not the primary path.

3. **Relax invariants that lack a clean transfer protocol.** Where the cure-by-handshake is structurally heavy, relax the invariant instead. "Exactly one active chunk per vault" was an accidental simplification; "transiently multiple, drain to one" is the cluster-native version that makes leader-transfer-active-orphan stop being a bug (gastrolog-2eclw).

4. **Reuse existing primitives.** Identity → `chunk.EventID`. Ordering → `IngestTS` + sorted index. Cluster-wide chunk residency → vault-ctl FSM's `placement_set - pendingDeletes.ExpectedFrom`. Per-peer fetch → `RequestReplicaCatchup` from gastrolog-19241. Don't invent new state when existing primitives cover the sub-problem.

## Child issues (concrete instantiations)

- **gastrolog-15fm8** — receipt-protocol finalize leak. Cure: fold finalize into `applyAckDelete`. Smallest landing point; structurally cleanest.
- **gastrolog-2eclw** — orphan active chunk after leader transfer. Cure: relax "one active per vault" to "transiently multiple, drain to one." Routing change is small; rotation policy must include time-based trigger.
- **gastrolog-617m6** — reconcile at seal (per-chunk EventID hash chain + record-level divergence resolution). Safety net under 2eclw's cure: when records have flowed through a chain of active chunks across leader transfers, seal-time reconciliation guarantees no records are silently lost. Depends on 2eclw's design direction being resolved first.

## Out of scope (related but distinct)

- gastrolog-19241 (closed) — peer-to-peer catchup for missing sealed chunks. Currently uses a periodic sweep on the leader; its follow-up is to convert that sweep into a takeover-triggered event with the sweep relegated to safety-net. Worth filing as a separate child under this epic when we're ready to revisit.

## Acceptance

- After a K8s rolling redeploy of 10 pods:
  - Zero "ret"-badged chunks that don't progress (gastrolog-15fm8's symptom).
  - Zero duplicate active chunks (gastrolog-2eclw's symptom — either eliminated by structural cure, or all chunks remain valid actives that drain naturally).
  - Sealed chunks are byte-identical across all replicas (gastrolog-617m6's guarantee).
- Audit of `vault_lifecycle_reconciler.go` finds no `if !IsRaftLeader() return; ... go Apply(...)` pattern remaining outside of explicit operator-triggered paths.

## Design audit (proposed first step before any implementation)

Grep the codebase for the leader-only-post-apply-callback shape:
- `r.vaultInst.IsRaftLeader()` / `r.vaultInst.HasRaftLeader()` checks gating a goroutine that calls `Apply...`.
- Every `SetOn...` callback in vault-ctl FSM (`OnRequestDelete`, `OnAckDelete`, `OnFinalizeDelete`, `OnPruneNode`, etc.) where the callback proposes a downstream Raft command.

Enumerate the full bug family in one pass. Some callbacks may be safely FSM-local; some may justify the sweep-as-safety-net pattern explicitly. The audit itself is the right starting point.

comments.text: Superseded by gastrolog-2i1g9 (FSM-authority migration epic). This epic was the right direction but limited to fixing convergence symptoms one at a time. title: K8s scale-down via kubectl scale strands Raft voters + NodeConfig entries; no auto-prune for unreachable voters
description:
## Symptom

Scaling a K8s StatefulSet down via \`kubectl scale\` (instead of the supported \`just deploy kubernetes-contract <count>\` path) leaves the cluster in a fragile-quorum state:

- Pods terminate cleanly.
- Raft membership keeps the terminated nodes as VOTERs forever.
- The system FSM keeps their \`NodeConfig\` entries forever.
- Quorum tolerance shrinks: an N-voter cluster with K dead voters needs (N/2)+1 reachable, but only (N-K) are reachable. If K > N - quorum, losing one more live node halts writes.

Observed on a 10→3 contract experiment in this session: \`gastrolog cluster status\` reports 5 voters (g-0, g-1, g-2 reachable + g-3, g-4 unreachable), \`config node list\` reports 6 entries (zombies g-3/g-4/g-5). Vault placements DID converge correctly to the live 3 nodes via the placement manager — the cluster is functional, just fragile.

From the operator's perspective it looked like "the cluster refused to let go of those last 2 nodes because they were needed for the replication." The cluster did not actively refuse; the design simply has no path that auto-prunes voters whose pods went away, and the vault with RF=5 generated replication-degraded alerts that read as "still need those nodes."

## Root cause

The supported scale-down recipe (\`deploy/justfile:461-490\` \`kubernetes-contract\`) does two things in order: (1) call \`gastrolog cluster remove-node gastrolog-N\` per pod-to-be-deleted, which fires \`RemoveServer\` against Raft + \`DeleteNode\` against the system FSM; (2) \`kubectl scale --replicas=<target>\`. \`kubectl scale\` alone only does step (2).

There is no automatic detection of "voter has been unreachable for N minutes — propose RemoveServer." [internal/cluster/cluster.go](backend/internal/cluster/cluster.go) has \`RemoveServer\` wired only as the implementation of the explicit \`cluster.RemoveNode\` RPC. Auto-prune isn't trivially safe — "unreachable for 10 minutes" could be a transient partition versus a true decommission, and getting it wrong evicts a real voter and loses one quorum slot worth of fault tolerance.

This is structurally the same shape as the leader-only-callback family captured in gastrolog-3qr8z: a multi-step convergence (pod terminate → Raft RemoveServer → NodeConfig DeleteNode) whose first step can fire independently of the others. The system trusts the operator to drive scale-down through \`cluster.RemoveNode\`, but K8s' default scale-down primitive has no awareness of that contract.

## Acceptance

At least one of the following, preferably both:

1. **K8s preStop hook in the StatefulSet pod spec** that calls \`cluster demote-self\` (or equivalent) before SIGTERM. Lets the pod tell the leader to RemoveServer / DeleteNode for itself before it goes away. Aligns the K8s lifecycle with the Raft lifecycle. Tradeoff: forced terminations (OOM, node failure) skip the hook — those still need (2).

2. **Periodic leader-side reconciler that proposes RemoveServer for voters that have not heartbeated in N minutes.** Configurable threshold (default high — 10 min? 30 min? — to avoid pruning during transient partitions). Logs a warning + alert before pruning. Operator override to disable.

3. **Document the failure mode prominently.** Anyone running \`kubectl scale -- replicas=X\` directly on the gastrolog StatefulSet should be warned in CLAUDE.md / docs that the supported path is the contract recipe.

After fix, the post-scale-down state should be: \`gastrolog cluster status\` reports exactly the number of currently-running pods as voters, \`config node list\` matches, and quorum tolerance is at the structural maximum for that node count.

## Workaround (current operator action)

For a cluster stranded as described, manually clean up each ghost voter:

\`\`\`
kubectl exec -n gastrolog gastrolog-0 -- /gastrolog --home /config cluster remove-node gastrolog-3
kubectl exec -n gastrolog gastrolog-0 -- /gastrolog --home /config cluster remove-node gastrolog-4
...
\`\`\`

Going forward: use \`just deploy kubernetes-contract <count>\` not \`kubectl scale\`.

## Related

- gastrolog-3qr8z (epic) — chunk-state convergence under cluster topology changes. Same disease shape: multi-step convergence whose first step can fire without the others. Worth parenting this issue under that epic.
- The vault placement manager's correct re-placement (placement.go:84-135) saved the cluster from being broken; the stranded-voter state is fragile but functional. Without the placement manager doing its job, this bug would be much worse.

title: DeleteNode FSM apply leaves IngesterAlive / NodeStorageConfig / IngesterAssignments entries stale
description:
## Symptom

Inspector renders ingester status as e.g. \`10/3\` (10 running of 3 selected) after a cluster scale-down + voter cleanup. The 10 reflects stale \`IngesterAlive\` entries in the FSM keyed by node IDs that have been removed via \`cluster remove-node\`.

Reproduces from any cluster contract: scale down N→M, run \`cluster remove-node\` for the departed nodes, refresh the inspector. The ingester-status badge counts stale alive entries forever.

## Root cause

[\`memory/store.go:501\`](backend/internal/system/memory/store.go) and [\`raftstore/store.go:376\`](backend/internal/system/raftstore/store.go) implement \`DeleteNode\` as a single-map mutation: \`delete(s.nodes, id)\`. It does not sweep related FSM state that references the deleted node ID:

- \`IngesterAlive[*][deletedNode]\` — every ingester's alive map keeps the deleted node's status flag.
- \`NodeStorageConfig\` for the deleted node — placement helpers carry a ghost storage.
- \`IngesterAssignments\` if any point at the deleted node — singleton ingesters can be assigned to a node that no longer exists.

Same disease shape as gastrolog-15fm8 (closed): an apply handler mutates one map but defers related state cleanup to a callback that may never fire. \`DeleteNode\` should be a full sweep — every reference to the node ID atomically removed.

## Acceptance

Backend (load-bearing):
- \`DeleteNode\` apply removes \`IngesterAlive[*][nodeID]\` for every ingester, \`NodeStorageConfig\` keyed by the node, and any \`IngesterAssignments\` pointing at it.
- Tests pin: after \`DeleteNode\`, no surviving FSM key references the deleted node.

Frontend (defense-in-depth, also worth doing):
- [\`ingester.ts:runningCount\`](frontend/src/api/model/ingester.ts) intersects the alive map's keys with the current \`liveNodes\` set before counting. Stale entries past the backend sweep don't inflate the badge.

After fix: inspector badge reads \`N/N\` for an AllNodes ingester running healthily on every alive node, regardless of how many nodes have been added and removed over the cluster's history.

## Related

- Parent: gastrolog-3qr8z. Same multi-step-convergence disease as gastrolog-15fm8 (fixed), gastrolog-6bfwk (sibling). \`DeleteNode\`'s apply handler is the natural home for the sweep.
- Sibling: gastrolog-6bfwk — K8s scale-down via \`kubectl scale\` strands Raft voters. Both bugs combine into the same operator-visible "scale-down doesn't fully scale down" complaint; fixing one without the other leaves the other half of the stranding visible.

title: Add runtime info to Help → About; move topic to top
description:
## Goal

Make the **About** topic in the Help dialog show useful runtime information about the running GastroLog process, and surface it as the **first** topic in the help sidebar.

Today [`frontend/src/help/about.md`](frontend/src/help/about.md) is a static markdown blob (project blurb, license, third-party libraries). It does not surface anything about the running instance, which is the first thing a user wants to know when they open About. The topic is also currently the **last** entry in [`frontend/src/help/topics.ts:108`](frontend/src/help/topics.ts#L108) — it should be the first.

## What to add (runtime panel)

Render a runtime-info panel **above** the existing static markdown content for the `about` topic, populated from live RPC data + a new environment detector:

- **Version** — from `HealthResponse.version` (set at build time via [`backend/internal/server/lifecycle.go:21-22`](backend/internal/server/lifecycle.go#L21-L22)). Show commit SHA / build date too if cheap to plumb.
- **Uptime** — from `HealthResponse.uptime_seconds`.
- **This node** — node id (short), node name, address, Raft role (leader/follower/candidate), suffrage (voter/nonvoter). All available from `GetClusterStatusResponse.local_node_id` + the matching `ClusterNode` entry.
- **Cluster size** — `len(GetClusterStatusResponse.nodes)` when `cluster_enabled`, otherwise show "Single-node" / "Cluster disabled".
- **Cluster leader** — leader id (short) + address from `GetClusterStatusResponse.leader_id` / `leader_address`.
- **Detected environment** — k8s / docker / docker-swarm / podman / bare-metal / unknown. **Requires a new backend detector** (does not exist today).

## Environment detection (new backend code)

Add a helper, e.g. `backend/internal/runtime/env.go`, that returns an enum:

| Env | Detection signal |
|---|---|
| `EnvKubernetes` | env var `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` set |
| `EnvPodman` | `/run/.containerenv` exists, or env `container=podman` |
| `EnvDockerSwarm` | Docker signals + Swarm-specific env (`SERVICE_NAME` injected by Swarm tasks) — best-effort; fall back to `EnvDocker` if uncertain |
| `EnvDocker` | `/.dockerenv` exists, or `/proc/1/cgroup` contains `docker` / `/proc/self/mountinfo` contains `/docker/containers/` |
| `EnvBare` | none of the above |

Detection runs **once at startup**, result cached. Expose it through the existing Health RPC (add a `string runtime_environment` field — or an enum) rather than adding a new RPC. Per project rules: delete and renumber proto tags, no `reserved`. Per cluster-first rules: this RPC is already cluster-aware via `WatchSystemStatus`, but About-panel data is per-node, so showing the **local** node's environment is acceptable; the cluster panel could optionally aggregate per-node environments later.

## Move About to the top

In [`frontend/src/help/topics.ts:108`](frontend/src/help/topics.ts#L108), move the `about` entry to be the **first** element of the exported topic tree (above `general-concepts`). Verify the help sidebar reflects the new order and that deep-links to `?topic=about` still resolve.

## Rendering approach

The current `HelpDialog` renders all topics as raw markdown via the `load` function. Two options:

1. **Special-case `about`** in [`HelpDialog.tsx`](frontend/src/components/HelpDialog.tsx): if `topic.id === 'about'`, render a `<RuntimePanel />` React component above the markdown.
2. **Generalize**: allow topic entries to declare an optional React `header` component.

Prefer option 1 — minimal blast radius; option 2 only if a second topic ends up needing the same hook.

The `<RuntimePanel />` component should use existing hooks (`useHealth`, `useClusterStatus` or whatever the current names are in `frontend/src/api/hooks/`) and degrade gracefully on partial data.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] About topic appears as the **first** entry in the help sidebar.
- [ ] Opening About shows a runtime panel listing: version, uptime, node id/name/role/suffrage, cluster size + leader (or "single-node"), detected environment.
- [ ] Static markdown (license, third-party libs) still renders below the runtime panel.
- [ ] Backend env detector lives in its own package, has unit tests covering each detection path (mock filesystem / env vars).
- [ ] `runtime_environment` field added to `HealthResponse` (or equivalent), proto regenerated on both sides via `just gen`.
- [ ] Multi-node test verifies that querying About from any node returns that node's local environment (per CLAUDE.md cluster-first rules — even though this is per-node data, the test confirms the field is populated correctly on every node, not just the bootstrap one).
- [ ] Help-system docs in [`frontend/src/help/about.md`](frontend/src/help/about.md) updated if the static section changes.

## Out of scope

- Aggregating environments across all cluster nodes into a single panel (could be a follow-up if useful).
- Detecting cloud provider (AWS/GCP/Azure metadata endpoints) — keep this issue focused on container/orchestrator detection.
- Showing per-node environment in the cluster topology view.
acceptance: About is the first topic in the help sidebar; opening About shows version, uptime, local node identity (id/name/role/suffrage), cluster size + leader (or 'single-node'), and detected runtime environment (k8s/docker/swarm/podman/bare/unknown); static markdown still renders below the panel; new env detector has unit tests; HealthResponse carries runtime_environment and is verified by a multi-node test.

title: Retention size policy uses logical bytes; UI shows on-disk bytes — confusing mismatch
description:
## Problem

When a vault has a SizeRetentionPolicy with maxBytes = N (e.g. 10 GB), the vault appears to plateau well below N in the UI (observed: ~6 GB for a 10 GB policy on the warm vault). Looks like retention is firing early or the policy is broken. It isn't — the two numbers measure different things.

- **Retention** sums chunks by **logical** `ChunkMeta.Bytes` (raw + attr + idx, uncompressed). See [backend/internal/chunk/retention.go:109](backend/internal/chunk/retention.go#L109).
- **UI / stats RPC** sums `ChunkMeta.DiskBytes` when populated (compressed `.glcb` size), falling back to `Bytes` only when `DiskBytes == 0`. See [backend/internal/server/vault_info.go:154-159](backend/internal/server/vault_info.go#L154-L159) (`accumulateChunkBytes`).

Net effect with typical zstd compression (~60% ratio on log records): a 10 GB logical cap displays as ~6 GB on disk. The cap IS firing where it should — the operator can't tell.

## Why it matters

Operators set retention limits to bound disk usage. Today the configured number and the displayed number measure different things, with no label distinguishing them. An operator who sees "vault is at 6 GB / 10 GB cap, plenty of room" is wrong about both halves of the fraction:

- The 6 GB is on-disk; the cap is logical.
- The headroom they think they have doesn't exist.

This is also why retention sweeps can appear ineffective during incident debugging.

## Options (pick one or combine)

1. **Dual-field stats (safest).** Expose both `logical_bytes` and `disk_bytes` in the VaultStats proto and surface them in the UI. Label the retention cap explicitly as "logical". Don't change retention math.
2. **Label-only fix.** Keep proto and behavior; just rename UI labels: "On-disk" for current DataBytes, and annotate retention-cap settings with "(uncompressed)".
3. **Switch retention to DiskBytes.** Tempting but bad: `DiskBytes` depends on the compression algo/level a given replica wrote with, so two replicas with different write paths would disagree on whether the cap is exceeded. Retention must be deterministic across replicas. **Do not pick this unless we also nail down `DiskBytes` as cluster-canonical, which is a bigger change.**

Recommendation: **option 1**. Operators want to see both numbers, and the cap-vs-display mismatch only confuses if the labels don't disambiguate.

## Acceptance

- VaultStats proto exposes logical and on-disk bytes as separate fields (single `data_bytes` field gone, or kept with a clear name).
- UI shows both, with the retention cap visibly aligned to the logical number (or whichever field retention uses).
- Settings UI for SizeRetentionPolicy explicitly labels the input as logical/uncompressed.
- Existing single-node and multi-node retention tests still pass.
- New test asserts: with a SizeRetentionPolicy of N logical bytes against a vault with compressed chunks where `DiskBytes < Bytes`, retention triggers at logical size N (not disk size N).

## Notes / open questions

- Does `DiskBytes` get populated reliably for all chunk sources (incl. cloud-backed chunks, transition destinations)? If it can be zero, the fallback path in `accumulateChunkBytes` masks the issue in some cases — worth auditing.
- Help page for the retention settings tab probably needs an update too (see CLAUDE.md rule on help/topics.ts + markdown).

## Discovered via

User asked: "why doesn't the warm vault go past ~6 GB with a 10 GB retention cap?" Traced to logical-vs-disk mismatch above.

title: Vault details: move above column header, restructure as labeled grid, add disk/cloud bytes + ingest rate + sparkline
description:
## Problem

The per-vault metadata strip currently lives **under** the chunk table's column header row, and is laid out as a wrapping inline-flex "sentence":

> FILE on GASTROLOG-8  5 chunks  448,659 records  RF=3  → GASTROLOG-6, GASTROLOG-1

This is hostile to scanning. The operator reads column headers (CHUNK ID / TIME RANGE / STATUS / RECORDS / SIZE), then hits a sentence-shaped row of badges and numbers that have no relationship to those columns, then finally hits the actual chunk rows. The vault-level summary is the most important orientation info on the page and it's buried under the table header pretending to be a row.

Source: [frontend/src/components/inspector/VaultCard.tsx:281-326](frontend/src/components/inspector/VaultCard.tsx#L281-L326) (the `<tr>` with the colSpan-5 inline-flex span at line 290).

## Goals

1. **Reorder.** Vault metadata renders **above** the chunk table's column header, not as a pseudo-row inside the table.
2. **Restructure.** Replace the inline-flex sentence with a labeled grid / definition-list layout. Each fact gets a label and a value, scannable column-by-column.
3. **Add the missing facts** an operator actually needs to assess the vault at a glance:
   - **Disk bytes** (sum of `ChunkMeta.DiskBytes`) — "how much storage is this vault consuming on this node"
   - **Logical bytes** (sum of `ChunkMeta.Bytes`) — pairs with disk to show compression ratio and aligns with the retention cap (see gastrolog-3gewc)
   - **Cloud bytes** when applicable — same split for cloud-backed chunks
   - **Records/sec ingest rate** — derived from ingest counter delta over a rolling window (already on backend in `NodeStats` / orchestrator counters)
   - **Sparkline** — ingest rate over the last N minutes, inline, single-row height. Quiet by default, no axes, just a shape.
   - Retention policy summary inline ("size: 10 GB logical" / "ttl: 7d" / "count: 1000") so the operator can compare current usage against the cap without leaving this page.

## Proposed layout (rough)

```
┌─ hot-vault ────────────────────────────────────  [5 chunks]  [448,659 records]  ⚙ ─┐
│                                                                                   │
│  TYPE        file on GASTROLOG-8 → GASTROLOG-6, GASTROLOG-1   RF 3                │
│  RETENTION   size 10 GB logical · ttl 24h                                         │
│  STORAGE     6.8 GB on disk · 10.3 GB logical · — cloud                           │
│  INGEST      ▁▂▃▅▇▆▄▃▂▁▂▃▄  1,245 rec/s · 1.2 MB/s                                │
│                                                                                   │
│  ─── chunks ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│  CHUNK ID         TIME RANGE          STATUS       RECORDS    SIZE                │
│  06f2g6up…7kgi8   May 14 22:09:34…    active 3     12,639     3.2 MB              │
│  ...                                                                              │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Exact labels and grouping are up for refinement, but the principle is: each row is **LABEL  VALUE**, top-aligned, monospace numbers, three-level text hierarchy (label = muted, value = normal, key numbers = bright).

## Notes / things to verify before implementing

- **Backend stats:** `GetStats` already returns `DataBytes` and `SealedChunks` per vault ([backend/internal/server/vault_info.go:154](backend/internal/server/vault_info.go#L154)). Adding logical-vs-disk split is the proto change tracked separately by **gastrolog-3gewc** — that issue is a prerequisite for the storage row above.
- **Ingest rate:** check whether per-vault rate is already aggregated in `PeerState` route stats / orchestrator counters. If not, this needs a new stat to flow up. Per multi-node memory rules, **must aggregate via PeerState broadcast** — single-node ingest counters won't reflect ingesters on other nodes.
- **Sparkline:** prefer reusing whatever histogram / chart primitive the dashboard already uses (search for existing sparkline / mini-chart components before writing one). Re-use the existing CSS palette tokens — no raw hex.
- **React Compiler:** no `useMemo` / `useCallback`; let the compiler handle memoization.
- **Help system:** if this exposes new operator-facing concepts (logical vs disk, cloud bytes), update the relevant help topic + markdown.
- **CLI parity:** `gastrolog inspect vault` and friends should expose the same numbers. Don't ship UI-only.

## Acceptance

- Vault metadata renders above the column header, not inside the table.
- Layout is a labeled grid / definition-list, not a wrapping inline sentence.
- Storage row shows disk bytes, logical bytes, and cloud bytes separately (depends on gastrolog-3gewc landing first or in parallel).
- Ingest rate (rec/s and bytes/s) shown per vault, aggregated across all cluster nodes (multi-node verified).
- Sparkline shows ingest activity over a rolling window. Quiet styling, no axes.
- Retention policy summary surfaced inline with current values, in units matching the cap (logical bytes for size cap).
- Works on all cluster nodes regardless of vault leader location.
- New multi-node test asserts ingest rate aggregation reflects ingesters on remote nodes.

## Discovered via

User screenshot review: hot-vault details row under column header reads like a sentence and lacks key numbers (disk/cloud bytes, ingest rate). Operator-hostile in incident-pressure scenarios.

title: FIFO-per-stream replication dispatch + simplified ack contract
description:
## Goal

Refactor leader-side replication dispatch to one FIFO writer goroutine per `(vault, follower)` pair, drop per-record bidi acks on the hot path, and simplify the documented ack contract to **"durable on the leader at ack time; cross-replica durability provided by the protocol up to retention."**

This is **step 1 of the gastrolog-617m6 reconcile-at-seal epic.** See parent c3–c7 for full design. Standalone refactor — no protocol change yet. The FIFO invariant is the precondition that makes the rolling-hash protocol from steps 3+ deterministic.

## Why

Today's leader-side dispatch is not strictly FIFO per `(vault, follower)`:

- `fireAndForgetRemote` (`backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go:547`) does `wg.Wait()` per record → ordering preserved per target. OK.
- `ackAfterReplication` (`backend/internal/orchestrator/replication.go:69`) runs in its own goroutine, parallel with the next record's dispatch. The per-target mutex in `ChunkReplicator.send` serializes the wire-send but is **not FIFO** — two concurrent ack-gated dispatches can race on the lock and land in either order on the wire.

The reconcile-at-seal protocol (steps 3+) folds a rolling `xxh3` hash over the active chunk's record sequence on every replica. The fold is order-sensitive. If leader-side dispatch is not FIFO, two replicas can see the same records in different orders → hashes diverge → reconcile fires on every seal, defeating the "rare path" assumption.

We also collapse the two ack paths: with reconcile-at-seal as the cross-replica durability proof, per-record follower→leader acks become redundant. Drop the `Record.WaitForReplica` field and the entire `pendingAcks` / `replicationTask` machinery.

## Design

### Per-(vault, follower) stream lifecycle

- Each leader maintains one outbound stream per `(vault, follower)` pair.
- One **writer goroutine** drains a bounded FIFO queue → `SendMsg` on the stream.
- One **reader goroutine** consumes whatever the follower sends back. Its only job: detect protocol errors / stream EOF / gRPC keepalive failure and call `closeStream` + `bumpReplicaBackoff`. No per-record decoding.
- gRPC keepalives (already enabled cluster-wide) handle "TCP died but no application traffic" detection.

### Enqueue contract

- Append path → enqueue record into each follower's stream queue.
- Rotation path → enqueue `SEAL N` into each follower's stream queue **before returning from rotate**. Ensures wire order: `... record_k (chunk N), SEAL N, record_{k+1} (chunk N+1) ...` on every follower.
- Bounded queue size. Default policy per c6: **drop on overflow** (slow followers fall behind silently; reconcile-at-seal catches them up at seal time). Increment a per-stream `enqueue_drops` counter and log at info on first drop in a window.

### Ack contract simplification

- `cm.Append` succeeds locally → ingester gets the ack. Single durability point.
- No per-record waiting for follower acknowledgments anywhere on the ingest hot path.
- Document the contract (deferred to step 7 of the epic; just note here that the user-visible behavior changes).

### Code that dies

- `Record.WaitForReplica` field in `backend/internal/chunk/types.go`.
- `pendingAcks` / `replicationTask` / `forwardTask` plumbing in orchestrator.
- `ackAfterReplication` goroutine path (`backend/internal/orchestrator/replication.go:69`).
- The `WaitForReplica`-driven branching at `AppendToVault` (`backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go:891-897`).
- RELP / HTTP X-Wait-Ack code paths setting `WaitForReplica` (grep `WaitForReplica` for the full list).
- The per-record `wg.Wait()` in `fireAndForgetRemote`.

### Code that lives, refactored

- `ChunkReplicator.send` (`backend/internal/cluster/chunk_replicator.go`) — driven now by the writer goroutine drain, not by per-call mutex acquisition.
- `fireAndForgetRemote` → renamed / inlined as the enqueue helper.
- `ImportSealedChunk` (`backend/internal/cluster/chunk_replicator.go:207`) — **stays for now**; killed in step 6 of the epic after reconcile-at-seal makes it unreachable.

## Acceptance

- Every `(vault, follower)` pair has exactly one writer goroutine and one reader goroutine.
- Wire order on every follower matches leader-side enqueue order, demonstrated by a test that ingests N records + rotations across a 4-node cluster (`setupMultiNode`) and asserts the follower-applied record sequence equals the leader's local sequence.
- `Record.WaitForReplica` field and all consumers are deleted.
- `pendingAcks`, `replicationTask`, `forwardTask`, `ackAfterReplication` are deleted.
- `enqueue_drops` counter is exposed per `(vault, follower)` stream; a slow-follower test (artificial sleep in the follower's apply path) shows ingest does not block on the leader and `enqueue_drops` increments on the slow target only.
- Existing replication tests pass with the new dispatch (`backend/internal/orchestrator/replication_test.go`, `forward_test.go`, `reliability_ingest_lock_test.go`).
- `just backend audit` passes (race + lint + vet + deadcode).
- No protocol additions yet — `CmdSealChunk`, `applySealChunk`, FSM state shape, etc. are unchanged.

## Test coverage required

Per CLAUDE.md "Test Coverage — MANDATORY": all dimensions.

- **Single-node**: dispatch refactor doesn't regress single-node ingest (existing tests cover this).
- **Multi-node**: FIFO order preserved across a 4-node placement; rotation `SEAL N` lands before any `chunk N+1` record on every follower.
- **Happy path**: ack returns to ingester after local durability only; never waits for followers.
- **Unhappy path**: follower-side stream EOF → reader goroutine closes the stream + bumps backoff; subsequent enqueues short-circuit until backoff expires.
- **Edge cases**: queue full → drop + counter increment, no ingest block; rotate path enqueues SEAL between record_k and record_{k+1} even under load; restart survives in-flight enqueues (lost on restart by design — pre-rotation records that hadn't reached the follower are subject to reconcile-at-seal at next seal).

## Out of scope

- The rolling-hash fold itself (step 3).
- Hash compare on `applySealChunk` (step 3).
- Reconcile sub-protocol (steps 4–5).
- Killing `ImportSealedChunk` (step 6).
- User-facing documentation (step 7) — note the contract change in the commit body and tag the docs work for step 7.

## Holes addressed

- **C1.1 (hash determinism)** — closed by this step's FIFO invariant.
- **#8 (slow-follower policy)** — closed by drop-on-overflow.

title: Single canonical append-and-fold path for active chunks (audit + invariant)
description:
## Goal

Make every code path that appends a record to an active chunk's record sequence go through a **single canonical append-and-fold function**, and enforce that with a compile-time + runtime check. Lays the groundwork for the rolling `xxh3` hash in step 3 of gastrolog-617m6.

**Step 2 of the gastrolog-617m6 reconcile-at-seal epic.** See parent c3–c7 for full design.

## Why

The rolling-hash protocol (step 3) folds `running = xxh3(running || event_id_bytes)` on every active-chunk append. The fold is order-sensitive **and append-path-sensitive**: if any code path appends to the active chunk without going through the canonical function, that replica's hash diverges from the leader's even though the records are identical.
