description.new:
## Why

Cleaning up dead chunks is currently spread across at least **eight distinct
code paths** in four files, each with different preconditions, different
trigger cadence, and different error-handling. The scattering has been a
documented stop-gap since early in the project; it is now actively obstructing
debugging and produces silent data divergence after node-down/up cycles.

Concrete pain we already paid for the scatter:

- **gastrolog-uccg6** — FSM-sealed-but-local-active chunk on node4 after
  crash recovery. None of the eight paths handled FSM-side seal divergence;
  required a full cluster restart to trigger the "multiple unsealed → seal
  all but newest" startup-only band-aid in `manager.go:812-829`.
- **gastrolog-3ayz3** — corrupted-chunk transition retry loop. The retention
  sweep had no idea other paths had already classified the chunk as
  unreadable; the sentinel-wrapping fix was a localized patch, not a
  structural one.
- **The catchup boundary is fundamentally broken.** When a node has been
  offline long enough that the rest of the cluster has snapshotted past
  the individual `CmdDeleteChunk` log entries, the rejoining node receives
  an `InstallSnapshot` that sets the FSM state via `FSM.Restore` — which
  does NOT fire the per-entry `onDelete` callback. The local Manager is
  never told to delete those files; the only thing that catches up is a
  periodic `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` walk via
  `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce` — a different code path with different
  preconditions. So we have one mechanism for steady-state and a
  different one for catchup, and neither owns the truth.

## Inventory of current cleanup paths

| # | Path | File | Trigger | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `reconcileTier` | `archival_sweep.go:230` | hourly cron | archive cloud chunks to glacier |
| 2 | `reconcileFollower` (alias) | `retention.go:416` | retention sweep | deprecated wrapper around #3 |
| 3 | `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` | `retention.go:423` | retention sweep, 1m | delete sealed local files NOT in FSM manifest |
| 4 | `expireChunk` | `retention.go:657` | retention rule eval | retention TTL/budget expiry |
| 5 | `maxTransitionStreamedStaleness` force-expire | `retention.go` | 30m grace | force-expire stuck `TransitionStreamed` chunks |
| 6 | `deleteChunkFromTierInstance` | `vault_ops.go:664` | RPC | CLI/UI explicit delete |
| 7 | `cleanOrphanTempFiles` | `manager.go:846` | Manager.Open | startup `.compress-*` / `*.tmp.*` cleanup |
| 8 | "multiple unsealed → seal all but newest" | `manager.go:812-829` | Manager.Open | crashed-mid-rotation seal recovery |

Plus FSM apply hooks:

| Command | Has callback to local Manager? |
|---|---|
| `CmdDeleteChunk` | yes (`onDelete`) — but bypassed by `FSM.Restore` after long offline |
| `CmdSealChunk` | **no** — gastrolog-uccg6 root cause |
| `CmdRetentionPending` | **no** |
| `CmdTransitionStreamed` | **no** |
| `CmdTransitionReceived` | **no** |
| `CmdCompressChunk` | indirect |
| `CmdUploadChunk` | yes (`onUpload`) |

## Target shape: receipt-based deletion list, single reconciler per tier

The redesign generalizes the existing `CmdTransitionStreamed` /
`CmdTransitionReceived` two-phase pattern into an N-way receipt protocol
that survives snapshot install — solving the catchup-boundary problem
structurally instead of with a periodic scrub.

### New FSM state

```go
pendingDeletes map[ChunkID]struct {
    expectedFrom map[NodeID]bool   // nodes still owing an ack
    proposedAt   time.Time          // for staleness / decommission cleanup
    reason       string             // retention-ttl, transition-source-expire, manual, ...
}
```

This map lives in the tier FSM and is part of the snapshot. A node restored
from a snapshot sees both the queued deletions and its own ack obligations.
No special catchup path; replaying becomes uniform with steady-state.

### Three new FSM commands

- **`CmdRequestDelete(chunkID, expectedNodes, reason)`** — proposed by the
  tier leader's retention sweep. Replicated. Adds entry to `pendingDeletes`
  with `expectedFrom = placement-membership-at-decision-time`.
- **`CmdAckDelete(chunkID, nodeID)`** — proposed by every expected node
  after handling its local side. "Handling" = either local file deleted, or
  the node never had it (immediate ack). Replicated. Removes `nodeID` from
  the `expectedFrom` set.
- **`CmdFinalizeDelete(chunkID)`** — proposed by the leader when
  `expectedFrom` is empty. Replicated. Removes the entry from
  `pendingDeletes`.

### Single reconciler per tier instance

```go
type TierLifecycleReconciler struct {
    tier   *TierInstance
    fsm    *vaultraft.TierFSM
    chunks chunk.ChunkManager
}
```

Two interaction modes:

1. **FSM-apply-driven (synchronous, common case).** The tier FSM's apply
   fans out to the reconciler for every chunk-lifecycle command —
   including the missing `CmdSealChunk`, `CmdRetentionPending`,
   `CmdTransitionStreamed`, `CmdTransitionReceived` callbacks alongside
   the existing `CmdDeleteChunk` / `CmdUploadChunk`. The reconciler is
   the only translator from "FSM said X" to "local chunk file changed".
2. **Snapshot-restore-driven (also synchronous).** When the FSM
   `Restore`s from a snapshot, the reconciler is told once. It walks the
   restored `pendingDeletes` map and `expectedFrom` set, processes any
   entries where this node is still expected, and proposes
   `CmdAckDelete` for each.

There is **no periodic disk-vs-FSM walk** in the steady-state design. The
reconciler is event-driven from FSM apply + restore. A defensive periodic
walk is added only if production reveals failure modes the apply path
can't handle (e.g. file-system corruption); it's not part of v1.

### Single deletion code path: `TierLifecycleReconciler.deleteChunk(id, reason)`

All eight current entry points become callers. Logged with `reason`
(`retention-ttl`, `transition-source-expire`, `fsm-delete`, `archived-to-glacier`,
`manual-delete-rpc`, `crash-recovery-seal`, `staleness-force-expire`,
`unreadable`). Audit trail is non-negotiable.

The active chunk is the one exception. The Manager retains authoritative
ownership of the single active chunk per tier until the FSM has applied
the corresponding `CmdSealChunk`. That's the one place local state leads
the FSM — by design, because the active chunk is the ingest sink.
Everything else is an FSM projection.

## Tradeoffs worth naming so the design doesn't backslide

1. **Log volume.** Every delete = `1 + N + 1` Raft entries (Request + N
   Acks + Finalize) where N = placement size. For a 4-node cluster doing
   10 deletes/sec, ~60 entries/sec. For a 50-node cluster doing 100
   deletes/sec, ~5.1K entries/sec. Worth measuring; not worth
   pre-optimizing. Optional `CmdAckDeleteBatch([]ChunkID, NodeID)` once
   the protocol is stable.
2. **FSM state size.** `pendingDeletes` size = in-flight deletes × unsatisfied
   nodes per delete. Bounded under healthy operation. GC pass for entries
   where all `expectedFrom` are decommissioned nodes.
3. **Membership-change semantics.** When a node leaves the placement, its
   pending obligations must be cleared eagerly on the conf-change apply,
   not lazily, otherwise pending entries linger forever waiting for a node
   that's gone.
4. **Decision point unchanged.** The tier (placement) leader still decides
   *what* to delete via retention rule evaluation. Receipt protocol changes
   *how* the deletion fans out. No new authority added.
5. **First-apply optimization (deferred).** A node that proposes the
   request and is also in the expected set could combine
   `CmdRequestAndAck` in one round. Skip until the protocol is stable.

## What this is NOT

- Not a re-architecture of existing FSM commands. `CmdCreateChunk`,
  `CmdSealChunk`, `CmdCompressChunk`, `CmdUploadChunk`,
  `CmdRetentionPending`, `CmdTransitionStreamed`, `CmdTransitionReceived`
  all stay; the issue is wiring (missing local-Manager callbacks for most
  of them) and adding the receipt commands.
- Not a change to retention POLICY evaluation (TTL/budget rules stay
  where they are; only the *execution* of "delete this chunk" goes
  through the receipt protocol).
- Not the indexing rework from gastrolog-4dh5i. Index lifecycle is a
  separate, parallel layer that should follow the same pattern but in a
  separate issue.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `pendingDeletes` map added to tier FSM state and included in
  snapshot serialization. Backwards-compat across format versions
  handled at the FSM serialization layer.
- [ ] `CmdRequestDelete`, `CmdAckDelete`, `CmdFinalizeDelete` commands
  added to `tier/raftfsm`.
- [ ] All current "delete a chunk file" sites converted to call the
  reconciler's `deleteChunk(id, reason)` API. Direct
  `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce`, `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)`, `Manager.Delete`
  calls outside the reconciler are forbidden by linter / commit hook.
- [ ] FSM apply hooks added for `CmdSealChunk`, `CmdRetentionPending`,
  `CmdTransitionStreamed`, `CmdTransitionReceived` so the local Manager
  learns about each lifecycle event without polling.
- [ ] FSM `Restore` triggers a one-shot reconciler pass that walks
  `pendingDeletes` and acks any obligations this node owes. Verified via
  the gastrolog-5ff7z `FollowerWipe_CatchupRebuilds` scenario, where the
  wiped node correctly drops orphan files it acquired before the wipe.
- [ ] Manager.Open's "multiple unsealed → seal all but newest" replaced
  by a reconciler pass that consults FSM and seals according to FSM state.
  Closes gastrolog-uccg6 structurally.
- [ ] `cleanOrphanTempFiles` becomes a reconciler responsibility, not a
  Manager-internal startup hook.
- [ ] Membership-change cleanup: when a node is removed from a vault's
  placement, the leader proposes a follow-up command that removes the
  removed node from every entry's `expectedFrom`. No pending deletes
  block on a decommissioned node.
- [ ] Single deletion log line per chunk includes: chunk ID, tier ID,
  vault ID, reason, ack-source-node-id (when CmdAckDelete fires).
- [ ] Reliability test matrix from gastrolog-5ff7z still passes.
  Specifically: leader kill mid-append, follower wipe + catchup, paused
  peer, ingestion stress, multi-vault isolation.
- [ ] gastrolog-3ayz3's corrupted-chunk-retry-loop scenario tested at
  the reconciler boundary: a chunk classified unreadable is removed via
  the same single deletion path with `reason="unreadable"`.

## Files implicated

- `backend/internal/tier/raftfsm/fsm.go` — new commands, new state,
  new apply branches, snapshot format change, new FSM callbacks
  (`onSeal`, `onRetentionPending`, `onTransitionStreamed`,
  `onTransitionReceived`).
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/retention.go` — paths #2, #3, #4, #5
  consolidated into the reconciler.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/archival_sweep.go` — path #1 routed
  through reconciler.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go` — path #6 routed through
  reconciler.
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` — paths #7, #8 + all direct
  file-deletion call sites; lint rule banning direct `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)`

- New: `backend/internal/orchestrator/tier_lifecycle_reconciler.go` —
  the single owner.

## Sequencing

Each step lands as its own commit (or small PR) so reliability-test

1. Add the missing FSM apply callbacks (`onSeal`, `onRetentionPending`,
   `onTransitionStreamed`, `onTransitionReceived`). Doesn't add behavior

2. Define the receipt protocol commands (`CmdRequestDelete`,

3. Build the `TierLifecycleReconciler` skeleton. Wire FSM callbacks +

title: Unify chunk lifecycle / dead-chunk cleanup behind a single reconciler

description.old:
## Why

Cleaning up dead chunks is currently spread across at least **eight distinct
code paths** in four files, each with different preconditions, different
trigger cadence, and different error-handling. The scattering has been a
documented stop-gap since early in the project; it is now actively obstructing
debugging and produces silent data divergence after node-down/up cycles.

Concrete pain we already paid for the scatter:

- **gastrolog-uccg6** — FSM-sealed-but-local-active chunk on node4 after
  crash recovery. None of the eight paths handled FSM-side seal divergence;
  required a full cluster restart to trigger the "multiple unsealed → seal
  all but newest" startup-only band-aid in `manager.go:812-829`.
- **gastrolog-3ayz3** — corrupted-chunk transition retry loop. The retention
  sweep had no idea other paths had already classified the chunk as
  unreadable; the sentinel-wrapping fix was a localized patch, not a
  structural one.
- **The catchup boundary is fundamentally broken.** When a node has been
  offline long enough that the rest of the cluster has snapshotted past
  the individual `CmdDeleteChunk` log entries, the rejoining node receives
  an `InstallSnapshot` that sets the FSM state via `FSM.Restore` — which
  does NOT fire the per-entry `onDelete` callback. The local Manager is
  never told to delete those files; the only thing that catches up is a
  periodic `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` walk via
  `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce` — a different code path with different
  preconditions. So we have one mechanism for steady-state and a
  different one for catchup, and neither owns the truth.

## Inventory of current cleanup paths

| # | Path | File | Trigger | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `reconcileTier` | `archival_sweep.go:230` | hourly cron | archive cloud chunks to glacier |
| 2 | `reconcileFollower` (alias) | `retention.go:416` | retention sweep | deprecated wrapper around #3 |
| 3 | `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest` | `retention.go:423` | retention sweep, 1m | delete sealed local files NOT in FSM manifest |
| 4 | `expireChunk` | `retention.go:657` | retention rule eval | retention TTL/budget expiry |
| 5 | `maxTransitionStreamedStaleness` force-expire | `retention.go` | 30m grace | force-expire stuck `TransitionStreamed` chunks |
| 6 | `deleteChunkFromTierInstance` | `vault_ops.go:664` | RPC | CLI/UI explicit delete |
| 7 | `cleanOrphanTempFiles` | `manager.go:846` | Manager.Open | startup `.compress-*` / `*.tmp.*` cleanup |
| 8 | "multiple unsealed → seal all but newest" | `manager.go:812-829` | Manager.Open | crashed-mid-rotation seal recovery |

Plus FSM apply hooks:

| Command | Has callback to local Manager? |
|---|---|
| `CmdDeleteChunk` | yes (`onDelete`) — but bypassed by `FSM.Restore` after long offline |
| `CmdSealChunk` | **no** — gastrolog-uccg6 root cause |
| `CmdRetentionPending` | **no** |
| `CmdTransitionStreamed` | **no** |
| `CmdTransitionReceived` | **no** |
| `CmdCompressChunk` | indirect |
| `CmdUploadChunk` | yes (`onUpload`) |

## Target shape: receipt-based deletion list, single reconciler per tier

The redesign generalizes the existing `CmdTransitionStreamed` /
`CmdTransitionReceived` two-phase pattern into an N-way receipt protocol
that survives snapshot install — solving the catchup-boundary problem
structurally instead of with a periodic scrub.

### New FSM state

```go
pendingDeletes map[ChunkID]struct {
    expectedFrom map[NodeID]bool   // nodes still owing an ack
    proposedAt   time.Time          // for staleness / decommission cleanup
    reason       string             // retention-ttl, transition-source-expire, manual, ...
}
```

This map lives in the tier FSM and is part of the snapshot. A node restored
from a snapshot sees both the queued deletions and its own ack obligations.
No special catchup path; replaying becomes uniform with steady-state.

### Three new FSM commands

- **`CmdRequestDelete(chunkID, expectedNodes, reason)`** — proposed by the
  tier leader's retention sweep. Replicated. Adds entry to `pendingDeletes`
  with `expectedFrom = placement-membership-at-decision-time`.
- **`CmdAckDelete(chunkID, nodeID)`** — proposed by every expected node
  after handling its local side. "Handling" = either local file deleted, or
  the node never had it (immediate ack). Replicated. Removes `nodeID` from
  the `expectedFrom` set.
- **`CmdFinalizeDelete(chunkID)`** — proposed by the leader when
  `expectedFrom` is empty. Replicated. Removes the entry from
  `pendingDeletes`.

### Single reconciler per tier instance

```go
type TierLifecycleReconciler struct {
    tier   *TierInstance
    fsm    *vaultraft.TierFSM
    chunks chunk.ChunkManager
}
```

Two interaction modes:

1. **FSM-apply-driven (synchronous, common case).** The tier FSM's apply
   fans out to the reconciler for every chunk-lifecycle command —
   including the missing `CmdSealChunk`, `CmdRetentionPending`,
   `CmdTransitionStreamed`, `CmdTransitionReceived` callbacks alongside
   the existing `CmdDeleteChunk` / `CmdUploadChunk`. The reconciler is
   the only translator from "FSM said X" to "local chunk file changed".
2. **Snapshot-restore-driven (also synchronous).** When the FSM
   `Restore`s from a snapshot, the reconciler is told once. It walks the
   restored `pendingDeletes` map and `expectedFrom` set, processes any
   entries where this node is still expected, and proposes
   `CmdAckDelete` for each.

There is **no periodic disk-vs-FSM walk** in the steady-state design. The
reconciler is event-driven from FSM apply + restore. A defensive periodic
walk is added only if production reveals failure modes the apply path
can't handle (e.g. file-system corruption); it's not part of v1.

### Single deletion code path: `TierLifecycleReconciler.deleteChunk(id, reason)`

All eight current entry points become callers. Logged with `reason`
(`retention-ttl`, `transition-source-expire`, `fsm-delete`, `archived-to-glacier`,
`manual-delete-rpc`, `crash-recovery-seal`, `staleness-force-expire`,
`unreadable`). Audit trail is non-negotiable.

The active chunk is the one exception. The Manager retains authoritative
ownership of the single active chunk per tier until the FSM has applied
the corresponding `CmdSealChunk`. That's the one place local state leads
the FSM — by design, because the active chunk is the ingest sink.
Everything else is an FSM projection.

## Tradeoffs worth naming so the design doesn't backslide

1. **Log volume.** Every delete = `1 + N + 1` Raft entries (Request + N
   Acks + Finalize) where N = placement size. For a 4-node cluster doing
   10 deletes/sec, ~60 entries/sec. For a 50-node cluster doing 100
   deletes/sec, ~5.1K entries/sec. Worth measuring; not worth
   pre-optimizing. Optional `CmdAckDeleteBatch([]ChunkID, NodeID)` once
   the protocol is stable.
2. **FSM state size.** `pendingDeletes` size = in-flight deletes × unsatisfied
   nodes per delete. Bounded under healthy operation. GC pass for entries
   where all `expectedFrom` are decommissioned nodes.
3. **Membership-change semantics.** When a node leaves the placement, its
   pending obligations must be cleared eagerly on the conf-change apply,
   not lazily, otherwise pending entries linger forever waiting for a node
   that's gone.
4. **Decision point unchanged.** The tier (placement) leader still decides
   *what* to delete via retention rule evaluation. Receipt protocol changes
   *how* the deletion fans out. No new authority added.
5. **First-apply optimization (deferred).** A node that proposes the
   request and is also in the expected set could combine
   `CmdRequestAndAck` in one round. Skip until the protocol is stable.

## What this is NOT

- Not a re-architecture of existing FSM commands. `CmdCreateChunk`,
  `CmdSealChunk`, `CmdCompressChunk`, `CmdUploadChunk`,
  `CmdRetentionPending`, `CmdTransitionStreamed`, `CmdTransitionReceived`
  all stay; the issue is wiring (missing local-Manager callbacks for most
  of them) and adding the receipt commands.
- Not a change to retention POLICY evaluation (TTL/budget rules stay
  where they are; only the *execution* of "delete this chunk" goes
  through the receipt protocol).
- Not the indexing rework from gastrolog-4dh5i. Index lifecycle is a
  separate, parallel layer that should follow the same pattern but in a
  separate issue.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `pendingDeletes` map added to tier FSM state and included in
  snapshot serialization. Backwards-compat across format versions
  handled at the FSM serialization layer.
- [ ] `CmdRequestDelete`, `CmdAckDelete`, `CmdFinalizeDelete` commands
  added to `tier/raftfsm`.
- [ ] All current "delete a chunk file" sites converted to call the
  reconciler's `deleteChunk(id, reason)` API. Direct
  `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce`, `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)`, `Manager.Delete`
  calls outside the reconciler are forbidden by linter / commit hook.
- [ ] FSM apply hooks added for `CmdSealChunk`, `CmdRetentionPending`,
  `CmdTransitionStreamed`, `CmdTransitionReceived` so the local Manager
  learns about each lifecycle event without polling.
- [ ] FSM `Restore` triggers a one-shot reconciler pass that walks
  `pendingDeletes` and acks any obligations this node owes. Verified via
  the gastrolog-5ff7z `FollowerWipe_CatchupRebuilds` scenario, where the
  wiped node correctly drops orphan files it acquired before the wipe.
- [ ] Manager.Open's "multiple unsealed → seal all but newest" replaced
  by a reconciler pass that consults FSM and seals according to FSM state.
  Closes gastrolog-uccg6 structurally.
- [ ] `cleanOrphanTempFiles` becomes a reconciler responsibility, not a
  Manager-internal startup hook.
- [ ] Membership-change cleanup: when a node is removed from a vault's
  placement, the leader proposes a follow-up command that removes the
  removed node from every entry's `expectedFrom`. No pending deletes
  block on a decommissioned node.
- [ ] Single deletion log line per chunk includes: chunk ID, tier ID,
  vault ID, reason, ack-source-node-id (when CmdAckDelete fires).
- [ ] Reliability test matrix from gastrolog-5ff7z still passes.
  Specifically: leader kill mid-append, follower wipe + catchup, paused
  peer, ingestion stress, multi-vault isolation.
- [ ] gastrolog-3ayz3's corrupted-chunk-retry-loop scenario tested at
  the reconciler boundary: a chunk classified unreadable is removed via
  the same single deletion path with `reason="unreadable"`.

## Files implicated

- `backend/internal/tier/raftfsm/fsm.go` — new commands, new state,
  new apply branches, snapshot format change, new FSM callbacks
  (`onSeal`, `onRetentionPending`, `onTransitionStreamed`,
  `onTransitionReceived`).
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/retention.go` — paths #2, #3, #4, #5
  consolidated into the reconciler.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/archival_sweep.go` — path #1 routed
  through reconciler.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go` — path #6 routed through
  reconciler.
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` — paths #7, #8 + all direct
  file-deletion call sites; lint rule banning direct `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)`
  outside the reconciler.
- New: `backend/internal/orchestrator/tier_lifecycle_reconciler.go` —
  the single owner.

## Sequencing

Each step lands as its own commit (or small PR) so reliability-test
regressions can be isolated to a single migration.

1. Add the missing FSM apply callbacks (`onSeal`, `onRetentionPending`,
   `onTransitionStreamed`, `onTransitionReceived`). Doesn't add behavior
   yet — wires the hooks. Smallest, low-risk start.
2. Define the receipt protocol commands (`CmdRequestDelete`,
   `CmdAckDelete`, `CmdFinalizeDelete`) and the `pendingDeletes` FSM
   state. Apply branches added; nothing calls them yet. FSM snapshot
   format updated to include `pendingDeletes`.
3. Build the `TierLifecycleReconciler` skeleton. Wire FSM callbacks +
   FSM `Restore` hook. The reconciler now SEES events but doesn't
   propose receipts.
4. Switch path #4 (`expireChunk` retention TTL/budget) from
   `applyRaftDelete(CmdDeleteChunk)` to `reconciler.deleteChunk(reason)`,
   which proposes `CmdRequestDelete`. Each node's reconciler responds
   with `CmdAckDelete`. Verify single-tier behavior end-to-end against
   the reliability matrix.
5. Migrate path #3 (`reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest`) and path #2
   (alias). Becomes a defensive backstop only — most cleanup now flows
   from the reconciler's apply hooks.
6. Migrate path #5 (`maxTransitionStreamedStaleness` force-expire) and
   path #1 (`archival sweep`'s reconcileTier). Same shape.
7. Migrate path #6 (RPC delete). Reconciler call.
8. Migrate paths #7 and #8 (manager.go startup). Manager keeps its own
   house clean *during operation*; reconciler owns lifecycle.
9. Land the lint/commit-hook rule banning direct
   `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce` / `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)` outside the
   reconciler.
10. Membership-change cleanup pass: when a node is removed from
    placement, prune its `expectedFrom` obligations from all pending
    entries.
11. Old `CmdDeleteChunk` (single-shot, no receipts) deprecated and
    removed once no callers remain. The receipt protocol is the only
    delete path.

  peer, ingestion stress, multi-vault isolation.
- [ ] gastrolog-3ayz3's corrupted-chunk-retry-loop scenario tested at
  the reconciler boundary: a chunk classified unreadable is removed via
  the same single deletion path with `reason="unreadable"`.
- [ ] gastrolog-uccg6's FSM-sealed-but-local-active scenario tested via
  a multi-node harness: a node restarted after the cluster sealed a
  chunk in its absence correctly recognises the chunk as sealed locally
  via the reconciler's `FSM.Restore` hook, with no further appends.

## Files implicated

- `backend/internal/tier/raftfsm/fsm.go` — new commands, new state,
  new apply branches, snapshot format change, new FSM callbacks
  (`onSeal`, `onRetentionPending`, `onTransitionStreamed`,
  `onTransitionReceived`).
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/retention.go` — paths #2, #3, #5
  deleted; path #4 reduced to thin caller.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/archival_sweep.go` — path #1 routed
  through reconciler.
- `backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go` — path #6 routed through
  reconciler.
- `backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go` — path #8 deleted; path #7
  optionally folded into reconciler; lint rule banning direct
  `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)` outside the reconciler.
- New: `backend/internal/orchestrator/tier_lifecycle_reconciler.go` —
  the single owner.

## Sequencing

Each step lands as its own commit (or small PR) so reliability-test
regressions can be isolated to a single migration.

1. Add the missing FSM apply callbacks (`onSeal`, `onRetentionPending`,
   `onTransitionStreamed`, `onTransitionReceived`). Doesn't add
   behavior yet — wires the hooks. Smallest, low-risk start.
2. Define the receipt protocol commands (`CmdRequestDelete`,
   `CmdAckDelete`, `CmdFinalizeDelete`) and the `pendingDeletes` FSM
   state. Apply branches added; nothing calls them yet. FSM snapshot
   format updated.
3. Build the `TierLifecycleReconciler` skeleton. Wire FSM callbacks +
   FSM `Restore` hook. The reconciler now SEES events but doesn't
   propose receipts.
4. Switch path #4 (`expireChunk` retention TTL/budget) from
   `applyRaftDelete(CmdDeleteChunk)` to `reconciler.deleteChunk(reason)`,
   which proposes `CmdRequestDelete`. Each node's reconciler responds
   with `CmdAckDelete`. Verify single-tier behavior end-to-end against
   the reliability matrix.
5. **Delete path #3 `reconcileTierDiskAgainstManifest`** and path #2
   alias. Verify cleanup is now driven entirely by the reconciler's
   apply hooks + FSM Restore pass. Reliability matrix must pass.
6. **Delete path #5 `maxTransitionStreamedStaleness`.** Migrate path #1
   `archival sweep`'s `reconcileTier` to thin caller through reconciler.
7. Migrate path #6 (RPC delete). Reconciler call.
8. **Delete path #8** "multiple unsealed → seal all but newest". Replace
   with reconciler's `FSM.Restore`-driven seal pass. Path #7
   (`cleanOrphanTempFiles`) optionally folded in or left as-is.
9. Land the lint/commit-hook rule banning direct
   `chunk.DeleteNoAnnounce` / `os.RemoveAll(chunkDir)` outside the
   reconciler.
10. Membership-change cleanup pass: when a node is removed from
    placement, prune its `expectedFrom` obligations from all pending
    entries.
11. Old `CmdDeleteChunk` (single-shot, no receipts) deprecated and
    removed once no callers remain. The receipt protocol is the only
    delete path.

title.new: Follower-side catchup for sealed chunks missed during pause

description.new:
## Symptom

After a follower node experiences a SIGSTOP / network partition / process
restart that brackets one or more chunk seal events on a tier where it
holds a replica, that follower can be missing the sealed chunk locally
even though its FSM has the manifest entry. The cluster looks healthy
in the inspector — replica count is correct in placement, but one node
is short — until the next placement-membership change forces a catchup.

Reproduces deterministically with SIGSTOP'ing a single node across at
least one rotation interval on a write-heavy tier. Concretely observed
on tier 1 in a 4-node cluster after a multi-minute pause/resume on
node-3: exactly one orphaned-on-follower chunk remained.

## Root cause

Sealed-chunk replication push from the leader fires once at seal time
via replicateToFollower → ImportSealedChunk gRPC. If the follower is
unreachable, the call fails and is logged at Warn — there is NO retry.

ScheduleCatchup (replication_catchup.go) IS the catchup mechanism, but
it is only invoked by the dispatcher when a follower is *newly added*
to placements (dispatch.go:530). A pause/resume of an existing follower
never triggers it because placement membership hasn't changed.

The follower side has no equivalent path either: ReconcileFromSnapshot
on the lifecycle reconciler handles pendingDeletes catchup and sealed-
state projection but does not walk fsm.List() vs tier.Chunks.List()
looking for chunks the FSM knows about that aren't present locally.

So the rejoin-correctness story is asymmetric:
  - Receipt-protocol deletes in flight: covered by SweepPendingObligations
  - Receipt-protocol deletes finalized while offline: covered by
    SweepLocalOrphans (gastrolog-51gme follow-up)
  - Replication pushes lost while offline: NOT COVERED — this issue.

## Proposed fix

Add a third local-state catchup sweep on TierLifecycleReconciler:
SweepMissingReplicas. Walks fsm.List() (sealed entries only), compares
against tier.Chunks.List(), and for each entry present in the FSM but
absent locally asks the placement leader to re-push it via the existing
replicateToFollower machinery.

A new follower→leader RPC (RequestReplicaCatchup) maps to a leader-side
handler that delegates to scheduleCatchupForNode for the requesting
node + chunkID set. No new transport — the leader uses existing
replicateToFollower / ImportSealedChunk plumbing.

Skip rules in the sweep:
  - chunk is CloudBacked → lives in shared object storage, not a
    local-replica concern
  - chunk is tombstoned → FSM contract violation if also in fsm.chunks,
    but defensive skip anyway
  - chunk is already present locally (sealed or active) → no-op

Wire into the existing pendingDeleteSweepAll cron (every 20s, phase-
offset 13/33/53s) so all three reconciler sweeps share a single
catchup tick. Rename the cron entrypoint to reflect the broader scope
(suggested: tierCatchupSweepAll).

Logs at INFO when chunks are pulled, so the recovery is visible in
cluster.log on both follower (request) and leader (push) sides.

## Why follower-driven not leader-driven

A leader-side per-follower retry queue would need to survive leader
change (so: in Raft) and would require persistent "confirmed delivered
to N" state we don't track today — too much infrastructure for the
value. Follower-driven catchup is local, leader-agnostic, and works
regardless of how the divergence arose (pause, partition, snapshot
install, manual rm of a chunk file).

## Test coverage

Per CLAUDE.md mandatory test matrix:
  - Single-node: positive (sweep detects + pulls), negative (no FSM
    entry → no-op), edge (cloud-backed skip, tombstoned skip)
  - Multi-node cluster: 4-node harness; pause one node across a seal
    event; verify chunk arrives within one sweep tick after resume
  - Unhappy path: leader unreachable → next sweep retries; leader
    changes between request and push → new leader's catchup fires;
    chunk gets deleted between request and push → tombstone rejects
    on receiver

## Out of scope

  - Active-chunk live-replication catchup. This issue is sealed-chunk
    only. Live record-stream re-establishment after a pause is a
    separate concern (likely handled by the existing record forwarder)
    and would be tracked separately if it turns out to be broken.

  - Leader-side push retry on transient failure. Could be a follow-up
    optimization but the follower-driven sweep already covers
    eventual consistency at the receiving end.

title.new: UI handlers hang when any cluster peer is paused or partitioned

description.new:
## Symptom

When any cluster node is paused (SIGSTOP, network partition, slow GC,
hung disk I/O), UI requests targeting other nodes hang indefinitely
instead of returning a partial result with the unreachable node
elided. The whole node-handling-the-request appears unresponsive
because each request blocks waiting for a gRPC that will never
respond.

Reproduces: 4-node cluster, SIGSTOP one node, browse the inspector on
any other node. Cluster-status panels work (PeerState heartbeats are
async), but every chunk-list / explain / pipeline-explain action
freezes. Confirmed on multiple non-paused nodes — symptom is
universal, not leader-only as initial observation suggested.

## Root cause

Two UI-facing handlers iterate peer node lists sequentially and
synchronously, with no per-peer timeout and no liveness filter:

  - server/vault_chunks.go ListChunks: for _, nodeID := range
    remoteNodes calls remoteChunkLister.ListChunks(ctx, nodeID, ...)
    inside the loop. A single paused peer blocks the loop until gRPC
    keepalive eventually closes the connection (minutes).

  - server/query_explain.go collectRemoteExplain: same shape; calls
    remoteSearcher.Explain sequentially per node.

Other paths (collectRemote in query_remote.go, peer broadcasts in
PeerState) parallelize via wg.Go or are async by design, so they
remain responsive. The two broken handlers were written before that
pattern was established.

## Proposed fix

Three changes per affected handler:

  1. Parallelize the per-peer calls via wg.Go + sync.Mutex over the
     accumulator (mirror collectRemote's pattern).

  2. Apply a per-peer context timeout (suggested 3-5s) so a hung peer
     fails fast instead of blocking on TCP keepalive. The full handler
     returns the partial-but-fast view operators expect.

  3. Optionally skip nodes already known unreachable via PeerState.
     Reduces cluster log noise; not strictly needed for correctness
     since per-peer timeout already bounds the wait.

After fixing the two known offenders, sweep the server package for
other sequential for _, nodeID := range … { … remoteX(ctx, nodeID, …)
} patterns and migrate them to the same shape.

## Test coverage

  - Unit: handler with a fake remote that blocks indefinitely returns
    the local-node subset within the per-peer timeout.
  - Multi-node cluster: 4-node harness with one node Paused via
    cluster.Server.Pause() (already exists for reliability tests);
    inspector requests on a non-paused node return within the
    per-peer timeout, marking the paused node's contribution as
    missing rather than hanging.

## Impact

  - Operator: the cluster currently fails to degrade gracefully when
    a node hangs — exactly the failure mode where operators most need
    the inspector to work. P1 reflects any node down breaks the
    inspector for everyone.
  - 2dgvj testing: the missing-replica catchup work cannot be
    verified until the fan-out bug is fixed, since the test recipe
    requires SIGSTOP'ing a node and the UI freezes when that happens.

## Out of scope

  - Async streaming across all UI calls. The simpler fix
    (parallel + per-peer timeout) is sufficient; full streaming is a
    separate optimization for very large fan-outs.

description.new:
## Symptom

On any node that is NOT the placement leader for a vault's tiers,
the inspector's chunk list goes stale over time. Newly-sealed
chunks created on the leader never appear on the follower's
inspector view until the user manually reloads the page. After
reload the list is fresh; subsequent chunks created on the leader
silently fail to appear again.

Symptom is more obvious when one peer is paused/partitioned —
fewer chunk events fire overall — but not caused by the pause:
a slow steady-state cluster shows the same drift.

Discovered while verifying gastrolog-csspr's per-peer-timeout fix.
csspr made the issue visible (inspector no longer hangs, so the
stale cache is plainly observable); the WatchChunks gap itself
predates csspr.

## Root cause

WatchChunks (server/vault_chunks.go:477) subscribes to the LOCAL
orchestrator's ChunkSignal. NotifyChunkChange() fires only when
events happen on the local node:

  - Local ingest/seal (ingest.go)
  - Local delete via reconciler (tier_lifecycle_reconciler.go:645)
  - Local retention actions (retention.go)

When a chunk is sealed on the placement leader and replicated to a
follower, the receiving path on the follower (ImportSealedChunk
handler → tier record import) does NOT call NotifyChunkChange.
So the follower's WatchChunks signal stays silent for events that
originated on the leader.

Compounded by the React Query polling pattern in
frontend/src/api/hooks/useVaults.ts:46-104:

  - Mount: full ListChunks → cache populated
  - Every 5s: ActiveOnly poll → updates record-count/bytes for
    chunks ALREADY in cache; does NOT append new chunks (avoids a
    replicaCount=0 visual glitch from the no-fan-out path)
  - Full re-fetch only on WatchChunks stream invalidation

So follower nodes' inspector caches never get refreshed; new chunks
created on the leader never enter the cache. Reload triggers a
fresh full fetch, which works briefly until the cache drifts again.

The placement leader doesn't show this symptom because every chunk
event in the cluster fires the signal locally on the leader.

## Proposed fix

Call NotifyChunkChange() at every follower-side mutation point that
matters to the inspector view:

  - Sealed-chunk import (cluster/forward.go ImportSealedChunk
    handler / chunk file/manager.go's import path)
  - Sealed-state projection on follower (TierLifecycleReconciler
    onSeal — already projects to local manager, just needs to fire
    the signal afterward)
  - Cloud-upload projection / RegisterCloudChunk on follower
  - Receipt-protocol delete is already wired (deleteLocalCopy fires
    NotifyChunkChange — confirmed)

Cleanest landing site: the chunk Manager's announcer hook, which
already exists for similar concerns. Wire the announcer-fired-event
through to NotifyChunkChange so the announcer is the single place
that says "something visible to the inspector just changed."

## Test coverage

  - Unit: a chunk Manager test that simulates an ImportSealed
    arrival fires the change-signal (via a fake announcer that
    records signal calls).
  - Multi-node cluster: 4-node harness, watch chunk events on a
    non-leader node's WatchChunks stream. Mount the inspector on
    node-2; create a chunk on node-1; assert node-2's stream emits
    a notification within a small bound (e.g. 200ms); assert
    node-2's full ListChunks gets re-fetched.

## Out of scope

  - Redesigning the React Query active-only merge to append new
    chunks. The current rule (no append from active-only path)
    is correct — appending would let replicaCount=0 chunks into
    the cache. Fix at the signal-firing layer instead.

  - Cross-cluster signal propagation (broadcast NotifyChunkChange
    over PeerState). Local firing on each node when the local
    state changes is sufficient — every node sees its own
    follower-side imports and thus fires its own signal locally.

## Related

  - gastrolog-csspr (just fixed) — made this stale-cache symptom
    visible by removing the inspector hang
  - gastrolog-1jijm — original WatchChunks design; assumed every
    chunk event would fire a local signal

title.new: Cloud upload's removeLocalDataFiles bypasses per-chunk lock — SIGBUS regression

description.new:
## Symptom

node2 SIGBUS-crashed with the identical stack trace as gastrolog-26zu1
(JSON indexer pass2 → mmapCursor.Next → DecodeIdxEntry →
encoding/binary.Uint64 fault on a now-invalid mmap region) AFTER the
26zu1 per-chunk lifecycle lock had landed. The lock fix was incomplete.

## Root cause

The 26zu1 fix wrapped CompressChunk and deleteInternal with the
per-chunk RWMutex but missed a third mutation site: uploadToCloud's
removeLocalDataFiles call (manager.go ~3506). uploadToCloud opens a
cursor (RLock), reads records, closes the cursor (RUnlock), uploads
to S3, then unconditionally removes the local raw.log/idx.log/
attr.log files via removeLocalDataFiles. That removal is NOT behind
the per-chunk write lock, so a concurrent indexer Build pass on the
same chunk can have its mmap regions invalidated mid-Next().

The race window is bounded by S3 upload latency (seconds — wide).
Triggered by backfillCloudUploads (cloud_health.go), which schedules
UploadToCloud asynchronously whenever a sealed chunk isn't yet
cloud-backed. PostSealProcess's own serial pipeline (compress →
build → upload) wouldn't trigger this because build's cursor closes
before upload's removeLocalDataFiles runs — but backfill is
independent of PostSealProcess and races against any concurrent
indexer Build on the same chunk.

## Why 26zu1's audit missed it

When introducing the per-chunk RWMutex, I audited paths by symbol
name (Compress, Delete) rather than by what the path actually does
to chunk files. removeLocalDataFiles is buried in step 6 of a
7-step uploadToCloud function whose name doesn't suggest "this
mutates chunk files." Grepping for os.Remove / os.Rename / os.Truncate
against chunk path helpers would have surfaced it; symbol-grep for
"Delete" / "Compress" did not.

## Fix

Take the per-chunk chunkLock.Lock() around uploadToCloud's
removeLocalDataFiles AND the subsequent metadata transition (set
cloudBacked=true, delete from m.metas, insert into cloudIdx) so
the disk transition and meta transition are atomic w.r.t. concurrent
cursors. The cursor-open phase earlier in uploadToCloud uses the
existing OpenCursor RLock and is unaffected.

OpenCursor also needs a defensive re-check: today it snapshots
meta.cloudBacked under m.mu BEFORE acquiring chunkLock.RLock; if
uploadToCloud transitions cloudBacked from false → true between
that snapshot and chunkLock.RLock, OpenCursor proceeds to construct
a local-mmap cursor on now-deleted files. After the fix, OpenCursor
re-checks cloudBacked under the chunkLock and falls back to
openCloudCursor if it changed.

## Audit lesson

When introducing a per-resource lock, audit every os.Remove /
os.Rename / os.Truncate on the resource's storage path, not just
every public method that names the resource. The 26zu1 RWMutex
audit memory should be updated with this rule.

Sweep for other paths beyond uploadToCloud:
  - replaceForwardedChunk in vault_ops.go (allow-listed for
    DeleteNoAnnounce)
  - cloud cache eviction in chunk/file/manager.go
  - any os.RemoveAll on chunkDir(id) outside deleteInternal

## Test coverage

  - Unit: race indexer Build (long-running cursor with per-record
    work) against UploadToCloud on the same chunk — cursor must NOT
    SIGBUS, must observe a clean error or read all records.
  - Multi-node cluster: same backfill-vs-Build scenario — already
    reproduced in production by node2's crash.
  - Existing TestIndexBuildRaceWithCompressionAndDelete should be
    extended to also race UploadToCloud, OR a new test should pin
    the upload-vs-cursor invariant separately.

## Severity

P1 — node-killing crash, recurs whenever cloud backfill races index
build (normal steady-state operation on cloud-backed tiers).
gastrolog-26zu1 was P1 for the same reason and did not fully close
the failure mode.

title.new: EnsureSealed steady-state skip-active breaks downstream-tier delete obligations

description.new:
## Symptom

Receipt-protocol delete obligations get stuck on follower nodes with
"delete chunk: cannot delete active chunk" warnings firing every 20s
on tier 2/3 chunks (downstream from ingest):

  delete obligation: local delete failed
    component=tier-lifecycle-reconciler
    chunk=06etoomtj5pnt0pa86s054hcmc
    reason=retention-ttl source=periodic-sweep
    error="delete chunk: cannot delete active chunk"

The chunk is sealed cluster-wide (FSM authoritative), retention-TTL
scheduled it for delete via the receipt protocol, but the follower's
local Manager active pointer is still pointing at it. fulfillObligation
calls deleteLocalCopy → deleteInternal → returns ErrActiveChunk →
ack never lands → pendingDeletes entry never finalizes → tombstone
never created. Sweep cycles forever.

Side effects:

  - SweepLocalOrphans can't clean up orphaned files on rejoining
    nodes because no tombstone gets created (finalize is blocked).
    Old chunks "reappear" on rejoining nodes and stay.

  - Storage / chunk count metrics drift over time as stuck chunks
    accumulate.

## Root cause

The uccg6-followup split (commit e12041ce) introduced two
EnsureSealed variants: EnsureSealed (steady-state, skip-active) and
EnsureSealedAndDemote (recovery, force-demote). The split was
motivated by log-spam from the steady-state path; the right fix
would have been a one-line log-level change (Info → Debug).

The steady-state-skip semantics rest on an assumption that doesn't
hold in all topologies:

> "the leader's record-stream's next TierReplicationAppend for the
> new active chunk authoritatively swaps the follower's active
> pointer within a few ms"

True for ingest tiers (tier 1) where records flow continuously.
False for downstream tiers (tier 2/3, fed only by transitions): no
continuous record-stream means no Append for a new chunk, means the
follower's active pointer never swaps, means it stays pinned at a
sealed-and-pending-delete chunk forever.

The original uccg6 fix (always force-demote) was correct. The split
was an over-correction motivated by perceived log noise. The user
caught both halves of the mistake.

## Fix

  1. Revert the EnsureSealed / EnsureSealedAndDemote split: single
     EnsureSealed method that always force-demotes when the local
     active matches the FSM-sealed chunk. Log at Debug level (not
     Info) to avoid the steady-state spam that motivated the
     incorrect split.

  2. Update reconciler.fulfillObligation to call EnsureSealed before
     deleteLocalCopy. The receipt protocol is itself an authoritative
     cluster decision; the local stale active pointer must yield.
     Calling EnsureSealed is the right way to compose the contract:
     "make this chunk sealed locally" is exactly what we need before
     deleting.

  3. Delete TestEnsureSealedSkipsLocalActiveInSteadyState — pinned a
     wrong invariant. Restore the recovery test as
     TestUccg6_EnsureSealedDemotesLocalActive (the original 26zu1
     name).

  4. Remove EnsureSealedAndDemote from chunk.SealEnsurer interface
     and from the file.Manager + test fakes.

## Audit lesson

Update the "don't conflate steady-state and recovery semantics"
feedback memory: a method's log firing on every normal operation is
a SYMPTOM, not always a behavior bug. Demote the log level FIRST.
Only split the API if there's a demonstrable correctness gap in one
of the contexts — not just because one context is louder than the
other.

Also: cluster invariants of the form "X happens because Y happens
continuously" are topology-dependent. Audit the assumption against
ALL tier topologies (ingest, transition-fed, cloud) before relying
on it. The "record-stream will swap active" invariant only holds
for ingest tiers; downstream tiers have no continuous record stream.

## Test coverage

  - Existing TestUccg6_EnsureSealedAndDemoteDemotesLocalActive
    (rename) verifies force-demote on local-active.
  - New TestFulfillObligationDemotesLocalActiveBeforeDelete:
    receipt-protocol fulfillObligation must call EnsureSealed first
    so a delete on a still-active chunk succeeds without
    ErrActiveChunk bouncing.
  - Multi-node cluster: a sealed chunk on a downstream tier's
    follower (no record-stream activity) must still delete cleanly
    on retention TTL.

## Severity

P1 — production cluster has stuck delete obligations spamming logs
every 20s; storage/chunk metrics drift; orphan cleanup blocked
chain-wise. Will reproduce on every cluster with downstream tiers
once any chunk reaches retention TTL.

## Related

  - gastrolog-uccg6 (closed): introduced force-demote semantics; correct.
  - gastrolog-uccg6-followup (closed): split EnsureSealed; this issue
    reverts that split.
  - gastrolog-26zu1 / gastrolog-2owzp (closed): per-chunk RWMutex
    introduction; orthogonal but same family of "FSM is authoritative"
    invariants.

description.new:
## Symptom

The inspector intermittently logs:

  level=WARN msg="rpc error response"
    procedure=/gastrolog.v1.VaultService/GetIndexes
    code=internal
    message="chunk not found: chunk <id> in vault <vault>"

Triggered when the inspector requests indexes for a chunk that has
migrated from the receiving node's local tier to a different tier
(tier 2/3 / cloud). The receiving node's findManagersForChunk walks
its LOCAL tier instances and doesn't find the chunk (because it now
lives on a tier this node doesn't host, or has been uploaded to
cloud and removed locally).

Doesn't break operation, but spams the log. Inspector UI shows the
"missing index" placeholder for chunks that should display indexes.

## Root cause

server/vault_chunks.go GetIndexes is RouteTargeted (forwards to the
"vault-owning node"). The route interceptor's notion of vault-owning
predates the multi-tier-multi-node distribution model: with chunks
moving across tiers, no single node "owns" the vault end-to-end.
The interceptor routes to whichever node it picks; that node may
not host the tier the chunk currently lives on.

orchestrator.findManagersForChunk searches the local node's tiers.
When the chunk has migrated, it returns ErrChunkNotFound. The
caller (server/vault_chunks.go) maps this to gRPC code=internal,
which the rpc_errors interceptor logs at WARN.

## Fix shape

Two layers of correctness possible:

  1. **Route fan-out** (analogous to ListChunks's per-peer fan-out
     via peerFanOut): GetIndexes asks every node hosting any of the
     vault's tiers; the one that has the chunk responds with index
     info; others say "not me" and are elided.

  2. **Cloud-aware lookup**: findManagersForChunk also consults the
     cloud index (m.cloudIdx) for chunks that have migrated to
     cloud. Cloud-backed chunks have indexes too (TS indexes
     embedded in the GLCB blob's TOC); the lookup should return
     those rather than ErrChunkNotFound.

(1) is more general and works for any tier-distribution shape; (2)
is narrower but the common case. Suggest implementing (1) since the
csspr peerFanOut helper makes it nearly free.

## Test coverage

  - Single-node: chunk migrates from tier 1 to tier 2; GetIndexes
    returns the tier-2 index info.
  - Multi-node: chunk lives on a tier this node doesn't host;
    GetIndexes fans out and returns the index info from the node
    that does host it.
  - Cloud-backed chunk: GetIndexes returns cloud-tier index info
    (TS index entries embedded in GLCB blob TOC).

## Severity

P3 — log spam, not an operational failure. Inspector still works
(individual missing indexes display as "no data"); just noisy.
Independent of the receipt-protocol / lifecycle fixes.

## Related

  - gastrolog-csspr: introduced the peerFanOut helper that this
    fix would reuse.
  - gastrolog-2yeht: orthogonal lifecycle fix; this issue does not
    depend on it.

title.new: Local-active chunks on rejoining node stay stuck if FSM has only tombstone

description.new:
## Symptom

After a node SIGBUS-crashes mid-write and rejoins later, chunks
that were active locally at crash time remain on disk as "active"
(unsealed) on the rejoining node, even though the cluster has
finalized their deletion (FSM has tombstone, no manifest entry, no
pendingDeletes entry).

Reproduces: node was active on chunk X at crash time. While
offline, the cluster sealed X, retention-TTL fired,
CmdRequestDelete → CmdAckDelete from surviving nodes →
CmdFinalizeDelete → FSM tombstone. node restarts; Manager.Open
picks X as active (newest unsealed on disk per tier); FSM restored
via snapshot has only the tombstone. None of the existing recovery
paths touch X:

  - projectAllSealedFromFSM iterates fsm.List() — tombstoned
    chunks aren't there.
  - fulfillObligation needs a pendingDeletes entry — finalize
    cleared it.
  - SweepLocalOrphans skips because chunk is !meta.Sealed locally.
  - SweepMissingReplicas only acts on FSM-known chunks; tombstoned
    is excluded.

## Root cause

SweepLocalOrphans was designed for sealed-on-disk chunks only.
gastrolog-2yeht handled the "FSM says sealed for chunk in
fsm.chunks, local says active" case via EnsureSealed force-demote
on the FSM apply / snapshot-restore paths. But the
"FSM-finalized-with-tombstone-only, local-active" case has no
recovery path — it's exactly the orphan sweep's territory but the
sweep's `!meta.Sealed { continue }` filter excludes it.

## Fix shape

Extend SweepLocalOrphans to handle local-active chunks too:

  for _, meta := range metas {
      if r.fsm.Get(meta.ID) != nil { continue }
      if r.fsm.PendingDelete(meta.ID) != nil { continue }
      if !r.fsm.IsTombstoned(meta.ID) { continue }
      // FSM-tombstoned, no live obligation. Demote first if local
      // active (yields m.active=nil + meta.sealed=true), then
      // delete. Same demote-then-delete pattern as fulfillObligation.
      if !meta.Sealed {
          if err := ensurer.EnsureSealed(meta.ID); err != nil { ... }
      }
      deleteLocalCopy(meta.ID)
  }

The four safety gates that made the orphan sweep correct still
apply (FSM tombstoned == positive proof of finalize); only the
"sealed locally" precondition is removed because the demote
handles unsealed local state by closing files first.

## Test coverage

Unit: in-process Manager test that:
  1. Appends records → chunk X is active.
  2. Simulates the FSM-tombstone-only state (call applyFinalizeDelete
     directly on the FSM with no prior CmdRequestDelete).
  3. Calls SweepLocalOrphans.
  4. Asserts the chunk file is removed AND m.active is nil.

## Severity

P1 — silent disk leak on every node SIGBUS / hard restart that
overlaps with retention TTL on the active chunk's tier.
Operationally observed today on node-2 (two stuck active chunks
after this morning's SIGBUS overnight).

## Related

  - gastrolog-2yeht: handled the FSM-still-tracking case
    (sealed/pending). This is the FSM-already-finalized case.
  - gastrolog-uccg6: introduced force-demote-on-FSM-sealed
    semantics.
  - gastrolog-26zu1: triggered the SIGBUS that put node-2 in
    this state.

## Symptom

Records imported via chunk.ChunkManager.ImportRecords (the
cross-node sealed-chunk replication path: leader → follower via
ImportSealedChunk RPC, plus catchup-replication, MoveChunk
fallback, etc.) land in the follower's idx.log with all-zero
EventID fields (IngesterID, NodeID, IngestSeq).

Direct consequences:

  - Histogram EventID dedup (streamedHistogramBuilder.add) skips
    the dedup branch when rec.EventID == zero — records counted
    unconditionally. Cross-node merge of follower-replicated
    records against leader-original records doesn't dedup,
    silently inflating histograms.

  - Any future invariant that relies on EventID identity
    cluster-wide (record forwarder dedup, search-result dedup,
    audit trails) fails for follower-replicated records.

  - Tier-transition cascade: if a chunk gets transitioned starting
    from a follower copy with zero EventID, the records propagate
    through downstream tiers carrying zero EventID forever.

## Root cause

backend/internal/chunk/file/manager.go importState.writeRecord
calls EncodeIdxEntry omitting IngestSeq, IngesterID, NodeID:

    EncodeIdxEntry(IdxEntry{
        SourceTS:   rec.SourceTS,
        IngestTS:   rec.IngestTS,
        WriteTS:    rec.WriteTS,
        RawOffset:  ...,
        RawSize:    ...,
        AttrOffset: ...,
        AttrSize:   ...,
        // MISSING: IngestSeq, IngesterID, NodeID
    }, idxBuf[:])

Compare to the regular Append path (manager.go:465-476) which
includes all three EventID fields.

The fix existed in a stash from gastrolog-4xusf
(commit 2507c8f7 "index on bug/gastrolog-4xusf-histogram-cloud-bars:
git outta here") but was never committed to main. The 4xusf issue
body listed sub-bug 1 as "FIXED" based on the local change, but
the actual main-branch code never received it.

## Fix

Add the three EventID fields to importState.writeRecord's
EncodeIdxEntry call. One-line change.

## Test coverage

  - Unit: append a record via Append (with explicit EventID),
    seal, transfer via ImportRecords to a fresh manager, cursor-
    read it back, assert EventID round-trips intact. Must fail
    pre-fix (zero EventID after import).

  - Defensive: existing chunk/file tests still pass.

## Severity

P1 — silent data-integrity gap that breaks any cluster-wide dedup
invariant. The histogram bump observed during transitions
(reported by user 2026-04-30) is at minimum partially attributable
to this when leadership rotation has caused leader-on-this-node
chunks to come from a previous follower-replica.

    landed in a stash and was never merged.

    has lost count) — landing this closes the cross-replica
    contribution; doesn't necessarily fix the in-flight

title.new: Refresh interval resets to Off on time-range change; off→Ns doesn't fire immediately

description.new:
## Symptom

Two related UX defects in the search-results refresh control:

  1. **Refresh interval silently resets to Off when the user
     changes the time range.** Operator picks "5s" / "10s" / etc.,
     starts a search, then changes the time range (e.g. clicks a
     different histogram bucket, edits last=N, etc.). The
     refresh-interval selector flips back to "Off" without any
     visible signal. Operator expects updates to keep flowing;
     none arrive. Counter-intuitive, costs minutes of confused
     waiting.

  2. **Switching from Off → 5s (or any non-Off) waits a full
     interval before the first refresh fires.** Operator picks
     "5s" expecting an immediate refresh; nothing happens for 5s,
     then the first tick. The picker change should kick a refresh
     immediately AND start the periodic timer.

## Expected behavior

  - Time-range change preserves the current refresh interval.
    Picker stays at whatever the operator selected; periodic
    refresh continues against the new range.
  - Off → non-Off transition fires a refresh immediately, then
    the timer ticks at the chosen interval.
  - Non-Off → Off cancels the next tick (already correct;
    no change needed).
  - Non-Off → different non-Off resets the timer to the new
    interval AND fires an immediate refresh (so the operator
    sees movement right after switching cadence).

## Files implicated

Refresh interval is the picker on the right side of the search
results header (Off / 5s / 10s / 30s / 1m). Likely lives in
SearchView.tsx / SearchResultsHeader.tsx area; the time-range
state probably lives in a higher-level hook (useSearchView or
similar) and a useEffect with a dependency on the time range
resets the interval.

Quick path for the fix (1):
  - Find the useEffect / useReducer reducer that's clearing the
    interval. It's almost certainly a "reset all transient state
    on time-range change" reflex that swept up the refresh
    interval as collateral damage.
  - Remove the interval from that reset.

Quick path for the fix (2):
  - When the interval picker changes from Off to non-Off, fire
    one refetch immediately before scheduling the next setInterval
    tick. Either explicit refetch() call, or cache invalidation,
    or rely on React Query's interval-restart semantics being
    "tick immediately on enable."

## Out of scope

  - Whether the refresh control should be remembered across
    page reloads (separate UX question — could go either way).
  - Adding a visual signal when refresh is paused (separate;
    related to the same area).

## Severity

P3 — UX papercut; not a data correctness issue. Costs operators
time waiting for refreshes that never come. Has thrown the user
"countless times."

description.new:
Every ingester must produce records with a complete EventID — IngesterID, NodeID, and IngestSeq all non-zero. A missing or partially populated EventID silently breaks downstream dedup, replication identity, and any future EventID-keyed correctness mechanism (gastrolog-5qwkw was a near-miss here: histogram dedup uses EventID equality, and zero-EventID records would collapse on shared timestamps).

Add a test per ingester that:

1. Constructs the ingester with a representative config + node identity
2. Drives a sample message through the full ingest path
3. Asserts the resulting record's EventID.IngesterID, EventID.NodeID, and EventID.IngestSeq are all non-zero
4. Asserts IngestSeq increments monotonically across multiple records from the same instance

Targets (one test per ingester package, under backend/internal/ingester/):
syslog, RELP, HTTP, MQTT, file-tail, journald, self, kafka, and any others.

Not a live bug — production paths assign these fields correctly today — but no test currently asserts the invariant, so a future ingester (or refactor) could regress it silently. Belongs in each ingester's own test file so the assertion lives next to the code that owns it.

description.new:
When placement reconfiguration unregisters a tier instance from a node (e.g. after follower nodes go unreachable and placement re-elects), in-flight seal and ImportSealed replication commands targeting that node fail with a misleading error.

The follower returns ErrVaultNotFound, which gets rendered in logs as:
- 'replication: failed to seal remote follower … error="follower rejected command: seal failed: vault not found"'
- 'follower rejected command: import failed: vault not found: tier <T> in vault <V>'

The vault almost always still exists cluster-wide — only the tier instance was evicted from this specific node by non-destructive placement churn (RemoveTierFromVault with deleteData=false in backend/internal/orchestrator/reconfig_vaults.go:375). The wording leads operators to think the vault was deleted, when in reality it is healthy on the surviving placement nodes.

Two source sites:
1. backend/internal/orchestrator/replication.go:32-36 — SealActiveTier returns bare ErrVaultNotFound when findLocalTier returns nil.
2. backend/internal/orchestrator/vault_ops.go:1037-1039 — ImportToTierStorage returns fmt.Errorf("%w: tier %s in vault %s", ErrVaultNotFound, tierID, vaultID) when the local tier ref is nil.

Both conditions are 'tier instance not registered on this node', not 'vault unknown'. The replication-handler then flattens this through 'seal failed: ' / 'import failed: ' string concatenation in backend/internal/cluster/tier_replication_handler.go:109,156, so errors.Is across the wire is already lost — operators only see the rendered string. Fixing the source message is the only lever.

Proposed fix:
1. Add new sentinel in backend/internal/orchestrator/reconfig.go alongside ErrVaultNotFound:
   ErrTierNotLocal = errors.New("tier not registered on this node")
2. Both call sites return: fmt.Errorf("%w: tier %s in vault %s", ErrTierNotLocal, tierID, vaultID)
3. Update the substring check in backend/internal/orchestrator/replication_catchup.go:133 (currently 'strings.Contains(err.Error(), "vault not found")') to also accept ErrTierNotLocal — or better, switch to errors.Is for both sentinels.
4. Audit the codebase for any other string-matching on 'vault not found' that needs widening.

Acceptance:
- Operators reading the log see 'tier not registered on this node: tier <T> in vault <V>' instead of 'vault not found'.
- replication_catchup behavior is preserved (no regression in the catchup path that currently relies on the substring match).
- Tests cover both error paths (SealActiveTier with missing tier, ImportToTier with missing tier) and assert errors.Is(err, ErrTierNotLocal).
- Multi-node test: simulate placement-driven tier eviction and verify the rendered log line on the leader.

Both MigrateVault and MergeVaults predate the multi-tier vault redesign:

- MergeVaults (backend/internal/server/vault_operations.go) calls Orchestrator.SupportsChunkMove, which only inspects ActiveTierChunkManager() — the first tier. For a multi-tier vault, the merge silently ignores chunks in tier 1+ (cloud, cold). Operators see "merge succeeded" but cloud-tier chunks remain orphaned in the source vault.

- MigrateVault treats the vault as having a single type/location, but with the tiered model each tier has its own type and storage placement. Migrating a vault doesn't have a clean meaning anymore.

Decide for each:

1. Remove the action entirely (button + RPC + handler).
2. Refactor to handle multi-tier semantics explicitly: move all chunks across all tiers? require operator to pick one tier? require dest to have matching tier topology?
3. Keep but gate on single-tier vault detection — UI hides the button for multi-tier vaults.

Lean (1) for both unless there is a real workflow that needs them. Neither button has been tested in months. Removing dead admin actions reduces the cognitive surface area of the settings page.

Related: gastrolog-25vur audit noted these as vestiges. Worth doing before any further admin-action additions.

description.new:
## Symptom

The histogram shows a recurring spike in the most recent buckets that
correlates with chunk transition windows. Reproducible at 5m time
range when chunks are rotating every few minutes — the spike appears
during the streaming window, then decays.

5qwkw landed partial mitigations (EventID preservation through
ImportRecords, chunk-level transitionStreamed filter) and was closed,
but the underlying bump is still visible in production.

## Why the existing mitigations are insufficient

- The chunk-level transitionStreamed filter only excludes the source
  chunk AFTER streaming completes (when applyRaftTransitionStreamed
  flips the flag). During the streaming window itself, the source
  chunk has not yet been flagged and contributes to the histogram
  alongside the destination tier's freshly-imported records.
- Record-level EventID dedup would catch the bump (records carry full
  cluster identity), but running computeDedupHistogram unconditionally
  is too expensive — a second eng.Search + collectRemote with Limit=0
  on every histogram refresh, observed to crater throughput under
  channel-pressure load. The previous attempt to drop the
  multiNodeVault gate was reverted.

## Fix shape: hybrid histogram

Compute the histogram in two passes:

1. Cheap chunk-metadata pass for chunks NOT in transition (the
   ComputeHistogram path that already exists). This dominates by
   chunk count and runs in O(chunks).
2. Record-iteration dedup ONLY over chunks where transitionStreamed
   is true OR streaming is actively in progress. Bounded to the
   small set of chunks in the transition window.

Cost scales with rotation rate, not query rate.

## Required: a "streaming-in-progress" flag

The transitionStreamed flag covers post-streaming. Need a complementary
"transitionInProgress" flag set at the START of streaming and cleared
when streaming completes (or fails). Either via a new FSM state or
via in-memory orchestrator state that the histogram path can consult.

Trade-off: marking the source chunk as in-progress and filtering it
during streaming would UNDERCOUNT (destination doesn't have all
records yet). The hybrid approach must dedup at the record level
during this window — chunk-level filter alone won't work either way.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Histogram refresh latency does NOT regress under heavy load.
- [ ] No bump visible in the histogram during chunk transitions in
      either single-node or multi-node clusters.
- [ ] The dedup pass executes ONLY on chunks in the transition
      window (verified via instrumentation or a unit test).
- [ ] Both single-node + multi-node integration tests cover the
      transition window, asserting no bump.

## Out of scope

- Reducing streaming duration itself (separate optimization).
- Removing the chunk-metadata histogram path (still needed for the
  bulk of chunks).

## Related

- gastrolog-5qwkw (closed; partial mitigations landed but bump persists).
- See also the retention staircase issue — collapsing it shrinks the
  total transitional-state window, which compounds with this fix.

title.new: Retention staircase: collapse multi-sweep pipeline to event-driven on FSM applies

description.new:
## Symptom

A chunk reaching its retention TTL takes ~4-5 minutes from "expired"
to "physically deleted". The staircase:

  RetentionPending → TransitionStreamed → RequestDelete → AckDelete → FinalizeDelete

Each state transition is gated on the NEXT retention sweep observing
the previous state. With the default 1-minute sweep cadence, that's
4-5 sweep ticks per chunk. Operationally:

- Chunks linger on disk far longer than necessary.
- Disk-vs-FSM divergence window widens, increasing the surface area
  for filter-bypass paths to misclassify a chunk in a transient state.
- Inspector view shows chunks in intermediate states for minutes at
  a time, even on a fast cluster with no actual problem.

## Fix shape: event-driven advancement

Drive the staircase via FSM-apply callbacks rather than polling sweeps.
The 2ob86 work already established this pattern for the local-state
projection callbacks (onSeal, onUpload, onDelete fire NotifyChunkChange
synchronously on the apply tick). Extend the same pattern to the
retention pipeline:

- onTransitionStreamed apply on a tier hosting a destination → leader
  immediately schedules the receipt-confirmation check (which is
  already implemented as confirmStreamedTransitions but currently
  invoked by the periodic sweep).
- Receipt confirmed (CmdTransitionReceived applies) → leader
  immediately proposes CmdRequestDelete on the source tier.
- CmdAckDelete applies (already wired in tier_lifecycle_reconciler) →
  proposeFinalizeDelete is already on a goroutine; that's fine,
  but the next CmdRequestDelete should not wait for the next sweep.

Each step's cost is small (one Raft apply, one local lookup); cron
sweeps remain as a safety net for catchup after restarts/membership
changes.

## Acceptance

- [ ] End-to-end "TTL expired → chunk gone" elapses in seconds, not
      minutes, on an idle local cluster.
- [ ] Periodic sweep continues to function as a catchup safety net
      (no regression in tests that exercise pause/resume / snapshot
      restore / late-arriving CmdRequestDelete).
- [ ] No new lock-inversion or apply-pump self-cycle hazards
      (recall gastrolog-51gme step 51gme apply-pump deadlock).
- [ ] Multi-node test: trigger retention TTL on a chunk, observe
      it gone from all replicas within a few hundred ms.

## Out of scope

- Reducing the sweep interval itself (orthogonal; cadence still
  needed for catchup).
- Changing receipt-protocol semantics — only the timing of
  next-step proposals.

## Related

- gastrolog-2ob86 (closed) — same FSM-apply-as-broadcast-point pattern.
- gastrolog-51gme (closed) — established the receipt protocol; this
  issue is about driving it event-driven instead of poll-driven.
- See also the histogram hybrid-dedup issue — collapsing this
  staircase doesn't directly fix the bump, but shrinks the lingering-
  chunk window where filter-bypass bugs can hide.

description.new:
## Diagnosis (revised; replaces the original record-dedup framing)

The histogram bug is **not** primarily about transition-window overlap (gastrolog-5qwkw and prior iterations). It's a much simpler arithmetic bug in the per-chunk bucket-count code, which has gone unnoticed because tier 1 happens to satisfy its hidden assumption.

backend/internal/query/histogram.go:timechartChunkByIndex computes per-bucket counts by:

  startPos := findIngestPos(chunkID, bStart)   // physical record position
  endPos   := findIngestPos(chunkID, bEnd)
  counts[b] += int64(endPos - startPos)

This subtraction is correct only when **physical record position monotonically increases with IngestTS** in the chunk file. That holds for tier 1 (records appended in steady ingest, IngestTS stamped at receive time, written immediately — physical position == IngestTS rank). It does NOT hold for chunks built via ImportRecords (i.e. tier 2 and beyond), where records are written in source-WriteTS order and the IngestTS values are scattered across positions.

The on-disk ingest index is sorted by IngestTS — entries are 12 bytes (int64 ts, uint32 pos), written in TS order. backend/internal/index/file/tsidx/format.go:searchTSIndexFile does a correct binary search on the sorted index and computes a correct **entry rank** (loop variable lo) but returns the **pos field** of the entry. Histogram uses the pos field; pos arithmetic is wrong on non-monotonic chunks.

Visible signature in production:
- Tier 1 (rightmost in the histogram, recent): smooth, matches expected ingest rate.
- Tier 2 / 3 (older): jagged, with bars whose heights vary erratically and don't correspond to the ingest rate.

The transition-overlap bump (5qwkw) is layered on top in the most recent buckets and is a separate, smaller-amplitude issue. Every prior fix targeted the overlap; none touched the position-arithmetic bug. That's why every fix appeared to help briefly under medium load (when the overlap component dominated) and regressed under sustained load (when the chunk-count distribution made the position-arithmetic component dominant).

## Fix

Add a method on both the index manager and chunk manager:

  FindIngestEntryIndex(chunkID, ts) (uint64, bool, error)

Returns the rank (entry index in the sorted-by-IngestTS index file) of the first entry with IngestTS >= ts. Unlike FindIngestStartPosition which returns the physical record position, this returns the rank — which is the correct value for "how many records have IngestTS in [bStart, bEnd)" via subtraction.

Implementation: reuse the binary-search loop in searchTSIndexFile, return uint64(lo) instead of the pos field. One-line change at the binary-search level, plus a method exposed on each interface.

Update timechartChunkByIndex to use entry-rank arithmetic:

  startIdx := findIngestEntryIndex(chunkID, bStart)
  endIdx   := findIngestEntryIndex(chunkID, bEnd)
  counts[b] += int64(endIdx - startIdx)

FindIngestStartPosition stays — it's still correct for its intended purpose (positioning a cursor to read records from a given timestamp). The histogram path was just using the wrong tool.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Tier 2/3 histogram bars look as smooth as tier 1 under steady ingest.
- [ ] No regression in tier 1 (where pos == rank, both arithmetics agree).
- [ ] The bucket counts sum to the same total records that ListChunks reports.
- [ ] Histogram refresh stays index-only (no record iteration introduced).

## Out of scope

- The transition-window overlap bump (separate issue, possibly already addressed by the chunk-level transitionStreamed filter; verify after this fix lands and the jaggedness clears).

title.new: Time-range 'All' button immediately bounces back to 5m

description.new:
Symptom: in the Search view's TIME RANGE selector, clicking 'All' visibly highlights briefly then snaps the active preset back to '5m'. The user cannot select an unbounded range from the UI.

Root cause: 'All' is encoded as the absence of any time-range token (no 'last=', no 'start='/'end='), but the search-effect detector treats that exact shape as 'no range chosen — inject the default'.

Trace:
1. User clicks 'All' → frontend/src/components/TimeRangePicker.tsx:131-146 fires onPresetClick('All').
2. Handler in frontend/src/hooks/useTimeRange.ts:12-31 sets timeRange='All', clears rangeStart/rangeEnd, then calls injectTimeRange(q, 'All', isReversed).
3. buildTimeTokens in frontend/src/utils/queryHelpers.ts:52-57 returns ONLY 'reverse=false' for range='All' — no 'last=', no 'start='.
4. URL navigates to that q, the route-q effect in frontend/src/hooks/useSearchView.ts re-runs.
5. resolveQueryEffectAction in frontend/src/utils/queryHelpers.ts:118-131 sees no 'last=' and no 'start=' → returns 'inject-default-range'.
6. The 'inject-default-range' branch in frontend/src/hooks/useSearchView.ts:345-357 hard-codes defaultRange='5m', calls setTimeRange('5m') and rewrites the URL with last=5m.

Net effect: 'All' → '5m' instantaneously, no visible search executes for the unbounded range.

Proposed fix (pick one — needs a small design call):
A) Distinguish 'no directive yet' from 'explicitly all' by encoding 'All' as a sentinel token (e.g. last=all). buildTimeTokens emits 'last=all reverse=…'; resolveQueryEffectAction sees a last= and returns 'search'; backend already accepts 'last=all' or we add a parser branch. Cleanest, also fixes the case where a hand-typed query without last= currently gets silently rewritten to 5m.
B) Track 'All' in component state separately from URL — keep timeRange='All' in useTimeRange even when URL has no last=, and skip the inject-default-range action when timeRange==='All'. Less clean but no backend change.

Acceptance:
- Clicking 'All' in TimeRangePicker stays on 'All' and runs an unbounded search (or whatever the explicit semantic is).
- The default-range injection still fires for genuinely empty/initial queries (URL with no q at all).
- Test: a unit test on resolveQueryEffectAction or useSearchView that asserts 'All' selection does NOT trigger inject-default-range.
- Hand-typed queries without any time directive should behave consistently with the chosen design (currently they silently get last=5m grafted on — surface this in the design call).

Reproduction: open Search view, click any preset, then click 'All' — observe the highlight briefly hits 'All' then the URL/active preset snap to '5m'.
